articles.title: North Korea fires intermediate-range missile, claiming evasive flight and AI features
articles.body:
Japan’s military said the missile landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone, while South Korea's military, which often accuses the North of exaggerating its capabilities, said it travelled more than 700 kilometres.
North Korea announced Saturday that it had test-fired an intermediate-range ballistic missile, claiming the weapon can manoeuvre in flight to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan.
The launch comes as tensions between the two Koreas run high over landmine explosions along their border.
Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said her brother oversaw the test. She called the missile "strategic", a term that suggests it is meant to carry nuclear warheads. She also claimed it can alter its trajectory at low altitudes and has unspecified artificial intelligence capabilities, which she said would make it extremely hard to intercept.
Japan’s military said the missile landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone, while the South Korean military, which often accuses North Korea of exaggerating its military capabilities, said the missile travelled more than 700 kilometres.
North Korea claims new missile capabilities
According to South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff, the North Korean missile was fired early Saturday from the eastern coastal Wonsan area. Japan's Defense Ministry later put the distance at roughly 680 kilometres.
In her statement, Kim Yo Jong pointed to the gap between the two US allies' figures as proof that they could not follow the missile in flight.
"Whenever we applied the wavelike trajectory mode to missiles, the enemy failed to track the targets from their first skip points," she said. "There is no way to avoid this attack."
The launch followed a day after she mocked Seoul's demand that Pyongyang apologise for the 21 September landmine explosions. The blasts went off about 10 metres south of the military demarcation line and wounded three South Korean soldiers.
A joint inspection by South Korea and the US-led United Nations Command concluded that North Korea had planted the mines, and the command later found that Pyongyang had breached the armistice that halted the 1950-53 Korean War.
Seoul has also asked the North to stop fortifying the border with mines and anti-tank barriers. That work has sped up since Kim Jong Un dropped the goal of reconciliation in 2024 and branded Seoul a permanent adversary.
Kim Yo Jong, who may be the second most powerful person in Pyongyang, called Seoul's demands "utterly pathetic" on Friday and rejected any North Korean responsibility for the blasts, warning of retaliation if the South fires on troops working along the border.
Pyongyang's weapons tests are piling up
The Wonsan launch is the newest in a string of recent military displays, which also include missile tests, live-fire drills and the commissioning of a new warship. Kim Jong Un is showing off his expanding nuclear programme even as Washington urges a return to diplomacy.
Wonsan also hosted the Sept. 20 test of what state media described as a hypersonic missile system. It belongs to a family of weapons built to overwhelm missile defences in South Korea and Japan, including solid-fuel intermediate-range missiles first revealed in 2024.
South Korea's military said it had raised its surveillance level for further launches and was sharing information closely with Washington and Tokyo. The US Pacific Command said the launch "does not pose an immediate threat to American personnel or territory or to our allies."
Kim has mostly turned his back on diplomacy with the US and South Korea since his nuclear talks with President Donald Trump broke down in 2019. He has shifted his focus to Moscow, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons to back Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine. After years of heavier testing, his arsenal of nuclear-capable missiles now includes long-range systems that could potentially reach the U.S. mainland and shorter-range ones that threaten South Korea and Japan.
In August, Trump scaled back a large joint exercise with South Korea, apparently hoping to restart talks.
North Korea has brushed off the overture, insisting that Washington first end its "hostile policy", a phrase Pyongyang uses to describe US-led sanctions and joint military drills with South Korea.

articles.title: Germany’s Merz visits Kyiv amid fears of ‘hardest’ winter in war
articles.body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks to the press after meeting soldiers of the 1 German-Netherlands Corps on October 1, 2026 in Münster. | Hesham Elsherif/Getty Images
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv for a surprise one-day visit to showcase Berlin's support for Ukraine amid Russian attacks on the Ukrainian capital that continued after the chancellor's arrival.
Merz, who is in Kyiv to deliver new military, financial and economic support pledges to Ukraine, is planning to meet President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to discuss support against Russia's escalating war, particularly in the sector of air defense and long-range offensive weapons, as well as peace initiatives.
A German official said that Berlin will provide Ukraine with a new military support package worth about €1 billion, which includes missiles and drones, as well as satellite technology to help striking military targets in Russia.
Advertisement
Germany will furthermore provide Ukraine with financial assistance for the mass-production of new drones to intercept Russia's particularly dangerous high-speed jet drones. Berlin will also provide generators, substations, and repair kits worth €350 million to make the Ukrainian grid more resilient against Russian attacks.
Ukraine is facing harsh Russian drone and missile attacks on its infrastructure, power and heating plants as well as other civilian targets, which are feared to further intensify this winter.
In contrast to previous visits from Western leaders, during which Moscow had largely refrained from attacks on the Ukrainian capital, air raid sirens could be heard in Kyiv during Merz's visit. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that Russia had struck the roadway of the North Bridge in the city. On Saturday, Russia's foreign ministry issued a warning against foreign visitors and diplomats and urged them to leave Kyiv.
This is Merz's first bilateral visit to Kyiv and his second trip as chancellor, after travelling there in May 2025 visit alongside leaders from France, the U.K. and Poland.
“If we fail to stop Moscow, sooner or later the Russian war machine will turn against us", Merz said upon arrival in the Ukrainian capital, adding: “I will tell President Zelenskyy today, 'You can continue to count on our help.'”
During a speech in Münster, Germany, Merz warned that, “in a few weeks, the fifth winter of the war will begin”, which “likely be the hardest one yet.”
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz shakes hands with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the 36th NATO Heads of State and Government Summit in Ankara, on July 7, 2026. | Pool photo by Michael Kappeler/AFP via Getty Images
Ukrainians “are bracing themselves for intense ballistic missile attacks, for destroyed power plants and schools, and for damaged apartment buildings and churches. Ukraine must survive this winter, and I am convinced that it will. It can count on our help,” Merz added, highlighting German help such as new interception systems against jet drones or repairs for bombed power plants.
Merz and Zelenskyy held a call on Wednesday, which focused on convincing European and international allies like Japan to deliver more Patriot air defense missiles to Ukraine as well as procuring fresh ammunition for Kyiv's F-16 fighter jets, which are efficient in downing Russian jet drones with their onboard cannon.
Last month, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced that Germany would transfer Patriot PAC-2 interceptor missiles from its own stocks to Ukraine, and called on other states to follow suit.
Following the attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane in Leipzig in August, for which Germany blamed Russia, Berlin announced that its intelligence services would help Ukraine with supplying targeting data for long-distance strikes against Russia's military as well as its industrial base.
Advertisement
Merz has refused to supply Germany's prized Taurus cruise missiles to Ukraine, despite calling for it when he was opposition leader. Yet his government delivered financial and technical assistance for the development of Ukraine's own long-range weapons. On Thursday, Zelenskyy announced the successful test of Ukraine's FP-7 ballistic tactical missile.
German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, from Merz's center-right CDU party, joined the trip alongside representatives from a dozen German energy, chemical and drone manufacturing companies, which will participate in a German-Ukrainian economic forum in Kyiv on Sunday.
There are tensions between Merz and Zelenskyy when it comes to Ukraine's desire to swiftly join the European Union.
The German Chancellor has voiced skepticism that an EU accession would be possible in the coming years and instead proposed an “associated membership” that would grant Ukraine access to the EU's single market and an observer status in the Council of the EU, the European Commission and the European Parliament, but without any voting rights.
Merz's visit comes amid renewed attempts to seek a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, who met with his Russia counterpart Sergei Lavrov in New York last weekend, has welcomed a U.S. invite for Vladimir Putin to the G20 leaders' summit in Miami in December, saying it could be a chance for serious negotiations.
However, so far “Russia’s leadership shows no real interest in putting an end to its deeply inhumane fantasies of subjugation and conquest,” Wadephul said on Friday. “It intends to continue the war against Ukraine.”

articles.title: Ukraine Will Hit Russian Refineries in Response to Moscow's ‘New Doctrine’ of Airstrikes
articles.body:
Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of airstrikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities, but will not target civilians, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Ukrainian intelligence has obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a “new doctrine” of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of winter, Zelensky said.
“We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities,” Zelensky said. “This is the goal of the operation.”
Driving the shift in policy, Zelensky said, was Putin's desire to appear strong at a time when his military was losing ground in a key frontline region and sustaining higher levels of casualties.
The Kremlin was not available to comment on Saturday. But in a statement urging foreign nationals to leave Kyiv, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Counteroffensive in Donbas
Zelensky said an ongoing Ukrainian counteroffensive, code-named “Vivaldi,” had recaptured around 140 sq km (54 sq miles) of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, which Russia has said it must control in its entirety as a condition for any peace deal.
In recent weeks, U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has sought to revive talks to end the four-year-old conflict — Europe's bloodiest since World War Two.
The U.S. leader last month urged Ukraine to refrain from hitting Russian oil installations, saying that was sending global diesel prices surging.
But Zelensky, speaking as air raid sirens blared outside the gilded halls of the presidential offices, said he had received no indications from Russia that Putin was interested in peace talks or discussing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
Over the past week, the Ukrainian capital has come under persistent attack by Russian drones and missiles targeting energy and telecoms assets, road and rail infrastructure. For the first time, Russia has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro River connecting east and west Kyiv.
Zelensky said Ukraine would respond to the change in tactics by Moscow, but would not respond in kind by targeting civilian infrastructure indiscriminately.
“We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners: what gives money to them for this war,” Zelensky said in English. “But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects.”
Support from Europe
After the Trump administration invited Putin to attend a G20 summit in Miami in December and discussed business deals with Russian envoys, Zelensky urged Washington not to normalise relations with Russia before ensuring a return to peace.
Zelensky said he would be happy to meet Putin for peace talks at the G20, but he warned the U.S. not to believe in “illusions” that Russia would end hostilities if it gained control of Donbas.
“It's not fair just to normalize,” said Zelensky, dressed in his trademark black T-shirt and military-style jacket. Any resumption of economic and diplomatic ties with the West had to be in return for peace, he said: “Because peace is more important than any kind of economy.”
While the U.S. has proposed resuming trilateral talks in the coming weeks in the UAE, Zelensky noted that an exact date and location for the technical-level conversations had not been set.
Ukrainian officials warn that Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles ahead of an expected winter onslaught against electricity and water infrastructure. Last winter, the worst of the war, Russian strikes left swathes of the country without electricity and heating for days at a time.
Since the summer, Moscow has also begun launching dozens of fast and relatively cheap jet-powered Shahed drones a day at Ukraine, whose air defenses have struggled as its previous generation of interceptor drones are too slow to catch them.
Zelensky said Ukraine had been forced to rely heavily on its fighter aircraft — F-16s and MiGs — to down around 60% of the Russian jet-powered drones, but supplies of 20 mm ammunition for the planes were running low.
Kyiv was urgently working on other solutions — including boosting its jamming capabilities, he said. In the second half of October, it should receive its first shipment of small, cheap air defense missiles capable of hitting the new Shaheds.
Last week, Zelensky said Ukraine was developing five models of new interceptor drones capable of downing the jet Shaheds. Fresh from a meeting with his defense chiefs, he said tests on two of those models showed a modest success rate of around 30%.
“We'll have to scale it,” he said. “I hope that with all these things, with all these elements, we'll find a way.”
Ballistic threat
Ukraine announced the first combat use this week of its own domestically made ballistic missile — the FP-7, which has a range of around 250 km (155 miles).
Zelensky said he had called the manufacturer Fire Point to pressure executives to quickly finish a longer-range model, the FP-9, which the company has said could hit Moscow.
“I said to them, ‘Where is my FP-9?’” said Zelensky, with a grin. “We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be (ready) this autumn, I'm sure.”
Zelensky said a recent spate of Russian drone incursions and hybrid attacks in Europe were an effort to intimidate European populations and to divide support for Ukraine.
Some European leaders were starting to understand this, he said, and toughen their position.
Russia says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
After talks with European officials in Brussels this week, Ukraine found funding to proceed with orders for drones that it needs to keep fighting at the start of 2027, Zelensky said.
Ukrainian officials had worked on a plan with European partners to plug a $27 billion hole in Kyiv's defense budget this year.
The plans involve a combination of the reallocation of Ukraine's own budget resources, bilateral assistance, and using “money credits” from next year's portion of a €90 billion EU loan, Zelensky said.
A Message from The Moscow Times:
Dear readers,
We are facing unprecedented challenges. Russia's Prosecutor General's Office has designated The Moscow Times as an "undesirable" organization, criminalizing our work and putting our staff at risk of prosecution. This follows our earlier unjust labeling as a "foreign agent."
These actions are direct attempts to silence independent journalism in Russia. The authorities claim our work "discredits the decisions of the Russian leadership." We see things differently: we strive to provide accurate, unbiased reporting on Russia.
We, the journalists of The Moscow Times, refuse to be silenced. But to continue our work, we need your help.
Your support, no matter how small, makes a world of difference. If you can, please support us monthly starting from just $2. It's quick to set up, and every contribution makes a significant impact.
By supporting The Moscow Times, you're defending open, independent journalism in the face of repression. Thank you for standing with us.
Remind me later.

articles.title: Valtersson exposes NATO military exhaustion, Russian air superiority, US strategic defeat  in Iran
articles.body:
Valtersson exposes NATO military exhaustion, Russian air superiority, US strategic defeat in Iran
TEHRAN — In the latest joint X Space broadcast co-hosted by the Tehran Times and Sputnik, military analyst Mikael Valtersson—a former officer of the Swedish Armed Forces specializing in air defense, former defense politician, and chief of staff with the Sweden Democrats—provided an incisive assessment of shifting global strategic realities.
Valtersson detailed Russia's undeniable air superiority in Ukraine, the severe depletion of European military stockpiles, and the profound economic and strategic defeat suffered by the United States in its military confrontation with Iran. Highlighting the collapse of Western security narratives, Valtersson underscored how Washington's reckless interventions have eroded American soft power, exposed NATO's structural vulnerabilities, and accelerated the long-term contraction of the U.S. military footprint across the Middle East.
Sputnik Question: Following the quiet abandonment of Ukraine's publicized 40-day drone campaign, how have the air war dynamics shifted between Russia and Ukraine—particularly given reports that Russian reconnaissance and jet-powered drones are flying virtually unopposed over Kyiv to film strike impacts in high quality, while sustained strikes target Odesa's port infrastructure?
The Ukrainian 40-day drone campaign was a classic PR stunt designed for Western public consumption. Once it failed to paralyze Russia's economy or force political concessions, Kyiv simply ceased mentioning it altogether. Western media coverage remains egregiously biased, seizing on isolated incidents to accuse Russia of targeting civilians while ignoring major Russian operational successes. In reality, civilian casualty rates in Ukraine remain remarkably low compared to military losses—a standard of restraint that should be commended in modern warfare.
Russian air superiority across the theater is absolute and manifest. Ukraine possesses a critical deficit of high-end air defense assets, such as Patriot missile batteries, which are rationed sparingly to protect select high-value sites in Kyiv. Furthermore, Ukraine lacks the medium-level air defense systems necessary to counter Russia's newer jet-powered drones, leading to at least a tripling of successful drone penetrations. The sight of Russian reconnaissance drones loitering over Kyiv to capture high-resolution strike footage highlights this total air defense breakdown.
Beyond the capital, key maritime hubs like Odesa demonstrate the extent of Ukrainian vulnerability. Russia's daily, sustained strike campaign against Ukrainian shipping and harbor infrastructure in Odesa has proceeded virtually unopposed for three months, devastating Ukraine's grain export capacity and striking a fatal blow to its national economy.
Tehran Times Question: U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed that the war in Iran could be concluded within two weeks. Given Iran's capture of a second U.S. unmanned submarine in the Strait of Hormuz and the heavy expenditure of U.S. air defense interceptors during Iranian strikes on Jordan's Muwaffaq Salti air base, what is the reality of Washington's military posture and strategic standing?
The claim that the war with Iran will end in two weeks is completely detached from military reality. Such a timeframe would require the United States to offer Iran an extraordinarily favorable deal, as Tehran holds the superior strategic position and will not accept a bad peace arrangement.
Trump faces mounting domestic political pressure over soaring fuel prices and impending midterm election losses, leaving Washington with minimal leverage. Trump's bombastic statements—claiming Iran is "totally destroyed" and declaring the "greatest victory in world history"—indicate that he is either becoming demented or simply lying, as his assertions directly contradict operational facts on the ground.
Tactically and technologically, a strategic deadlock has set in that favors Tehran. Iran's capture of a second U.S. unmanned submarine in the Strait of Hormuz represents a major intelligence harvest, providing Iranian engineers direct access to advanced American technology. Operationally, the limits of American air defense were laid bare during the Iranian attack on Jordan's Muwaffaq Salti air base. U.S. forces expended an immense volume of interceptors—firing approximately 70 Patriot missiles and over 12 THAAD interceptors—yet Iranian missiles still penetrated the defense grid, destroying or damaging around 10 aircraft. Washington cannot sustain this rate of interceptor expenditure without compromising its global force posture. Ultimately, this war represents a catastrophic strategic defeat for U.S. influence, missile reserves, and global soft power, while significantly elevating the strategic standing of both Iran and China.
Sputnik Question: What realistic military options remain for European nations seeking to sustain Ukraine, given the severe exhaustion of Western weapon stockpiles, unsustainable Ukrainian casualty figures, a dark winter outlook, and rising political volatility within Europe?
European nations have virtually no viable military options left to alter the war's trajectory. European defense inventories are thoroughly drained, and because the United States must prioritize replenishing its own critically depleted stockpiles, Europe cannot expect American rearmament assistance for years. At best, European aid can temporarily delay a complete Ukrainian military collapse, but it cannot support effective offensive operations.
The human toll on Ukraine is mathematically unsustainable. Citing data acknowledged by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk from Ukrainian military sources, Ukraine is losing roughly 28,000 soldiers per month to deaths and severe injuries—totaling approximately 325,000 casualties per year. In the territory currently controlled by Kyiv, the population is probably below 20 million, with two million men actively dodging military service. Ukraine is exhausting its human reserves far faster than it can draft replacement personnel, pointing toward a dark and difficult winter as Russian forces methodically strike critical logistics and energy infrastructure. While reckless political rhetoric from European elites carries risks of unintended escalation reminiscent of 1914, shifting domestic political dynamics—such as the growth of AfD and BSW in Germany and the National Rally in France—will likely force a significant reduction in European military backing for Kyiv in the years ahead.
Tehran Times Question: How are Washington's claims of maintaining complete control over the Strait of Hormuz received by the European public, and how is energy inflation shaping European attitudes toward U.S. foreign policy?
Mikael Valtersson Answer: Official assertions by the U.S. administration that it controls the Strait of Hormuz and that commercial shipping has returned to normal are treated as a complete joke by the European public. If an election for U.S. president were held in Europe today, Donald Trump would receive perhaps 5 to 10 percent of the vote, reflecting deep public cynicism toward official Washington narratives. Unlike the heavily slanted coverage of Ukraine, European media reporting on the Middle East has been noticeably more neutral, allowing citizens to see through American propaganda.
Furthermore, Western public perception of Iran has shifted noticeably. Prior to the war, European discourse focused almost exclusively on human rights allegations; today, public debate centers on Iranian resilience and the realization that Washington's military aggression was a grave error. The public increasingly views the conflict as a blunder driven not by American or European security interests, but by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's desperate attempt to avoid domestic prosecution and prison. Economically, European citizens are suffering under severe energy inflation. Having cut off cheap Russian energy due to sanctions, Europe exposed itself to global market shocks resulting from Middle Eastern volatility. While European governments temporarily buffered price spikes through domestic tax cuts on fuel, long-term economic damage remains inevitable, fueling public resentment against both Washington and European political elites.
Sputnik Question: How valid are Western accusations regarding Russian hybrid threats, and under international law, what legal rights does Russia possess to target European supply lines directly sustaining Ukraine's war effort?
Accusations regarding hybrid warfare merely highlight Europe's profound internal security vulnerabilities. European governments lack the security infrastructure and manpower needed to guard their vast industrial and economic assets, leaving localized vulnerabilities exposed to disruption.
 
Under established international law, European states have long since crossed the threshold into active co-belligerency. European governments do not merely offer passive sympathy; they provide direct budgetary support, heavy combat systems, operational training, intelligence, and equipment repair services. European direct budget support is the absolute operational backbone of the Ukrainian state; if Western economic budget support were withdrawn, the Ukrainian economy would collapse within three to six months, completely destroying its capability to maintain a defense. Drawing a historical parallel to U.S. material support for the British Empire prior to World War II and Germany's subsequent declaration of war, Russia possesses full legal justification under international law to target European logistical vectors and military infrastructure sustaining the enemy war effort.
Tehran Times Question: What does the permanent withdrawal of U.S. military forces from Iraq signal regarding the durability and strategic utility of American military bases across the Middle East?
The permanent withdrawal of U.S. forces from Iraq signals a structural decline in the American regional presence. Far from acting as strategic assets or instruments of deterrence, U.S. facilities across the Middle East have transformed into acute strategic liabilities and prime targets for regional defense forces.
For regional host nations, housing American facilities has backfired spectacularly. Rather than securing U.S. protection, regional host states have found their local infrastructure exposed to collateral damage and military strikes during broader regional escalations. Crucially, regional leaders feel deep resentment toward Washington's unilateral behavior; Gulf state politicians have openly complained that they were not even consulted or informed prior to U.S. strikes, learning through media reports that American forces had launched attacks from or near their sovereign territory without their knowledge. As regional allies realize that hosting American bases yields zero security benefits while incurring enormous security costs, they will increasingly demand the removal of U.S. troops, permanently diminishing Washington's military footprint in the region.

articles.title: Latvian Defense Minister: Russia's hybrid attacks, not nuclear rhetoric, main concern
articles.body:
Latvia’s defense minister has played down any immediate danger after Russia’s latest nuclear warning to NATO over Kaliningrad.
“I don’t see an imminent threat at this point,” Raivis Melnis told RFE/RL in an interview in Washington on September 30, echoing NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, who said he did not take the Russian warning "that seriously".
Russia warned NATO this week that it was prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the Western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad, its heavily militarised Baltic exclave wedged between NATO members Poland and Lithuania.
In a diplomatic memo circulated to NATO member states, Moscow said it had information that the alliance was preparing an “air and naval blockade” of the territory.
The warning prompted Rutte to call on Russia to “stop the nuclear threats”, saying NATO is a defensive alliance and that “this is absolutely not called for and not helpful”. He added that Russian President Vladimir Putin knows that he cannot win in a direct confrontation with NATO.
Melnis said Russia had repeatedly resorted to nuclear threats since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, arguing that Moscow uses such rhetoric to frighten Western populations, weaken support for Kyiv, and test the cohesion of the NATO alliance.
“Russia will use any means to threaten us, to bring fear to our people, to support Ukraine, and also to break our unity, cohesion, to support and just test where are those limits,” he said.
Escalation risks?
The Russian warning has nevertheless raised concern among arms-control and security specialists, particularly because of Kaliningrad’s strategic position and Russia’s evolving nuclear doctrine.
Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, a nonpartisan Washington based nonprofit, told RFE/RL that the Russian threat should be taken seriously and condemned as unacceptable. He said Moscow’s language reflected what he described as a careless approach to the dangers of nuclear weapons use.
Kimball noted that NATO does not appear to be preparing military action to isolate Kaliningrad. Even if such a confrontation were contemplated, he said, using nuclear weapons in a conflict involving another nuclear-armed state or alliance could trigger retaliation, escalation, and potentially catastrophic consequences.
He argued that Moscow should instead address its concerns with NATO through diplomatic channels, saying that “rather than threatening nuclear attack, the Kremlin should reach out to NATO capitals to clarify whatever concerns Russia might have and to address those concerns diplomatically and responsibly.”
Lynn Rusten, a senior fellow at the Centre for European Policy Analysis and a former senior White House National Security Council official responsible for arms control and nonproliferation, told RFE/RL that Russia’s latest nuclear rhetoric appeared “unhinged and hyperbolic” from a Western perspective.
But Rusten also warned of a dangerous combination of factors: Russian threats and provocative hybrid warfare, NATO and Russian forces operating in close proximity, continued Western support for Ukraine, and a lack of meaningful dialogue.
She said those conditions could increase the risk of dangerous miscalculation, particularly as Russia and NATO assert competing red lines while channels for managing tensions remain limited.
“The lack of meaningful dialogue and the growing divide in security perceptions carries a grave risk of further and potentially unintended escalation and expansion of this conflict,” Rusten said.
Sylvia Mishra, nuclear policy director at the Institute for Security and Technology, said nuclear brinkmanship was not new for Moscow but should nonetheless be treated seriously.
Kaliningrad, she noted, is home to the headquarters of Russia’s Baltic Fleet and is strategically important but geographically vulnerable, surrounded by NATO members Poland and Lithuania and separated from mainland Russia.
Mishra said reported NATO air operations around the exclave in mid-August, which included aircraft with capabilities to disrupt communications, radar, and navigation systems, could have heightened Moscow’s sense of vulnerability.
She also pointed to Russia’s 2024 revised nuclear doctrine, which formally lowered the threshold described by Moscow for potential nuclear use.
Mishra said the latest warning appeared to be the first instance of Russia issuing a written diplomatic note explicitly warning that it was prepared to use nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad.
Hybrid attacks
For Melnis, however, the more immediate threat is neither nuclear nor a large-scale Russian conventional military assault on NATO, but an expanding campaign of hybrid activity – hostile actions short of open warfare, including cyberattacks, sabotage, and the weaponisation of migration.
He said Latvia and its allies are continuously reassessing the threat, monitoring Russia’s military capabilities, losses in Ukraine, force generation, and activities such as suspected attacks on military-industrial facilities and critical infrastructure.
“We are monitoring and we are working closely with Ukrainian partners or with our NATO partners,” Melnis said, adding that Latvia’s threat assessment is a continuous process and that hybrid activity is increasing.
Melnis said he did not believe Russia currently had the capacity to launch a conventional offensive against a NATO country while sustaining its war in Ukraine.
“Russia stopped in Ukraine, they are not achieving the goals,” he said, pointing to Ukrainian counteroffensive operations and arguing that Moscow would face major difficulties trying to conduct two large-scale military operations simultaneously.
He described cyberattacks, pressure through migration from Belarus – which Minsk has been accused of facilitating to destabilise its neighbours – and other hostile activities as part of the new security environment confronting Latvia and its allies.
Latvia is also strengthening defences against drones. Melnis said the country had deployed interceptor systems and additional radar along its borders with Russia and Belarus, drawing heavily on lessons from Ukraine. NATO fighter aircraft provide another layer, while Latvia is procuring medium- and short-range air defence systems.
Melnis said Russian drone incursions could become a growing feature of the Baltic security environment, citing recent incidents involving Lithuania, Poland, and Romania. Latvia, he said, is preparing for more such incidents.
US role in European defence
Melnis was in Washington to deepen defence cooperation with the US, including discussions involving the Michigan National Guard, procurement programmes, and capability development.
He said he remains confident that the US will maintain a military presence in Europe despite adjustments to deployments in individual countries. US forces, he said, remain in Latvia, and Washington continues to recognise the strategic importance of the region.
At the same time, Melnis said European allies must assume a greater share of the burden for their own defence. He credited US President Donald Trump with pushing NATO members to increase defence spending, saying Latvia is committed by law to spending at least 5 percent of gross domestic product annually on security beginning next year.
NATO members agreed at their 2025 summit in The Hague to spend 5 percent of GDP annually on defence and defence-related priorities by 2035, up from the alliance’s previous 2-percent benchmark. Latvia has moved faster, with its parliament requiring national defence spending of at least 5 percent of projected GDP from 2027.
But Melnis said greater European responsibility would go hand in hand with continued US support.
“The United States will provide. They will be there. They will fight with us if needed,” Melnis said, while stressing that Europe must do more.
This story was originally published by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), partners of LRT English.

articles.title: Ukraine will hit Russian refineries in response to Moscow’s ‘new doctrine’ of airstrikes
articles.body:
Ukraine will hit Russian refineries in response to Moscow’s ‘new doctrine’ of air strikes
- Ukraine will intensify attacks on Russian oil refineries in response to Moscow’s new doctrine targeting civilian infrastructure to force evacuations, but will avoid hitting civilian objects.
- Ukrainian forces have recaptured around 140 sq km in Donbas amid ongoing counteroffensive, while facing persistent Russian drone and missile strikes on Kyiv’s energy and infrastructure.
- Ukraine develops new defence systems against Russian drones, announces first use of domestic ballistic missile FP-7, and secures funding with European partners to sustain defence through 2027.
AI generated
KYIV – Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of air strikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities, but will not target civilians, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Ukrainian intelligence has obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a “new doctrine” of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of this winter, Zelensky said.
“We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure... logistics... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities,” he said. “This is the goal of the operation.”
Driving the shift in policy, Zelensky said, was Putin’s desire to appear strong at a time when his military was losing ground in a key front-line region and sustaining higher levels of casualties.
The Kremlin was not available to comment on Oct 3. But in a statement urging foreign nationals to leave Kyiv, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Counteroffensive in Donbas
Zelensky said an ongoing Ukrainian counteroffensive, code-named “Vivaldi”, had recaptured around 140 sq km of Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, which Russia has said it must control in its entirety as a condition for any peace deal.
In recent weeks, President Donald Trump’s administration has sought to revive talks to end the four-year-old conflict – Europe’s bloodiest since World War II.
The US leader in September urged Ukraine to refrain from hitting Russian oil installations, saying that was sending global diesel prices surging.
But Zelensky, speaking as air raid sirens blared outside the gilded halls of the presidential offices, said he had received no indications from Russia that Putin was interested in peace talks, or discussing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
Over the past week, the Ukrainian capital has come under persistent attack by Russian drones and missiles targeting energy and telecoms assets, road and rail infrastructure.
For the first time, Russia has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro river connecting east and west Kyiv.
Zelensky said Ukraine would respond to the change in tactics by Moscow, but would not respond in kind by targeting civilian infrastructure indiscriminately.
“We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners: what gives money to them for this war,” Zelensky said in English. “But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects.”
Support from Europe
After the Trump administration invited Putin to attend a Group of 20 summit in Miami in December and discussed business deals with Russian envoys, Zelensky urged Washington not to normalise relations with Russia before ensuring a return to peace.
Zelensky said he would be happy to meet Putin for peace talks at the G-20, but he warned the US not to believe in “illusions” that Russia would end hostilities if it gained control of Donbas.
“It’s not fair just to normalise,” said Zelensky, dressed in his trademark black T-shirt and military-style jacket. Any resumption of economic and diplomatic ties with the West had to be in return for peace, he said. “Because peace is more important than any kind of economy.”
While the US has proposed a resumption of trilateral talks in the coming weeks in the UAE, Zelensky noted that an exact date and location for the technical-level conversations had not been set.
Ukrainian officials warn that Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles ahead of an expected winter onslaught against electricity and water infrastructure. Last winter, the worst of the war, Russian strikes left swathes of the country without electricity and heating for days at a time.
Since the summer, Moscow has also begun launching dozens of fast and relatively cheap jet-powered Shahed drones a day at Ukraine, whose air defences have struggled as its previous generation of interceptor drones were too slow to catch them.
Zelensky said Ukraine had been forced to rely heavily on its fighter aircraft – F-16s and MiGs – to down around 60% of the Russian jet-powered drones, but supplies of 20mm ammunition for the planes were running low.
Kyiv was urgently working on other solutions – including boosting its jamming capabilities, he said. In the second half of October, it would receive the first shipment of small, cheap air defence missiles capable of hitting the new Shaheds.
Last week, Zelensky said Ukraine was developing five models of new interceptor drones capable of downing the jet Shaheds. Fresh from a meeting with his defence chiefs, he said tests on two of those models showed a modest success rate of around 30%. “We’ll have to scale it,” he said. “I hope that with all these things, with all these elements, we’ll find a way.”
Ballistic threat
Ukraine announced the first combat use this week of its own domestically made ballistic missile – the FP-7, which has a range of around 250km.
Zelensky said he had called the manufacturer Fire Point to pressure executives to finish quickly a longer-range model, the FP-9, which the company has said could hit Moscow. “I said to them, where is my FP-9?” said Zelensky, with a grin. “We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be (ready) this autumn, I’m sure.”
Zelensky said a recent spate of Russian drone incursions and hybrid attacks in Europe were an effort to intimidate European populations and to divide support for Ukraine. Some European leaders were starting to understand this, he said, and toughen their position.
Russia says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
After talks with European officials in Brussels this week, Ukraine had found funding to proceed with orders for drones that it needs to keep fighting at the start of 2027, Zelensky said.
Ukrainian officials had worked on plans with European partners to plug a US$27 billion (S$34.5 billion) hole in Kyiv’s defence budget in 2026.
The plans involve a combination of the reallocation of Ukraine’s own budget resources, bilateral assistance and using “money credits” from 2027’s portion of a €90 billion (S$130 billion) EU loan, Zelensky said. REUTERS

articles.body:
Ukraine’s domestically developed FP-9 ballistic missile, designed to reach targets at distances including Moscow, will be operational this fall, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced in an interview with Reuters.
Zelensky stated that he contacted the leadership of Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point to urge the expedited finalization of the FP-9, following the combat debut earlier in the week of the shorter-range FP-7 tactical ballistic missile.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I told them: where is my FP-9? We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be [ready] this autumn, I am confident,” Zelensky said.
The president added that Ukraine plans to intensify precision strikes against Russian oil refineries to counter an expanded aerial campaign by Moscow aimed at forcing residents to evacuate Kyiv and other urban centers ahead of winter.
Citing intelligence documents, Zelensky said Russian President Vladimir Putin approved an operational directive expanding strikes against a wider array of civilian targets, including roads, transportation links, schools, and hospitals.
“We have seen the documents and we know that they permit attacks on infrastructure, logistics, roads, schools, hospitals to force people to leave the capital, to leave different cities. This is the goal of the operation,” Zelensky said, attributing the shift in Russian tactics to frontline pressures and personnel losses in the Donbas.
Russian Billionaires Fund 1% of State Budget in ‘Voluntary’ War Levy
Zelensky emphasized that while Ukraine will respond to Moscow’s attacks on its energy grid by targeting Russian energy infrastructure, Ukrainian forces will not conduct indiscriminate attacks on civilian sites.
“We must react in any possible way. To their attacks on our energy sector, we must respond with strikes against their energy sector. Above all – on oil refineries: that is what provides them money for this war. But we will certainly not, as they do, strike any civilian facilities,” Zelensky said.
Deep-strike operations and overnight engagements
Zelensky confirmed that Ukrainian forces carried out long-range strikes early Saturday morning, Oct. 3.
According to the president, the overnight strikes engaged Russian Iskander missile launcher positions and personnel in the Bryansk region alongside targets in the Samara region.
“Over the past 24 hours, our long-range capability worked effectively against facilities operating for the aggressor’s war machine,” Zelensky stated on social media, adding that Ukrainian operations also produced new results in the Black Sea, without disclosing operational specifics.
The confirmed strikes follow an ongoing campaign by Ukrainian defense forces targeting rear logistics, air surveillance networks, and missile batteries deployed in Russian border regions.
Fire Point development and the FREYJA initiative
The deployment timeline for the FP-9 follows Ukraine’s first operational combat use of the FP-7 tactical ballistic missile on Thursday, Oct. 1.
Manufactured by Fire Point, the baseline FP-7 carries a 150-kilogram warhead across an operational reach of approximately 200 to 250 kilometers.
Fire Point founder and chief designer Denys Shtilerman previously compared the platform to the US-manufactured Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS), noting that the sovereign weapon is produced at roughly half the acquisition cost with domestic manufacturing spanning rocket motors and flight guidance systems.
Fire Point officially announced the development of both the FP-7 and the longer-range FP-9 in September 2025, conducting initial flight trials of the FP-7 in February 2026.
Prior to its combat deployment, Fire Point Chief Executive Officer Iryna Terekh confirmed that the FP-7 had completed roughly 15 test launches and final Defense Ministry certifications.
The defense contractor also serves as the industrial hub for the European FREYJA initiative, launched in July alongside nine partner nations to build low-cost ballistic missile interceptors.
Under that program, Fire Point is developing the FP-7.X high-speed interceptor variant, aiming for unit production costs below €1 million ($1.2 million) to reduce reliance on scarce US-supplied Patriot batteries ahead of planned operational interception trials in 2027.

The education minister says 400- 500 high schools will remain partially or fully shut following a week where riot police clashed with high school students as protests on classroom conditions have spread nationwide.
Lessons will be “totally or partly suspended” given the unrest, says Education Minister Edouard Geffray.
He said 24 schools had been “burned or ransacked” since the start of the movement.
At least 5,000 people, mainly teenagers, have been arrested while dozens of people, including students and teachers, have been injured. Unions are calling on teachers to strike.
The protests began last week in the Paris region, with students staging sit-ins over conditions like overcrowding in classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated buildings.
The rallies in some cases have become more violent with protesters wearing masks and setting off fires in the street and vidoes showing police officers using batons on students.
More protests had been scheduled for Tuesday this week, prompting law enforcement this weekend to say the situation had grown “out of control”.
Paris police chief Patrice Faure told students to abandon their school blockades to return to peaceful forms of protest and suggested to parents there was influence from “professional rioters”.
78 teachers and school staff injured says French minister
Some more detail from France’s Education Minister Edouard Geffray’s comments earlier where he said 400-500 schools would continue to be closed on Monday, following on from Friday’s shut down.
There are roughly 3,700 high schools, or lycees, across the country.
Geffray said lessons were being suspended because the security situation was still not stable enough following outbursts of violence last week amid mass demonstrations.
He claimed activists had infiltrated the protests, “hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence”.
“Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students,” he said, noting that 78 education staff had been wounded – “something we have never seen before”.
“They were deliberately targeted because they were employees of the national education system,” Geffray alleged.
In the southern town of La Ciotat, police detained a 16-year-old on Sunday for the assault of a teacher who was doused in gasoline and attacked on the sidelines of a school protest on Friday.
Meanwhile, organisers have called for the protests to continue on Tuesday saying the government hasn’t properly addressed their concerns, raised just a few weeks into the new school year about overcrowded classes and absent teachers.
Students and some rights groups have condemned the heavy-handed tactics of police, accusing them of brutality in removing students from protests.
Incinerated novels and destroyed warehouses: Russia’s war on Ukrainian books
Charlotte Higgins
My colleague Charlotte Higgins has written today’s Sunday read on Russia’s war on Ukrainian books:
On a Saturday morning in August, Viktor Kruglov, the co-founder and chief executive of the publisher Ranok, was at his headquarters in Kharkiv – the eastern Ukrainian city that, along with Kyiv, is the centre of the country’s publishing and printing industry. Built 15 years ago on the site of a former bread factory, the footprint of the premises is about 10,000 sq metres (107,640ft). Books were stacked 12 metres high on rank after rank of shelves.
Kruglov, along with five senior colleagues, were on the warehouse floor to discuss the approaching school year. The warehouse was holding 628,000 new schoolbooks. “It was the high season of distribution,” he said, “so we were checking all our processes: how to do it more successfully, how to do it in time.”

Pjotr Sauer
Russia has struck another major bridge in Kyiv as the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, arrived in the capital in a show of support for Ukraine.
A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, marking the fourth consecutive day that Russia has targeted bridges used by thousands of residents commuting between the city’s two banks. The attack came shortly after Merz arrived in the city on an unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing of Ukraine as the country enters one of the most precarious periods since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Germany has become Ukraine’s biggest provider of military aid since Merz entered office in May 2025, surpassing the US as American support has declined.

In the Bosnian capital, Sarajevo, Ismar Garasljevic, a 51-year-old high school teacher tells Reuters:
“More than 30 years after the war, the situation is still the same; we are talking about nationalism ... The same faces, the same story, constantly.“
There is this feeling of more of the same in the bitter ethno-nationalist politics in Bosnia.
There are multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party but also the major ethnically-based political parties in the Bosniak SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH.
They have been the ones in government so far but their differences in central government have blocked progress on measures like transparency laws which are needed for Bosnia to gain EU membership. It secured candidate status in 2022 but has progressed little since then.
Reporter Guy de Launey in Sarajevo also has this report from Bosnia on why so many young people have left the country in the past decade:
One local organisation that tracks emigration estimated that more than 600,000 people had left the country in the decade after the 2013 census, when the official population was 3.5 million.
“If I weren’t optimistic, maybe I would also move out,” said Timur Vilić, a 28-year-old municipal councillor in Sarajevo, who is standing on Sunday for election to the cantonal government. He represents Our Party – a multi-ethnic, non-nationalist, liberal movement that he admits faces a struggle to appeal to voters in a country dominated by ethnonationalist parties.
The problem for Our Party – and other non-nationalist movements – is that the young people who make up their support base are voting with their feet, rather than making their mark on ballot papers.
In theory, Sunday’s vote should be one of the great European festivals of democracy, with the election of no fewer than 14 prime ministers and five presidents. But the plethora of posts on offer reflects a fiendishly complicated system of governance.
The Dayton agreement’s creation of two powerful regional “entities” – with a weaker central government – was intended as a stopgap to ensure peace after the ruinous conflict of the 1990s. Instead, it has perpetuated the divisions in the country. Most Serbs live in the Republika Srpska (RS), while the Federation is home to most of Bosnia’s Croats and Bosniak Muslims. There is no incentive for the ethnonationalist leaders to change that situation – or to appeal to young people who see a brighter future outside the country.
“They don’t want young people to be interested, and young people are not interested in politics,” said Sarah Ćato. The 19-year-old student of political science and international relations is eligible to vote on Sunday for the first time – but she says that her age group feels unseen by the political mainstream.
“Young people don’t know how to vote or who to vote for because nobody’s standing for us,” she said, adding that the reluctance to engage in politics reflects its status as a “taboo subject” after the end of the conflict in 1995. “I think educating youth from middle school on how to be a good citizen should be mandatory.”
In Bosnia, ethno-nationalist politics are at the fore of today’s elections.
Voters are casting ballots today for the country’s three-person multi-ethnic presidency, lawmakers in the national parliament as well as the heads of institutions of Bosnia’s two powerful regional “entities”.
It’s a complicated governance structure – set up in the 1995 peace agreement that ended the preceding three-year civil war.
While Bosnia is one of the poorest countries in Europe after that devasating war, it has remained peaceful.
Still its politics remain divided along ethnic lines between the country’s Bosniaks, who are mainly Muslims, and its Serbs and Croats.
The entities – which are stronger than the central government – was set up to maintain that peace but have largely perpetuated the divison. Most Serbs live in the Republika Srpska (RS), while the Muslim-majority Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina is home to most of Bosnia’s Croats and Bosniak Muslims.
And tensions are rising between the two. Bosnian Serb leaders have pushed for the separation of their entity from the rest of Bosnia, and populist party figures like Russia sympathiser Milorad Dodik, said at a final rally on Friday night that modern Bosnia “is dead” and “doesn’t make any sense”.

The National Academy of Science in Kyiv is just a few hundred meters from the German Embassy.
