Zelensky noted that the strikes on Kyiv had continued even amid the chancellor’s visit.
Pro-Ukraine and EU Latvian PM wins parliamentary vote
In Latvia, the small republic right on Nato’s eastern flank, Prime Minister Andris Kulberg’s centre-right party has won the most support in the country’s parliamentary election.
The vote on Saturday had been dominated by concerns over neighbouring Russia as well as cost-of-living and economic issues- and saw about 51% turnout.
Kulberg’s United List party – which won 42 of the 100 seats in parliament, an unprecedented result- will now go about forming a coalition to govern.
Kulberg became prime minister in May after a political crisis over the handling of stray drones suspected to have come from Ukraine, brought down the governing coalition that was in place.
Kulberg, then in opposition, then secured parliamentary approval to lead a new coalition.
He has vowed to push on with his pro-Ukraine and EU direction. Latvia, a small country with a 1.8 million population, which borders both Russia and Moscow-allied Belarus has always supported Ukraine against Russia’s invasion.
Germany is Ukraine’s largest donor and has sent Kyiv more than €43.3 billion ($48.8 billion) since the war began, along with equipment and weapons.
Zelenskyy thanked Merz for visiting the Ukrainian capital describing him as “A leader of a country that consistently demonstrates leadership in protecting the lives of Ukrainians from Russian strikes.
We are grateful for all the support, and today we are preparing decisions to give us in Ukraine, and all of Europe, greater capabilities to defend ourselves. There will be important agreements between Ukraine and Germany. Russia must be stopped together.”
At least one killed in strikes on Kyiv, Kharkiv, Sumy, Dnipro, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia
Zelenskyy in the past hour has been tweeting about the strikes and the German chancellor’s visit, thanking Merz for his support.
On the Kyiv strike this morning he confirmed it had been a drone on the Northern Bridge (Pivnichnyi Bridge).
He noted too a drone attack on a pharmaceutical warehouse in Sumy which killed one person and a strike on a communications facility in Dnipro.
“Overnight, the Russians launched 135 attack drones against Ukraine, more than 50 of them jet-powered. Kyiv, the Dnipro, Kharkiv, Donetsk, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia regions came under attack.
"And among the main targets of these terrorists, as always, are ordinary residential buildings, critical infrastructure – everything that makes up normal everyday life.
"This week alone, the Russians have used more than 1,900 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 25 missiles against Ukraine. More than 800 of the drones were jet-powered, and Russia must be held accountable for this escalation.”
Western diplomats say publicly that they intend to remain in Kyiv, mindful that leaving would hand Moscow a propaganda victory and risk creating the impression that Ukraine was being abandoned.
However, privately two senior diplomats said contingency plans were being drawn up to relocate embassies to Lviv or eastern Poland if Russia began deliberately targeting foreign missions.
“The situation is obviously deteriorating fast,” the diplomat said.
My colleague Pjotr Sauer, the Guardian’s Russian affairs reporter in Kyiv this week, has described the onslaught of around-the-clock attacks we’re seeing on the Ukrainian capital:
Kyiv is entering its most difficult period since the early days of the invasion, as intensifying Russian attacks reshape everyday life in a capital that Moscow is seeking to plunge into darkness.
For weeks, the main worry in the capital had been the coming winter, when Russia is expected once again to try to plunge Ukraine into darkness and cold. But a sharp escalation in Russian attacks has left many residents feeling that some of the hardship they had been bracing for is already here.
“The capital is in a very dramatic situation. And it’s no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we do in peacetime,” the Kyiv mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said on Friday. “The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart.”
This week alone, Russian missiles and drones have struck offices, datacentres, a school and hospital and one of Kyiv’s main bridges. Moscow has also started its attacks on Ukraine’s energy, targeting a thermal power plant and other energy facilities, leaving several neighbourhoods without power and water by morning.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy underlined the apparent shift in Russian tactics in an interview with the Financial Times this week, saying Vladimir Putin had recently ordered his commanders to abandon the rules of war.
“They want Ukrainians to leave the capital … and show that if you don’t have the capital you don’t have the country,” Zelenskyy said in separate comments to reporters.
Until recently, Kyiv had retained a deceptively normal rhythm, while cities closer to the front, including Kharkiv and Dnipro, absorbed the brunt of daily missile and drone attacks. Now, residents joke grimly that the balance is beginning to shift, with those cities at times feeling safer than the capital.
The city is confronting a particularly dangerous combination of an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors for ballistic missiles and a new generation of faster, jet-powered Russian drones that are harder to shoot down.
Kyiv is racing to fast-track a new generation of interceptor drones capable of taking down the jet-powered models. Several are already in use, according to three defence industry sources, though they said it could still take weeks or months to deploy them at a scale sufficient to provide meaningful protection for the capital.
Merz tours science academy targeted in Monday daytime strike
Some more pictures through as the visit unfolds – the leaders have also toured the site of the National Academy of Science which was struck in a daytime attack just on Monday. Two people were killed.
The 19th-century building, in the heart of Kyiv, stands close to the German embassy, the National Opera, St Volodymyr’s Cathedral and several government buildings.
You can see Merz and his delegation assessing the damage and detritus outside the building.
Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, who greeted Merz at the station this morning, had this week accused Russia of cynicism for targeting a scientific institution during the working day.
“Russia is deliberately expanding the boundaries of what it believes the world will tolerate. Every attack left without a strong response only encourages the next one,” he said.
On Saturday, Russia’s foreign ministry had issued the message saying it was carrying out “mass retaliatory strikes” on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, urging foreign nationals and diplomats to leave the country. It last issued a similar warning in May.
The Russians have increasingly been using ballistic missiles on Ukrainian cities in recent months – which are near impossible to defend against without Patriot interceptor missles. The US continues to ignore Ukraine’s desperate please for new stocks.
Meanwhile Ukraine since the summer has also escalated its drone strike campaign targeting Russian oil refineries and energy sites as well as Wildberries warehouses– the Russian equivalent of Amazon – bringing the war home to consumers.
This is the German chancellor’s second visit to Ukraine during his 18 months in office so far.
Merz is facing significant domestic pressure back home with record-low ratings and major losses against his party in three recent regional elections.
But along with the leaders of France, the UK and Poland, with whom he last travelled to Ukraine in May 2025, he has been among the most staunch of Ukraine supporters and has pushed to increase aid as well as work on defence co-operation with Zelenskyy’s government.
He is expected to announce in his visit today the release of €1 billion in military aid and €350 million for repairs in Ukraine’s energy sector – the sites of which have been heavily targeted by Russian strikes and need to be restored going into winter.
He is also expected to finalise a deal for drone production between German and Ukrainian manufacturers. He’s been accompanied by several German CEOs including from Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defence, Quantum Systems and other firms as well as his Economic Affairs Minister Katherina Reiche.
In his X post this morning he’d repeated the pledge “You can count on us” adding: “Germany’s security also depends on the outcome of this war. That is why we are helping out of our own self-interest as well.”
Earlier this week, Zelenskyy had also said that Ukraine would close a deal soon on the joint production of drones, missiles and their software with Germany.
Merz has met Ukraine’s President Voldymyr Zelenskyy at the main war memorial on the Maidan in Kyiv.
Both men lay tributes at the central site, which features thousands of Ukrainian flags and framed portraits of the soldiers who’ve been killed in the war that’s gone on for more than four-and-a-half years.
Attack on Kyiv as Merz arrives shows upsurge in Russian attacks on capital
The North Bridge – one of several connecting central historic Kyiv to the residential suburbs across the Dnipro river -was struck not long after the German chancellor’s arrival in the Ukrainian capital.
The incident has been confirmed by Kyiv’s mayor Vitali Klitschko this morning who wrote on Telegram: “Impact on the road surface of the Northern Bridge. Emergency services are heading to the scene.”
There’s no word of casualties yet. Pictures and footage being shared online appears to show a missile slamming into the cable bridge and the resulting fireball explosion.
It follows strikes by the Russians on the South Bridge on Friday and Saturday, and several earlier this week that had shut three of the city’s six road bridges over the Dnipro.
Merz has arrived in the thick of it, as Kyiv, which was largely spared direct aerial strikes in the first years of the war has increasingly come under attack since April.
The Russians have launched strikes day and night, hitting schools, petrol strations, government buildings and churches as well as rails and communication infrastructure.
Good morning and welcome to our Europe live blog, I’m Frances Mao.
We begin in Kyiv where one of Ukraine’s strongest European backers, the German chancellor Friedrich Merz, has arrived this morning in an unannounced visit.
Soon after his arrival, the Russians struck the city’s North Bridge, just a 20-minutes drive from the central railway station where Merz had pulled into.
Sirens have rung out across the city and smoke can still be seen rising from the Dnieper River bridge. Yesterday, Russian drones also struck another bridge, causing injuries; the Kremlin has stepped up attacks on the capital this year and Ukrainians say they are steeling for another autumn blitz ahead of a tough winter.
Elsewhere across the continent today, Bosnians are voting in a national election likely to determine the course of their strained EU accension path so far.
And I’ll also bring you an update on the rent protests we saw across Spain’s largest cities yesterday.

articles.title: Russia strikes Kyiv bridges with drones as Putin escalates attacks on Ukraine
articles.body:
Russia continued its extensive assault on bridges in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv on Sunday, first-person view (FPV) drones on roads crossing the Dnipro River for a fourth straight day. The bridges connect the eastern and western parts of the city, and the attacks appear aimed at sowing panic among Ukrainians and disrupting supply routes while causing massive traffic jams. At least four air raid alerts sounded in Kyiv Sunday morning, and a Russian drone exploded on the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro as vehicles were crossing it. No injuries have been reported so far in that incident.
Russia began attacking Kyiv’s bridges on Thursday, saying it was seeking to sever supply routes to the Ukrainian military from central Ukraine to the east. On Thursday and Friday, it repeatedly attacked the city’s Southern Bridge with drones, forcing its closure and causing massive traffic jams across the Kyiv metropolitan area, home to about 3 million people.
The strikes were Russia’s first significant attacks on a major bridge in Kyiv since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. On Saturday, it also attacked the Northern Bridge, which it struck again Sunday. Ukraine has now been forced to partially or fully close three of the six bridges over the Dnipro that carry vehicle traffic, causing severe congestion across large parts of the city throughout the weekend.
Russia is attacking Kyiv’s bridges with domestically produced jet-powered drones, which it has increasingly deployed in recent weeks. The drones are fast and relatively inexpensive, and their speed makes them more difficult for Ukrainian air defense systems to intercept. Russia has used them to strike not only bridges but also residential buildings, supermarket warehouses, gas stations and server farms.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky acknowledged in an interview with Reuters on Saturday that his country is managing to intercept only about 60% of the drones and has been forced to rely heavily on its F-16 and MiG fighter jets, whose ammunition stocks are running low. He said Kyiv is urgently seeking other solutions, including upgrades to its electronic jamming capabilities. Ukraine is expected to receive its first shipment of small, inexpensive air defense missiles capable of striking the new drones in the second half of October.
Russia describes its broad assault on Ukraine in recent days as a campaign of retaliation. On Saturday, it urged diplomats and foreign nationals in Kyiv to leave the city ahead of further “mass retaliatory strikes,” which it said would target military sites in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities. Russia says it is seeking to make Ukraine pay for its repeated drone attacks in recent months against oil refineries and storage facilities deep inside Russia, strikes that caused a Russian fuel crisis over the summer, as well as attacks on warehouses belonging to Russian e-commerce giants Wildberries and Ozon, which caused significant disruptions for Russian consumers. The strikes on Russian refineries have also repeatedly drawn criticism from U.S. President Donald Trump, who argues that they are worsening the global diesel shortage.
Zelensky defies Trump: We will double attacks on oil refineries
Russia’s retaliatory attacks in recent weeks have included almost daily drone strikes. On Friday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko described the situation in the capital as “extremely dramatic,” saying Moscow was “destroying” the city by systematically targeting its infrastructure and logistics. Nevertheless, Zelensky said in his Reuters interview Saturday that the Ukrainian military would double its attacks on oil refineries in Russia.
Zelensky said Ukrainian intelligence services had obtained documents indicating that Russian President Vladimir Putin had formulated a “new doctrine” for military attacks against a far broader range of civilian targets ahead of the coming winter. According to Zelensky, the doctrine is intended to pressure Ukrainians to leave the capital and other cities. Zelensky attributed the shift to what he described as Putin’s battlefield setbacks, particularly in “Operation Vivaldi,” in which he said Ukraine recaptured about 140 square kilometers (54 square miles) of territory in the eastern Donbas region that had previously been seized by Russia.
Despite Russia’s call Saturday for diplomats to leave Kyiv, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the Ukrainian capital Sunday morning. Merz traveled to Kyiv by train and was greeted upon stepping off the train by Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. The chancellor said he had come to demonstrate his support for Ukraine because it “needs all our support in the coming weeks.” He warned: “If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will be turned against us.”
Merz, whose country is among Ukraine’s largest supporters in its war against Russia, arrived in Kyiv accompanied by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and senior business executives. He is expected to announce a new military aid package for Ukraine worth about 1 billion euros, specifically intended to help counter Russia’s jet-powered drones. He is also expected to pledge 350 million euros in assistance for Ukrainian infrastructure ahead of winter, a critical period in which Ukraine fears massive Russian attacks on its power plants, similar to those in 2025 that repeatedly left millions of people without electricity or heating in freezing temperatures.
Merz, who is deeply unpopular at home, arrives in Ukraine after stinging defeats in regional elections to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which advocates ending aid to Kyiv and normalizing relations with Moscow. Polls show that nationwide, the AfD is currently Germany’s most popular party.

articles.title: Japan’s island-defense glide missile seen at Camp Fuji
articles.body:
- New video shows Japan's Type 25 Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile launcher arriving, raising into firing position and withdrawing at Camp Fuji.
- Japan deployed the missile to Camp Fuji on March 31 and plans new units in Hokkaido and Kyushu during fiscal 2026.
New video from Camp Fuji shows Japan’s Type 25 Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile launcher driving onto a firing site, raising its missiles into launch position and packing up again, giving a rare look at how the country’s first domestically built long-range strike missile is operated.
The three-minute clip was posted on X by Japanese military photographer @yahou5, who described it as the full sequence from arrival through moving into firing posture to withdrawal. It shows a heavy 8×8 truck carrying two large missile canisters on its back. The post was tagged with Camp Fuji and the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force’s Fuji School, which runs the service’s artillery training.
Japan deployed the weapon to Camp Fuji in Shizuoka Prefecture on March 31, the same day the Defense Ministry gave it its official name. Developed as the Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile for island defense, it was redesignated the Type 25 HVGP, also known as 25HGP. The unit at Camp Fuji is the Field Artillery Training Unit, which is using the first systems to train crews and work out how the weapon will be used.
Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said at the time that the deployment, together with the Type 25 surface-to-ship missile sent to Camp Kengun in Kumamoto, was the first time domestically produced stand-off missiles had been delivered to Japanese military units. Stand-off weapons are meant to hit an enemy force from outside the range of its own weapons.
The HVGP works differently from a cruise missile. A rocket booster carries it to high altitude, where the warhead section separates and glides toward the target at very high speed, maneuvering on the way down. That combination of speed and an unpredictable flight path makes it harder to intercept than a conventional ballistic missile. Japanese outlet Jiji Press has described it as a type of hypersonic glide weapon, flying at more than five times the speed of sound.
The Defense Ministry says the current Block 1 version has a range of several hundred kilometers. Japanese media have reported figures of up to 900 km (560 miles). The ministry is developing longer-range versions, with a goal of 1,000 to 2,000 km, and a later Block 2 with a more advanced glide body is planned for the 2030s.
The launcher made its first public appearance at the Fuji Firepower Review, Japan’s largest annual live-fire demonstration, at the East Fuji Maneuver Area on June 7. There, it raised its two launch tubes upright to show its firing posture. No missile was fired.
Camp Fuji is only the first stop. The Defense Ministry plans to form new HVGP units at Camp Kamifurano in Hokkaido and Camp Ebino in Miyazaki Prefecture on Kyushu during fiscal 2026, which ends in March 2027.
The deployment has drawn attention from local officials. The ministry told the town of Oyama, home to Camp Fuji, that launch equipment would be stationed there, but it has declined to say whether warheads are kept at the base.

articles.title: Ukraine to Deploy Small Missiles, Turrets Against Jet Drones, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Ukraine will begin deploying domestically produced small missiles by late October to counter Russian jet-powered strike drones, alongside expanding networks of automated gun turrets around the capital region, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced during a joint press briefing with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on Sunday, Oct. 4.
According to Ukringrom, Zelensky confirmed that Ukrainian defense enterprises have developed several types of specialized, lower-cost interceptor missiles engineered to neutralize high-speed unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), with initial combat deployments anticipated during the second half of the month.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The small missile program – I will not state the name now, there are several types – we will evidently see results in the second half of this month. We expect to see results,” Zelensky said.
While the missiles are not yet in serial mass production, the president stated that manufacturing can be scaled up rapidly once operational performance is confirmed.
Zelensky noted that Ukrainian forces currently intercept roughly 50 to 60 percent of incoming turbojet Shahed drones, with combat aviation demonstrating the highest efficacy against high-velocity targets.
“Right now, high-quality interception of [jet UAVs] is about 50 percent, 55 percent, sometimes 60 percent – that is our aviation,” Zelensky said.
“F-16s are helping very significantly, and 20mm ammunition is working well.”
Germany Pledges €1.3B Defense Package During Merz Kyiv Visit
Automated defensive turrets in Kyiv
To reinforce ground-level interception networks, Zelensky announced that Ukrainian defense units have installed more than 12 automated counter-drone turrets across the capital, with plans to deploy eight additional systems in the surrounding Kyiv region.
The automated modules are configured to fire 50-caliber (12.7mm) ammunition to destroy incoming loitering munitions on terminal approach vectors. Zelensky explained that the installations form part of a layered, combined defense posture required to address Moscow’s evolving air assault doctrine.
“The Russians will now focus precisely on jet-powered drones and ballistics,” Zelensky observed. “Regarding mass strikes similar to what we are seeing now, I believe they will move toward quality rather than quantity, transitioning from conventional Shaheds to maximum utilization of jet variants.”
The technological adaptation arrives as Russian forces have increasingly paired high-speed loitering munitions with ballistic missile salvos to overwhelm mobile air defense fire teams and deplete inventories of high-end surface-to-air guided missiles.
Bilateral drone agreement
The technical announcements coincided with the formal conclusion of a bilateral agreement between Ukraine and Germany to deepen operational cooperation in counter-drone warfare, enabling German defense manufacturers to integrate Ukrainian combat lessons directly into joint production ventures.
Chancellor Merz emphasized that defense cooperation between Berlin and Kyiv functions as a reciprocal partnership, noting that German corporate representatives accompanying his delegation are studying Ukrainian battlefield adaptations while establishing joint high-tech industrial facilities.
Merz referenced a thwarted Russian-directed sabotage plot at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4 as a clear demonstration of why counter-drone technologies are critical for Germany’s own domestic security.
Addressing Russian rhetoric, Merz stated that public threats issued by the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs warning foreign diplomats of “mortal danger” in Kyiv did not influence his decision to visit the Ukrainian capital.
“Despite the threats that reached us from Moscow in recent days, I came today. Together with me came a colleague from the government, Federal Minister for Economic Affairs Katharina Reiche, a large delegation from my government, and a major economic delegation,” Merz said.
“This shows: we will not allow ourselves to be intimidated.”
The chancellor added that ongoing Russian drone attacks on the capital during his visit underscored Moscow’s conduct, reaffirming that Berlin’s solidarity remains steadfast on his second visit to Kyiv as head of government and fourth overall.
Diplomatic resilience
Merz’s presence in Kyiv follows public assurances from EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová, who confirmed that no EU member state embassy is preparing to evacuate the capital despite Moscow’s threats and infrastructure strikes.
Mathernová confirmed regular coordination with the diplomatic missions of 25 EU member states based in Kyiv, stating that both the EU Delegation and the EU Advisory Mission (EUAM) Ukraine remain fully operational.
The ambassador characterized Moscow’s escalatory statements as an attempt to compensate for military setbacks on the battlefield, echoing statements by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine that standard diplomatic protocols mandate prior notification and that zero relocation requests have been received.

articles.title: As Russia expands attacks on Kyiv, Ukraine prepares to hit Moscow’s oil industry harder in response
articles.body:
Ukraine will intensify strikes on Russian oil refineries in response to Moscow’s expanded campaign against Ukrainian infrastructure, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview with Reuters on 3 October.
Russia has increased attacks on Kyiv in recent weeks, hitting energy and telecommunications infrastructure, roads, railways, and bridges across the Dnipro. Zelenskyy said Ukraine would respond by targeting the Russian energy infrastructure that helps finance the war.
Russia expands attacks on Kyiv
Russian forces have broadened their strikes on infrastructure in and around Kyiv in recent weeks, with attacks increasingly affecting systems that support civilian life.
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence obtained documents indicating that Russian authorities had approved a broader policy for targeting infrastructure, including logistics, roads, schools, and hospitals. He said the goal is to put pressure on residents to leave Kyiv and other major cities.
Russia has also begun targeting bridges across the Dnipro, which connect the eastern and western parts of the capital.
Ukraine targets Russia’s war economy
Ukraine plans to keep striking Russian oil refineries because they generate revenue that supports Moscow’s war effort, Zelenskyy said.
The policy puts Kyiv at odds with US President Donald Trump, who has urged Ukraine not to attack Russian oil facilities, arguing that such strikes contribute to higher global diesel prices.
Zelenskyy said he sees no indication that Moscow is prepared for either peace talks or an agreement to halt attacks on energy infrastructure.
Ukraine prepares for a new wave of air attacks
Ukraine is also preparing for intensified Russian attacks on its energy system over the winter. Ukrainian officials say Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles for a new campaign against electricity and other critical infrastructure.
Russia has also expanded its use of fast jet-powered Geran drones, launching dozens each day since the summer.
Ukrainian F-16s and MiG aircraft are intercepting around 60% of these drones, according to Zelenskyy, but ammunition for their 20 mm cannons is running low. Ukraine is increasing the use of electronic warfare and expects a first shipment of small, inexpensive air defense missiles designed to counter the jet-powered drones later in October.
Ukraine is developing five interceptor drone models to counter Russian Shaheds. Two have already undergone testing, with Zelenskyy putting their current interception rate at around 30%.
Ukraine expands its strike capabilities
Ukraine is also expanding its long-range strike capabilities. It has used its domestically produced FP-7 ballistic missile in combat for the first time, with a range of about 250 kilometers, while work continues on the longer-range FP-9.
At the same time, Kyiv is working with European partners to secure additional funding for its defense needs. Ukraine has found financing to order drones for early 2027 and is working to close a $27 billion gap in this year’s defense budget through its own resources, bilateral assistance, and financing linked to the EU’s €90 billion loan package.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s ability to sustain its defense and expand its strike capabilities will remain central as Russia prepares for another winter campaign.

- Moscow trains its military pilots at Khanskaya. Locals report a fire there after drones attacked overnight
- Ukraine’s bomber drones, ones that dropped ground robots in its recent Donetsk counteroffensive, are getting 2.4-kilogram jammer to shield them from FPVs

articles.title: The winter war: Ukraine is prepping for another season of Russian attacks before the cold sets in
articles.body:
On Sept. 23, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov once again voiced Moscow’s rejection of a Ukrainian proposal to halt fighting along the current front line. Now Kyiv is preparing for another series of strikes on its critical infrastructure that appear intended to freeze the country during the upcoming winter and result in a humanitarian disaster. Ukraine’s military and civilian institutions have already begun preparing for what they expect to be an especially difficult Russian campaign, with energy companies inspecting equipment and stockpiling fuel while apartment associations buy up generators.
In September, air raid alerts have sounded in Kyiv every day — and almost continuously. Jet-powered Shahed drones circle over the city, disrupting the work of municipal services, shops, businesses, and public institutions. A new operating protocol took effect on Sept. 10, introducing a “yellow” alert level for Shaheds and a “red” level for missiles. Under a yellow alert, most businesses and institutions now remain open.
The changes do not apply to schools, which are still required to suspend classes during air raid alerts. Schools without underground classrooms have moved children to online learning. Across Ukraine more broadly, local authorities have been given discretion over how to respond to alerts.
In August and September, central government officials held a series of meetings with businesses. Entrepreneurs were advised to consider setting up air defenses on their own, to cooperate with existing volunteer territorial defense formations (known by the Ukrainian acronym DFTG), and to move warehouses underground.
Russian forces have been striking warehouses belonging to home improvement retailer Epicentr and delivery company Nova Poshta for years, but the logistical networks of supermarket chains recently started coming under systematic attacks for the first time. Strikes on warehouses reduced the range of goods available in stores in August, though the situation had largely stabilized by mid-September.
As fall begins, everyone in Ukraine seems to be asking the same question: how can the country make it through a winter of relentless strikes? It is already clear that the infrastructure responsible for heating and other fundamental civilian services will be among Russia’s targets.
The military shield and the front line
Ukraine needs interceptors to defend against ballistic and cruise missiles. But increasingly frequent attacks by jet-powered drones have created another challenge.
A volunteer (call sign Max) with a Kyiv Region DFTG told The Insider that his unit formed teams of interceptor-drone pilots in preparation for the winter campaign, alongside its regular gun and mobile fire teams. Training began in mid-spring, and by the end of summer, most volunteers had passed examinations and received certificates — along with combat interceptor drones.
But a problem emerged: older interceptor drones work well against conventional Shaheds traveling at speeds of up to 250 kilometers per hour, but new interceptors designed to take out jet-powered Shaheds have only recently completed testing. Russia is expected to use both conventional and jet-powered Shaheds during the fall and winter, meaning crews are expected to use different interceptors depending on the target.
Volunteer formations are part of Ukraine’s Territorial Defense Forces (TDF) and their supply system tends to lag somewhat behind those of the Unmanned Systems Forces, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), and the National Guard. Newer technologies only reach the TDF and volunteer groups after they have been tested by regular units.
By Sept. 20, videos had emerged showing jet-powered Shaheds being intercepted by high-speed fixed-wing interceptor drones and Sting S quadcopters.
“We have to remember that there is no such thing as 100% effective air defense. Some missiles and Shaheds will get through any defenses. That is why residents should always follow the recommendations of Ukraine’s Defense Forces. New Ukrainian interceptor drones are more maneuverable and can engage targets at greater distances and altitudes than the usual weapons used by ground-based fire teams. But they cannot offer a complete guarantee either. The same applies to Russia, where they are also technologically behind. So if power stations, thermal power plants, and combined heat-and-power plants burn here this winter, there is an even greater likelihood that they will burn in Russia as well,” Max said.
Ukraine’s new interceptor drones are more maneuverable and can hit targets at greater ranges and altitudes, but they cannot provide a complete guarantee against Moscow’s aerial attacks
A Kyiv volunteer territorial defense formation commander called Asgard said his unit has gun teams equipped with a wide range of weapons “from 5.45 mm up to 23 mm,” along with interceptor-drone crews. “The biggest target was probably a cruise missile we shot down in 2024. Believe it or not, we brought it down with a 7.62 mm Maxim machine gun manufactured in 1942.” Unsurprisingly, Asgard’s unit also engages jet-powered Shaheds.
There has been no particular need for “retraining” this year, the Kyiv DFTG commander said. “Every day we face new challenges and learn. Before, they were ordinary Shaheds. Those are very easy targets for us now. We still have work to do with the jet-powered ones.”
Ukraine’s small mobile air defense units shoot down conventional Shaheds in 95% to 99% of cases, but their success rate against jet-powered versions is no more than 40% to 60%. Volunteer formations hope that rate will increase soon as interceptor-drone teams receive more high-speed drones of their own.
At the front itself, winter could provide Ukraine with some advantages, according to Silver, an FPV drone pilot who flies fiber-optic-controlled drones.
“There will be more work in winter. First, the leaves will fall, which will make things easier. Even now we manage to fly fiber-optic drones through forests, but without the ‘greenery’ [the military term for dense seasonal foliage] we will create far more problems for the Russians. Second, we will rely on skill, quality, and careful planning rather than quantity. We are changing our approach, adapting technically and improving our skills. Everyone is talking about AI-equipped drones now, but artificial intelligence will not replace the person who still decides which target to send it toward. I’ve worked with AI-assisted terminal guidance, and it works!”
Even if Russia carries out another mobilization, conditions will become harder for Russian soldiers in winter, according to a Nemesis bomber-drone pilot who has flown 1,000 combat missions over a year and a half.
“The Russian military is adapting too, changing tactics and infiltrating our lines. Maybe they have something new prepared for us. But overall, we’re ready. We’ll see how their mobilization goes and how many more targets we have along the line of contact,” the pilot said.
Front-line cities
About 127,500 people live in the Ukrainian-controlled portion of the Kherson Region — about a quarter of the prewar population. In the city of Kherson itself, 63,000 out of the prewar population of 283,000 remain — roughly 22%.
The situation there is difficult. Russian forces deliberately target energy and heat-generating facilities in an effort to deprive residents of basic services. Strikes take place around the clock, with explosions heard roughly every two minutes. Since the area was liberated in November of 2022, the regional administration has recorded 400,000 Russian attacks involving more than 900,000 munitions.
Elvina Osmanova, head of the Kherson regional administration’s domestic and information policy department, told The Insider that between three and 10 guided aerial bombs (known by the Russian and Ukrainian abbreviation KAB) are dropped on Kherson each day. “They hit infrastructure sites one after another, including the combined heat-and-power plant, and essentially everything responsible for electricity, heating, gas, and water supplies.”
Alongside guided bombs, Russian forces make extensive use of conventional drones, a particular problem for Kherson, Nikopol, and other cities within a 20-kilometer range of the front line. Osmanova lists off the drone types that most frequently attack the city: “FPV drones, Mavics, cheap Molniya kamikaze drones, and other systems. Most of them use fiber-optic control, which makes them difficult to stop. As many as 5,000 drones can be launched at Kherson in a week.”
Still, food deliveries still make it to central Kherson, Osmanova said:
“The city has a sufficient supply of food. But the Russians deliberately destroy trucks and kill drivers transporting bread and other foodstuffs, so issues with deliveries cannot be ruled out. Due to constant shelling, some parts of Kherson are already effectively dead — riverside areas such as Antonivka, Voyenne, Korabel, and several others near the Dnipro. They haven't had normal municipal services for a long time.
Last winter, there were times when people went 10 days without electricity or water. Right now, one district of the city has been without power for 14 days. In other areas, electricity has been restored through the heroic efforts of utility workers. Many have unfortunately been wounded or killed. Drones deliberately target workers while they repair infrastructure.
We understand that the Russians will only increase their attacks in the fall and winter. The number and severity of enemy attacks are increasing every day. Kherson may end up without electricity and heating not just for hours or days but for prolonged periods, and we're preparing for that. We're adapting our anti-drone system — detection systems, electronic warfare, and mobile fire teams — and increasing physical protection for important facilities.”
Shelters are another major focus. Osmanova said 307 protective structures have been repaired and 439 mobile shelters installed in crowded public areas. Protection for critical infrastructure is also being strengthened through backup power, additional physical defenses, and alternative systems intended to allow facilities to continue operating after Russian attacks.
“The Russians attack any kind of transportation with drones: mopeds, passenger cars, trucks, ambulances, municipal vehicles, and public transit,” Osmanova said. “Last week alone, about 40 vehicles were damaged or destroyed. We are doing everything possible to protect the city’s supply routes, including covering roads and streets with anti-drone nets. About 270 kilometers of roads have already been protected that way.”
Zarina Zabrisky, an American journalist with Byline Times who lives in Kherson, told The Insider that residents are preparing for winter however they can. Residents with standalone, private houses were able to heat their homes with firewood in previous winters and are preparing to do so again — and many of them have generators. Zabrisky’s apartment has access to a supply of natural gas, which she used to heat her home last winter.
At the same time, the local administration is advising residents — particularly older people, those with limited mobility, and families with children — to seriously consider temporarily relocating to safer parts of Ukraine. The authorities say they are prepared to assist at every stage, including organizing evacuation, finding housing, providing humanitarian aid, and offering psychological and legal assistance.
Kyiv
Locals in Kyiv are not counting on an energy ceasefire. Instead, they are preparing for something resembling a repeat of last year. The main difference is that the upcoming winter is expected to be milder, with frequent thaws.
Vyacheslav Hryb, who heads three condominium associations in Kyiv, told The Insider how preparations are going:
“We’re buying additional inverters, checking the generators, and connecting elevators to them. If the power goes out, our calculations show the elevators can operate for five to six hours. Heating should also be fine. We have a large building and a 110-kilowatt generator that powers the cold-water supply, hot-water supply, and heating.
Last year, the unprecedented cold made everything harder, and after the strikes, many buildings had to drain water from their heating pipes. Restarting the heating at minus 22 Celsius [about negative 8 degrees Fahrenheit] was what you might call an advanced-level challenge. The instructions say it’s impossible, but we pulled together and managed to get it running.”
Kyiv’s energy situation is among the most difficult among Ukrainian cities not located near the front. Last winter, residents of several buildings on the eastern bank of the Dnipro went without centralized heating for around a month after heating pipes burst. Electricity schedules were largely maintained, with power generally available for four hours followed by four hours without it.
Kyiv’s energy situation is among the most difficult of Ukraine’s non-frontline cities
Residents are now buying batteries and inverters in order to be more self-sufficient. Buildings with condominium associations are generally better prepared, often with generators or high-capacity battery and inverter systems that can keep heat, water and elevators running during outages. But only about 2,000 of Kyiv’s more than 10,000 residential buildings have these associations.
Other buildings are serviced by municipal housing offices, commonly known by the Soviet-era abbreviation ZhEK. Their residents therefore often have to go to special “Points of Invincibility” set up by city authorities and Ukraine’s State Emergency Service to warm up and charge their devices.
The Zhytomyr phenomenon
The city of Zhytomyr is located less than 100 miles from Kyiv, but last winter it did not even suffer widespread short-term power cuts. Vitaliy, a Zhytomyr resident, told The Insider that while Kyiv spent days at a time without electricity, Zhytomyr experienced only a handful of outages, none lasting more than an hour:
“Specialists had told me before that Zhytomyr had inherited many military factories from the Soviet era. It was also an early adopter of power systems designed for wartime conditions. The city developed a distributed energy system, which is why, despite repeated attacks, we did not face major disruptions or prolonged power outages last winter or the winter before.”
In Ukrainian cities where power distribution has been managed effectively, utility services remain close to prewar levels. Residents of Kyiv — and perhaps soon Moscow and St. Petersburg — can only look with envy at Zhytomyr.
The overall state of Ukraine’s energy system
The risk of new large-scale attacks remains one of the most serious and unpredictable factors facing Ukraine this winter. DTEK, the country’s largest private energy company, is preparing for a range of possible scenarios.
“First and foremost, we are repairing and restoring thermal power plants around the clock after attacks,” the company told The Insider. “There is not a single DTEK generating unit that has not been damaged or destroyed during the years of the full-scale war, and some units have had to be rebuilt several times.”
At the same time, the company is carrying out scheduled equipment repairs in order to improve reliability during the winter. It is also stockpiling fuel and supporting the operation of mines, machine-building facilities, and repair businesses. DTEK spent more than 7.6 billion hryvnias ($170 million) on those efforts in the first half of 2026 alone. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, it has spent more than 51 billion hryvnias ($1.2 billion) restoring thermal generation, supporting its businesses, and preparing for wartime winters.
In the first half of 2026, DTEK invested 3.3 billion hryvnias ($74 million) in repairing and modernizing power grids. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, investment in that area has exceeded 15 billion hryvnias ($335 million). The company says its central goals are to restore as much available capacity as possible, maintain sufficient supplies for emergency repairs, and be prepared to respond as quickly as possible to new attacks.
DTEK is advising Ukrainians to use electricity carefully, particularly during periods of peak demand, and says it will do everything possible to minimize the effects of attacks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, meanwhile, said the government would prepare the country’s air defense network for the winter.
“This is extremely difficult, but it has to be expanded. Absolutely everyone is working on it: the Defense Ministry, the Foreign Ministry, and the Foreign Intelligence Service. The obvious challenge, as you know, is missiles for the Patriot system. But we are working on that as well,” Zelensky told reporters Sept. 25. “Separately, we are working on our own anti-ballistic air defense system. That is the FREYJA system. We will work on all of this so there is no collapse.”
Zelensky also said Ukraine would retaliate for attacks on its energy system by striking not only Russian oil refineries — but its energy facilities as well.

articles.title: Defense Forces Hit Kaluga Radio Tube Plant Producing Components for Kh-101 and Iskander-M
articles.body:
The Defense Forces of Ukraine hit Voskhod-KLRZ, also known as the Kaluga Radio Tube Plant. This electronics manufacturer produces components for Kh-101 and Iskander-K cruise missiles, as well as Iskander-M ballistic missiles.
The OSINT project Supernova+ reported this on the evening of October 3, citing local residents.
Judging by videos published by local residents, cruise missiles or jet-powered drones were used in the strike. A characteristic jet-engine sound can be heard before the explosion.
Meanwhile, the governor claimed that Russian forces had destroyed 13 UAVs over the Kaluga region and Kaluga itself.
The Varta OSINT project reported that the Voskhod JSC, or the Kaluga Radio Tube Plant, specializes in developing and manufacturing high-reliability microelectronics, semiconductor components, specialized materials for the electronics industry, and equipment for testing components.
The plant produces digital integrated circuits, operational amplifiers, transistor arrays, optocouplers, semiconductor lasers and photodiodes. In a 2012 presentation, the company stated that more than 90% of its products were intended for Russia’s defense industry.
According to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, Voskhod is involved in producing Kh-101 cruise missiles. The company manufactured OSM140UD17A and UD601A operational amplifiers for the K003 computing unit, as well as 544UD16U3 amplifiers and N590KN13 analog switches for the Monoblock-L unit.
For the 9M727 missile of the Iskander-K system, the plant supplies trunk transmitters for the Zarya-61M onboard computer. It also manufactures converters, operational amplifiers, logic elements, and analog switches for circuit boards of the GIB-123-4 inertial navigation system.
The company is also involved in the production of 9M723 ballistic missiles of the Iskander-M system. According to Ukrainian intelligence, Voskhod manufactures and supplies RUD20 microchips for these missiles.
Another military-related area of the plant’s work is equipment for maintaining armored vehicles. Its catalog includes the UChS-1G system for chemical cleaning of 125mm tank gun barrels and the PPSG-2-2 device for testing generator systems of BMP-2 and BMP-3 infantry fighting vehicles, as well as the starter-generator system of the T-72 tank. The company’s public catalog also offers the PKV-003 device for crimping, or mechanically securing, fuzes screwed into artillery ammunition ranging from 37mm to 152mm in caliber.
Ukraine imposed sanctions on Voskhod under Decree No. 227/2023 dated April 15, 2023, for a period of 10 years. At the same time, the company is not subject to sanctions imposed by the United States, the European Union, or the United Kingdom.
In early September, it was reported that almost half of the 155 companies owned by the Russian Roselectronika industrial holding, which specializes in developing and manufacturing radio-electronic components, remain outside sanctions.

articles.title: 1 killed, 6 injured in Ukraine as another Kyiv bridge comes under Russian attack, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
04 October 2026•Update: 04 October 2026
At least one person was killed and six others injured in overnight Russian attacks on Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday.
Zelenskyy said a Russian drone again struck the Pivnichnyi Bridge in Kyiv, as key bridges in the capital were targeted for a fourth consecutive day.
He said Russia also struck a medical supply warehouse in Sumy and a communications facility in Dnipro.
Zelenskyy said Russia launched 135 attack drones at Ukraine, more than 50 of them jet-powered, targeting residential buildings and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Dnipro, Kharkiv, Donetsk and Sumy regions, as well as Zaporizhzhia.
“There are power outages in some communities. Our services are working at the impact sites,” he said.
He said Russia had used more than 1,900 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 25 missiles against Ukraine this week alone.
“More than 800 of the drones were jet-powered, and Russia must be held accountable for this escalation,” he said.
Zelenskyy also welcomed German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s visit to Kyiv after he arrived Sunday morning, saying Germany had consistently supported efforts to protect Ukrainian lives from Russian strikes.
“We are grateful for all the support, and today we are preparing decisions to give us in Ukraine, and all of Europe, greater capabilities to defend ourselves. There will be important agreements between Ukraine and Germany. Russia must be stopped together,” he said.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces continued to strike Ukrainian port infrastructure and maritime vessels allegedly supporting Ukrainian troops. It said a dry-cargo vessel carrying military supplies for the Ukrainian armed forces was hit by a drone at sea east of Odesa.
The ministry also said a UAV command post and temporary deployment sites of Ukrainian forces in the Donetsk and Sumy regions came under airstrikes.
It added that Russian air defenses intercepted or destroyed 559 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over several Russian regions, annexed Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.

articles.title: Germany announces $1.46 billion in aid for Ukraine, including interceptor drones
articles.body:
Germany announces $1.46 billion in aid for Ukraine, including interceptor drones
Germany on Oct. 4 announced a new support package worth more than €1.3 billion ($1.46 billion) for Ukraine, including funding for interceptor drones and energy assistance.
The package was announced by President Volodymyr Zelensky and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz at a joint press conference in Kyiv.
Zelensky said the package included weapons needed immediately, support for Ukraine's energy sector, and funding to produce new interceptors specifically designed to counter Russia's jet-powered attack drones.
"These are weapons that will help now, support for our energy sector — this is very important," Zelensky said.
The package includes €1 billion ($1.13 billion) in military aid, including financing the production of interceptor drones capable of countering Russian jet-powered weapons, Merz said.
Additionally, the chancellor announced around €350 million ($394 million) in energy assistance, including support for generators and repairs to infrastructure damaged by Russian attacks.
"This will quickly and noticeably strengthen Ukraine's air defense, and this reinforcement is urgently needed," Merz said.
He added that the energy package was intended to mitigate the impact of Russian attacks on Ukraine's power infrastructure ahead of winter.
Earlier in the day, Merz visited the National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv, which was damaged in a Russian drone strike on Sept. 28.
"Mr. Putin, stop this senseless war," Merz said during the visit, according to dpa. "We are ready for talks, we are ready to speak with one another about ending this war. But these barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop."
The announcements come as Russia continues to terrorize Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure with jet-powered attack drones. "Just this week, Russia has used more than 1,900 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 25 missiles against Ukraine. More than 800 of the drones were jet-powered," Zelensky said.
Zelensky described air defense as Ukraine's current "number one priority," saying he and Merz had discussed additional measures the two countries could take together.
Germany and Ukraine have also expanded joint defense production. In May, Berlin and Kyiv launched "Brave Germany," a joint initiative backed by Ukraine's Brave1 defense-tech platform to support Ukrainian and German defense companies and accelerate development of new military technologies.
The new package was announced during Merz's visit to Kyiv on Oct. 4, where he arrived with German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and executives from the country's defense and energy sectors.

articles.title: Iran warns US: More firepower will not end Mid-East war
articles.body:
Iran warns US: More firepower will not end Mid-East war
- Iran’s top diplomat said there is no military solution to the US war and only negotiations based on justice and fairness can end the conflict.
- The US has rejected Iran’s demands to end sanctions and lift a naval blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, but says it remains open to talks.
- The US has increased military presence in the Middle East, deploying missile batteries and aircraft carriers to counter Iran.
AI generated
TEHRAN – Iran’s top diplomat insisted on Oct 4 that there would be no military solution to the US’ war against Iran, with talks on ending the conflict apparently at an impasse.
A campaign of heavy bombardment failed to bring a decisive close to the war launched by the US and Israel in late February, and Washington in recent weeks has dialled back military operations in favour of economic pressure.
The main point of contention remains Iran’s attempt to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, a vital conduit for Gulf oil and gas where a British maritime agency reported on Oct 4 another tanker struck by an unknown projectile.
“If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before and we will defend ourselves with even more force,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said at a gathering of foreign ambassadors.
“There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions,” he said, adding that “only negotiations based on justice and fairness” could end the conflict.
The two sides agreed on a memorandum of understanding in June that spelled out a framework for a permanent resolution, but Iranian attacks on vessels in the Hormuz prompted a return to US military operations.
Iran has sought to impose its control over the vital shipping lane since the start of the war, striking vessels that attempt to transit without its authorisation.
The US has imposed its own counterblockade of Iranian ports, and has also struck vessels it accuses of violating it.
On Oct 4, the British maritime security agency UKMTO said a tanker in the Hormuz “reported being struck by an unknown projectile, causing damage to the engine room”, though the crew were reported safe and no environmental impact was recorded.
The agency did not specify the date of the incident, the vessel’s origin or destination, or whether it was an oil tanker or LNG carrier.
Focused on Hormuz
Iranian and US officials last week held indirect talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, with Tehran saying it presented seven conditions for reopening the strait.
Iran has demanded, among other things, a ceasefire across the Middle East, the unfreezing of its assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade.
Trump, however, rejected the proposal, while leaving the door open both to further talks or renewed military operations.
Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei on Oct 4 characterised the latest US counterproposal as being “in line with their previous proposals concerning nuclear issues”.
“We have clearly indicated that we are focusing on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said, adding that reopening the waterway required “an end to the disruptions to Iranian commercial maritime traffic and the lifting of sanctions”.
The US and Israel have characterised the war as being necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons – a goal it has long denied pursuing – though the focus soon shifted to reopening the Hormuz after its closure sent shockwaves through world energy markets.
The US has not struck Iran since Sept 1 1, but it has recently pursued a fresh military buildup in the region.
US media outlet Axios reported that Washington has deployed additional Patriot missile batteries to Saudi Arabia and Qatar to help protect key energy facilities from possible Iranian retaliation.
It also reported that the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and its strike group were heading to the Middle East, where they could join two other US carrier strike groups already in the region.
Axios reported that top Trump Cabinet members met on Oct 2 to discuss the war in Iran, as well as the conflict in Yemen, where the Tehran-backed Houthis have been fighting government forces and attacking Saudi Arabia. AFP

articles.title: What a US-China thaw could cost India
articles.body:
What a US-China thaw could cost India
When the leaders of the world’s two largest economies meet, the whole world watches the theatrics, the body language and the substance. Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the US and summit with President Donald Trump took place against the backdrop of a surge in China’s global trade, while Trump has been struggling with falling approval ratings at home.
The high-stakes summit centred on symbolic gestures, personal rapport, and major economic and technology tensions. It yielded few breakthroughs on structural disputes. The most tangible outcome was an agreement to extend a critical trade war tariff truce by an additional two months, shifting the deadline to mid-January 2027. China’s export boom defied Trump’s tariff campaign.
From a position of strength, Xi was in no rush to make concessions while Trump was constrained by the costly Iran war that was hurting both his popularity and American wallets. The tariffs to address a trade imbalance with China were actually “killing” the US.
View from Delhi
Few nations have been monitoring the proceedings in Washington with greater scrutiny than India, as Xi-Trump discuss AI governance, tariff truces, critical minerals, regional maritime flashpoints, Taiwan and Indo-Pacific security. The outcome could affect New Delhi’s trade ambitions, supply chains, border security, Quad strategy, energy costs and influence.
New Delhi has been closely monitoring shifts in bilateral ties and supply chain vulnerabilities, and wondering about regional security frameworks like the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad). Indians have been also wondering why they were being singled out for 100% tariff for trading with Russia, while China was being wooed due high US economic dependences. As China has grown in global stature, it was clear that economic and military strength brings prestige and respect.
The largest and oldest democracies, India and the US, were meant to have congruence of interests and common global perceptions. That a day would come so quickly when the US would woo the communist arch rival and competitor from a relative position of weakness, was not anticipated.
At the core of it all, for some time now, India’s calculations have been based on an enduring fear of the emergence of a US-China “G2.” Something that could position India as a “second fiddle.”
The new emerging duopoly could establish a bilateral framework to partition spheres of influence, resolve global disputes, and manage international security above the heads of leading middle powers or an aspiring great power like India. China could get emboldened towards Asian dominance. Early signals were visible during Trump’s second term that Washington preferred a highly transactional foreign policy. Trump’s tariffs were bound to actually give greater leverage to China which monopolizes critical minerals and technologies and has a balance of payments advantage with all.
Despite structural mistrust between the US and China, these baby-steps towards managed coexistence present challenging outcomes for India. On the other hand, a total breakdown of US-China relations would be even worse for New Delhi and the world.
Washington’s policing failures around the world over the decades, and now never-ending Iran war, have lowered America’s global standing and influence. The tariffs have caused a level of distrust in New Delhi. NATO allies and West Asian friends of the US are running helter-skelter looking for alternative security arrangements and umbrellas.
For a long time India was hoping US support for technology and military capability building would allow it to remain a peer to China in Asia. A cosy bilateral understanding between Washington and Beijing could marginalize India’s diplomatic leverage. India also risks diluting regional bargaining power. In fact, US-China competition also indirectly supported India’s “strategic autonomy.”
In the recent past, India was looking for alternative sourcing through what is called the ‘China Plus One’ manufacturing strategy. American industrial giants that have been eager to exit China dependence have been investing billions of dollars into Make-in-India, especially in consumer electronics, pharmaceuticals, automotive parts, and solar equipment. This has helped boost manufacturing’s share of India’s GDP and expand the country’s exports.
But now if Xi and Trump move towards a comprehensive trade deal, securing American industry interests, then the move towards India could slowdown. A transactional Trump has been vocal about India’s protective trade policies and domestic market restrictions. He may now push for opening India’s agriculture and technology sectors to American firms. Global commodity price volatility is also being watched closely by India. A reconciliation between Washington and Beijing could stabilize global demand, and be good for New Delhi.
China controls roughly 70% of global rare-earth element extraction and nearly 85% of refining capacity. Essential for military hardware, electric vehicle batteries, wind turbines, and advanced electronics, they give Beijing significant leverage over Washington. Any US-China understanding on critical minerals will be good for the world and India.
Just days before the bilateral summit, on September 18, Trump signed into law a bill that allows a 100% tariff on top buyers of Russian energy, primarily China and India. Days later, the US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that Washington and Beijing had extended their Busan Agreement until January 10, 2027, under which the two sides agreed to avoid new tariffs and trade restrictions on each other.
Will India receive a similar concession? For now, it remains exposed to the tariff threat. Does Trump see India as a softer target? While US threatens India and Brazil, it is more considerate towards China because Beijing exercises much more leverage. Peter Navarro, an American economist and Trump’s senior counsellor for trade and manufacturing, at one point called Ukraine ‘Modi’s war’ - because of New Delhi’s oil imports from Russia. Nobody in Trump’s administration has ever tried to call the Ukraine crisis ‘Xi’s war’. Recall that in July 2025, Washington spared China but imposed an additional 25% on India for buying Russian crude. There is thus increased suspicion that India is in the crosshairs while Beijing keeps escaping US scrutiny.
The US has been concerned about AI malpractice by China and has sought structured AI safety dialogues. India, which aims to become a global hub for AI deployment and digital public infrastructure, is monitoring the discussions closely, so that it does not lose the early mover advantage.
India’s Indo-Pacific strategy relies heavily on the Quad alongside the United States, Japan, and Australia. But under Trump 2.0, the grouping has faced growing uncertainty, with the US president clearly favoring bilateral deals over multilateral frameworks. If Washington ends up softening its position on the South China Sea in exchange for economic concessions, it would send a deeply troubling signal — not only to New Delhi, but to the wider world.
As China becomes a peer power with the US, a weakening American position on Taiwan could embolden the People’s Liberation Army (PLA). While India’s immediate focus remains sovereignty over its territory along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) and its influence across South Asia, an emboldened PLA could be a threat for India. It could weaken India’s position on the painstaking negotiations after the 2020 border conflict. Beijing might become less accommodating toward Indian border positions. Conversely a stable China-US relationship could also bring stability in China-India relations, and reduce the trust deficit. India also does not want Chinese or US influence in South Asia as it considers it detrimental to its security.
India hopes that the Xi-Trump discussions bring stability to the global energy trade. Spiking oil prices are already worsening India’s current account deficit and driving domestic inflation.
Reenergized US-China relations could reduce Russia-China dependency on each other. Russia may then edge closer to India.
Long strategic game
The export juggernaut that Trump sought to tame has kept roaring in what economists are increasingly referring to as ‘China Shock 2.0’. China’s global trade surplus is on pace to top $1 trillion for a second straight year. The Trump administration thought they could use massive unilateral pressure to force China to make concessions, but that did not occur.
The US president had hoped to use the pending $14 billion arms package for Taiwan as a “negotiating chip” with Beijing. With Xi clearly in the driver’s seat it will further unnerve US allies in Asia, especially Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, Taiwan, and the Quad partners. Washington’s resolve to defend Taiwan is again in question.
Washington also sees Xi as uniquely able to exert pressure on Iran to negotiate, but Xi has shown little inclination to do so. Beijing is selling billions of dollars’ worth of goods to Iran through sanctions-evasion. Xi had urged the US and Iran to return to negotiations to end the war, but Xi has not publicly commented on Chinese support for Iran. China is moving from indirect influence to signalling readiness for a direct role. Could China become the next mediator in the US-Iran war?
Xi pressed Trump on Taiwan saying he hoped the US would “handle the Taiwan question with prudence.” Meanwhile, Senate Democrats criticized Trump for failing to publicly address China’s military pressure on Taiwan and called for the immediate delivery of approved military aid and arms sales to the island.
In his characteristic way, Trump said America was “very happy” about Xi’s visit, and hoped that China is “very happy also.” Xi said the US-China relationship had developed into a constructive one of “strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity,” thus positioning Beijing as an equal to the US on the global stage.
“In some ways, the best thing that we accomplished in this visit is to continue the conversation,” US Ambassador to China David Perdue told Fox News. Showmanship of bonhomie and current positive mood in the relationship could be temporary, given disputes over technology controls, rare earth exports, agricultural trade, and over Iran, Russia, and Taiwan.
The US and China remain strategic competitors across trade, technology, security and geopolitics, yet both governments have simultaneously demonstrated an interest in preventing competition from degenerating into confrontation. There was a talk about a possible hotline between the two countries, and some sort of a broad deal for sharing a progress report of sorts. Nothing of that sort happened.
Xi Jinping is playing a long strategic game. Washington continues to be at war and mired in multiple geopolitical and domestic crises. Beijing is quietly consolidating its economy, political control, restructuring its military and expanding its strategic footprint. China does not need to defeat America, it may only need to outlast American attention. “America is very happy about this visit, and I’m sure China is very happy also,” Trump said. Whether India is happy will be dissected in the corridors of power in New Delhi.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: Germany's Merz visits Kyiv to pledge more support to Zelensky
articles.body:
Kyiv’s North bridge was hit in a new Russian attack on Sunday, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said, soon after German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Ukraine's capital. Merz is on a surprise visit to demonstrate European support in the face of an upsurge in Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. Follow our liveblog for all the latest developments.
Germany's Merz unveils new military and energy aid for Ukraine
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced military aid for Ukraine worth around €1 billion ($1.13 billion) and an energy support package during a visit to Kyiv, as the Ukrainian capital came under renewed attack from Russian drones.
Merz, who was accompanied by a senior minister and several company executives, said his visit "demonstrates that we will not be intimidated. Nor will we be intimidated by a drone attack occurring at the very time of our visit."
Zelensky meets with Germany's Merz at Kyiv Russian drone strike site
Russia to intensify strikes on Ukraine after Zelensky remarks, defence ministry says
Russia said it would ramp up its pummelling of Ukraine after President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that Kyiv would increase its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
"Following Zelensky's statement ... strikes by the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation on military and military-industrial facilities, as well as related infrastructure in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine, will be intensified," Russia's defence ministry said in a statement.
Russian strikes hit Kyiv Northern bridge as Germany's Merz visits
Moscow has once again bombed one of Kyiv’s bridges, despite the presence of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in the Ukrainian capital. The visit was unplanned, but Merz says it was intended to show Germany’s support for Ukraine.
FRANCE 24's correspondent Gulliver Cragg, reporting from Kyiv, says traffic has resumed on the bridge, though slowly. Video shows a large hole in the roadway. Experts say the bridges are extremely solid and difficult to destroy, even with ballistic missiles.
Three injured after drone debris triggers fire at Krasnodar industrial site, authorities say
A fire broke out at an industrial site in Russia's Krasnodar region after falling drone debris struck the site in the Temryuk district, regional authorities said.
Three people were injured and were receiving medical treatment, while emergency services were working at the scene.
Germany's Merz in Kyiv as Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian cities
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Ukraine's capital Kyiv on Sunday on an unannounced visit in a show of support for the country in its war with Russia. Merz's visit comes just a day after Russia warned foreigners and diplomats to leave the Ukrainian capital, saying that "massive" new air strikes would hit the city.
FRANCE 24's correspondent in Kyiv Gulliver Cragg has more.
Latvian PM on track to lead pro-Ukraine coalition after election win
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs was set to retain power and form a pro-Ukrainian coalition after his centrist United List secured the biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence in 1991.
With 97 percent of ballots counted after Saturday's election in the NATO and European Union country bordering Russia, United List was on 35.3 percent, enough for 42 seats in the 100-seat parliament.
Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which stray Ukrainian military drones flew undetected into Latvia.
Russia strikes hit Kyiv soon after Merz's arrival
A bridge in Kyiv was hit in a Russian attack, the city's mayor Vitali Klitschko said, soon after the arrival of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
"Impact on the road surface of the Northern Bridge. Emergency services are heading to the scene," the mayor wrote on Telegram. Air raid sirens had earlier blared, warning of drones approaching the city.
Germany's Merz in Kyiv to hold talks with Zelensky
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Chancellor Friedrich Merz would hold talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Writing on X, Sybiha said the agenda would focus on "strengthening Ukraine, our defense and resilience, and our shared European security”.
Germany's Merz arrives in Kyiv as Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian cities
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv in a show of support as Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukrainian cities.
The aerial war has intensified, with Moscow menacing cities across Ukraine with hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, while Kyiv has been striking Russia’s oil industry and businesses
“Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I traveled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us,” Merz wrote on X, noting that Germany’s own security “also depends on the outcome of this war".
Good morning and welcome to our liveblog on the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: FP-9 ballistic missile capable of reaching Moscow will be ready this autumn
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: FP-9 ballistic missile capable of reaching Moscow will be ready this autumn
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has stated that Ukraine's FP-9 ballistic missile, which is capable of reaching Moscow, will be ready this autumn.
Source: Zelenskyy in an interview with Reuters
Details: Reuters noted that Ukraine reported the first combat deployment of its domestically produced FP-7 ballistic missile this week. The missile has a range of approximately 250 km.
Zelenskyy said he had phoned the manufacturer, Fire Point, to urge them to speed up development of the longer-range FP-9 model, which the company says will be able to strike Moscow.
Quote from Zelenskyy: "I said to them, where is my FP-9? [with a grin – ed.] We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be [ready] this autumn, I'm sure."
Details: Zelenskyy also pointed out that Ukraine has had to rely heavily on its F-16 and MiG fighter jets to shoot down about 60% of Russian jet-powered UAVs, but stocks of 20mm ammunition for these aircraft are running extremely low.
He said Kyiv is urgently seeking alternative solutions, particularly by enhancing its electronic warfare capabilities. The first delivery of small, inexpensive air defence missiles capable of shooting down the new Shaheds is expected in the second half of October.
Last week Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine is developing five new interceptor models designed to down jet-powered Shaheds. Having just returned from a meeting with the leadership of the Ministry of Defence, he mentioned that the testing of two of these models had demonstrated a moderate success rate of around 30%.
Quote: "We'll have to scale it. I hope that with all these things, with all these elements, we'll find a way."
