articles.title: Moscow unveils 'new doctrine' targeting Ukrainian civilians, Zelensky vows to respond with more energy strikes
articles.body:
Moscow unveils 'new doctrine' targeting Ukrainian civilians, Zelensky vows to respond with more energy strikes
In response to a new airstrike policy targeting Ukrainian civilians by Moscow, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 3 that Ukraine would increase attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
Zelensky told Reuters that Ukrainian intelligence obtained documents revealing that Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a "new doctrine" allowing Russian forces to launch broader strikes against Ukrainian civilian targets this upcoming winter.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them [to] attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities," Zelensky said. With this shift, Putin wants to appear strong even as Russian troops continue to lose ground while suffering massive casualties, said Zelensky.
The president's comments come as Russian forces have increasingly battered Ukrainian civilian infrastructure in recent weeks, including attacks on key bridges and medical and educational facilities.
In response to Moscow's changing tactics, Zelensky vowed to increase strikes on Russian energy sites, though without indiscriminately targeting Russian civilians.
"We have to respond in any way [we can]. With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refineries: what gives money to them for this war," Zelensky said. "But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects."
For weeks, U.S. President Donald Trump has been pressing Ukraine and Russia to halt energy strikes in order to help lower high oil prices brought on by his war with Iran. While Zelensky has expressed his willingness to try an energy ceasefire, the American president's pleas appear to have gained little traction in Moscow.
In order to help double down on striking Russian energy sites, Ukraine will continue to produce its own long-range ballistic missiles. On Oct. 1, Zelensky announced Ukraine's domestically developed FP-7 ballistic missile was used in combat against Russia for the first time.
Zelensky told Reuters he has already called on the missile's manufacturer, Fire Point, to prepare longer-range missiles.
"I said to them, where is my FP-9? We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be [ready] this autumn, I'm sure," Zelensky said.
On Oct. 3, Zelensky said Ukraine had responded to Russian strikes on civilian targets by using long-range missiles to hit a facility in Russia's Samara region as well as an "Iskander" missile systems in the Bryansk region.
"Russians continue to turn our infrastructure and everything that supports normal life into targets," said Zelensky. "It is important to note that our soldiers always find ways to respond justly to these attacks and to return the war to where it came from."

articles.title: Germany's Merz arrives in Kyiv to pledge more support
articles.body:
Germany's Merz visits Kyiv amid Russian strikes
Published October 4, 2026last updated October 4, 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, on Sunday and called on Russian President Vladimir Putin to stop his "barbaric attacks" and end what he called a "senseless war."
Speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the badly damaged building of Ukraine's Academy of Sciences, where at least two people died in a drone strike last week, Merz said:
"We are ready for talks, we are ready to discuss bringing this war to an end, but these barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop. I can only repeat once again: Mr Putin, put an end to this senseless war."
Merz arrived in Kyiv by train early on Sunday morning, accompanied by German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and a delegation of leading figures from Germany's arms industry, including executives from Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defense and Quantum Systems.
"If Russia is not stopped, it will turn its war machine against us sooner or later," Merz said upon arrival.
Air raid sirens blared across the Ukrainian capital throughout the morning, as Kyiv's mayor announced one of the city's bridges had been hit by a Russian drone.
President Zelenskyy condemned the attacks and said the capital was experiencing a "terrible situation" with "horrific days and nights." He labeled the Russian attackers "absolute barbarians" and said: "It is vital that Ukraine is not left alone in the face of this terror."
Focus on ramping up drone production
Merz pledged further military and energy assistance during his visit, with Zelenskyy announcing a German support package worth more than €1.3 billion ($1.5 billion).
The package includes €1 billion in military aid and €350 million for energy sector repairs ahead of winter.
Zelenskyy said the two countries had agreed 15 documents worth more than €8.5 billion ($9.6 billion), covering defense cooperation, production, procurement and joint projects in Ukraine.
According to German government sources cited by Reuters and the DPA news agency, the planned cooperation includes the development and delivery of thousands of interceptor drones capable of countering the fast, jet-powered drones Russia increasingly deploys against Ukrainian infrastructure.
The plans also envisage expanding production of long-range weapons capable of striking targets more than 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) away.
Merz emphasized that the partnership would also benefit Germany, with companies from both countries developing technology to strengthen their security.
"German and Ukrainian companies are jointly developing technologies that benefit both countries. That makes us safer and stronger," he said.
Russia strikes Kyiv bridge during Merz visit
The visit came just hours after the Russian Foreign Ministry warned foreign diplomats and other visitors to avoid the Ukrainian capital, and military and government buildings in particular.
"The responsibility for any negative consequences lies entirely with those who ignore this warning," read a statement, which claimed that Russian strikes were responses to "terrorist acts by the Ukrainian armed forces against our country's civilian infrastructure."
In recent days, Russia has attacked several bridges across the Dnipro river as well as energy infrastructure, and the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, on Friday said that Kyiv was in a "very dramatic situation."
Further strikes followed on Sunday during Merz's visit, with Klitschko confirming that a bridge had been struck.
"Impact on the road surface of the Northern Bridge. Emergency services are heading to the scene," the mayor wrote on the Telegram messaging service.
But the German delegation was not deterred, with Merz saying upon arrival that "Ukraine will need all our support in the coming weeks" as winter approaches and Russian attacks intensify.
"A fifth winter of war is about to begin," he said. "Russia is bombarding cities, apartments and power stations. I will tell President Zelenskyy today: 'You can count on our help.'"
Merz: 'If Germany wavers, Ukraine wavers'
Merz's arrival in Kyiv marks the fourth such visit to Ukraine by a German chancellor since the full-scale Russian invasion began in February 2022.
His predecessor, Olaf Scholz, visited twice during his three-year tenure, while Merz himself first traveled to Kyiv in May 2025 – just four days after taking office. He was accompanied on that occasion by French President Emmanuel Macron, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
Sunday's visit comes just days after Merz had assured Ukraine of Germany's support, despite isolated resistance and criticism at home.
"If we in Germany waver, Europe wavers," he said on Thursday after conferring the international Westphalian Peace Prize upon the NATO military alliance and its secretary general, Mark Rutte. "And if Europe wavers, Ukraine wavers."
Germany remains Ukraine's most important backer, both militarily and financially, but state elections in September saw significant gains for parties at both ends of the political spectrum who are critical of expenditure on Ukraine: the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the socialist Left Party in Berlin.
In his speech on Thursday, Merz called out in particular "the AfD and their Russian backers" and promised Ukraine that Germany would not be divided.

articles.title: Germany Pledges €1.3B Defense Package During Merz Kyiv Visit
articles.body:
Germany has committed a comprehensive military and energy assistance package valued at more than €1.3 billion ($1.5 billion) to Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced in Kyiv on Sunday, Oct. 4.
According to Ukrinform, the newly allocated assistance package comprises roughly €1 billion ($1.13 billion) in military aid focused on air defense, long-range strike capabilities, combat drones, and satellite communications, alongside approximately €350 million ($396 million) to reinforce Ukrainian power substations and emergency generation ahead of winter.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Speaking during a joint press briefing in the capital, Zelensky stressed that the agreements combine emergency battlefield deliveries with sustainable industrial integration.
“There is a new support package for Ukraine – a comprehensive package of more than €1.3 billion,” Zelensky stated. “This is weapons that will help right now, as well as support for our energy sector ahead of winter – an important energy package. Naturally, we discussed the need for air defense, which is crucial at this time.”
In parallel with the emergency assistance, the two governments and corporate partners concluded 15 bilateral agreements and industrial documents valued at more than €8.5 billion ($9.6 billion), focusing on long-term arms manufacturing, joint defense ventures on Ukrainian soil, and direct state orders for German industrial manufacturers.
No EU Embassies Leaving Kyiv Despite Russian Threats, Envoy Says
“To date, we have 15 agreements and documents, and most of them concern security cooperation, manufacturing, corresponding procurement, our orders for German industry, and joint projects in Ukraine,” Zelensky said.
“The total weight of today’s agreements is more than €8.5 billion.”
Military breakdown, long-range systems, and winter energy aid
Details outlined by Chancellor Merz during the briefing confirmed that the €1 billion ($1.13 billion) military component prioritizes long-range standoff capabilities and advanced communications to allow Ukrainian forces to target Russian launch installations directly.
“We are launching another military support package worth around one billion euros,” Merz said, noting that Berlin will supply long-range strike weapons, combat drones, and satellite technologies.
“Regarding the details of the military support, I ask for understanding that we do not wish to disclose them in detail.”
Merz emphasized that German military assistance is concentrating on two foundational capabilities: expanding layered air defense and reinforcing space-based satellite communications to ensure Ukrainian units receive real-time operational data.
The chancellor added that German funding is accelerating serial assembly lines for newly developed interceptors engineered to neutralize jet-powered strike drones following recent technological breakthroughs.
Addressing the civilian heating sector, Merz announced approximately €350 million ($396 million) in targeted energy assistance to procure mobile generators, repair damaged electrical substations, and restore transmission infrastructure battered by Russian aerial strikes.
“We are facing what may be a very difficult winter. Moscow is deliberately targeting energy supply infrastructure – thermal power plants, substations, fuel stations, and railway infrastructure,” Merz said.
“The goal is entirely obvious: to break the morale of Ukrainians. Despite the attack that occurred this morning, I see here a determined people and a determined government.”
Industrial ventures and Berlin winter summit
A core component of the newly finalized accords is a dedicated bilateral agreement on joint counter-drone operations, established to counter Russia’s accelerating use of turbojet-powered loitering munitions against Ukrainian urban centers and power generation facilities.
The agreement aligns with Chancellor Merz’s pledge, announced upon his arrival in the capital, that Berlin intends to ensure the expedited transfer of 1,000 newly developed interceptor systems designed specifically to defeat turbojet-powered Shahed drones directly from German production lines.
Merz traveled to Kyiv accompanied by German Minister for Economic Affairs Katharina Reiche alongside a 10-member delegation of chief executives and senior managers representing Germany’s defense and energy industries.
The corporate representatives conducted working sessions with Ukrainian defense officials to advance collaborative assembly lines, technology transfers, and resilient industrial supply chains.
The industrial focus comes as German defense planners and corporate partners seek to deploy lower-cost interceptors capable of neutralizing fast-moving strike drones without depleting high-end surface-to-air missile stockpiles such as the IRIS-T or Patriot.
Looking ahead to multilateral diplomatic coordination, Merz announced that Germany intends to convene a high-level summit in Berlin this winter alongside France and the UK.
“Together with France and Great Britain, we want to hold a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin this winter, particularly to coordinate further assistance,” Merz confirmed, though specific calendar dates and formal agendas remain under development.
Academy of Sciences visit
Following their formal talks, Zelensky and Merz traveled together to inspect the site of a recent Russian drone strike on the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv.
The strike on the academic institution killed two people and injured seven others, causing severe structural damage to the historic scientific complex.
Zelensky stated that video records confirmed the facility was deliberately targeted by Russian loitering munitions, characterizing the strike as an intentional effort to destroy Ukrainian scientific infrastructure.
The joint inspection took place against the backdrop of recurrent air raid sirens and ongoing drone strikes across the capital on Sunday morning, which included a repeat strike that damaged the road deck of Kyiv’s North Bridge.
Zelensky commended the German chancellor for maintaining his itinerary and visiting the damaged research complex despite operational security warnings, describing the gesture as an important signal of personal and national solidarity from Berlin.
Merz’s visit follows statements delivered in Berlin on Sept. 29, in which the German leader identified territorial air defense as Ukraine’s “weakest point” ahead of the winter heating season, confirming that Germany is coordinating with EU partners to finalize additional military aid packages ahead of the European Council summit in Brussels on Oct. 15–16.

articles.title: From a drone-downing pastry chef to the company commander who carried a wounded soldier for miles on foot: 10 stories of Ukraine's defenders
articles.body:
From a drone-downing pastry chef to the company commander who carried a wounded soldier for miles on foot: 10 stories of Ukraine's defenders
2026 has been a year of victories great and small for the Ukrainian military, and the whole country has celebrated along with them.
Nazar Daletskyi, a serviceman believed to have been killed three years ago – a funeral had even been held for him – came home alive from captivity.
Vladyslav Polskyi, a company commander in the 475th Assault Regiment (Code 9.2), single-handedly evacuated two wounded soldiers in a civilian pickup truck as Russian drones circled overhead.
The National Guard awarded the title of Hero of Ukraine to a woman for the first time – machine gunner Oleksandra Davydenko.
Ukraine's defence forces in the south reclaimed up to 435 sq km of territory. The 3rd Army Corps stunned the public with the successful Operation Vivaldi counteroffensive in Donetsk Oblast.
Ahead of Defenders' Day, Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life) looks back to 10 of this year's most interesting stories about our defenders. Read them all – you won't regret it!
"Four of them couldn't walk": how a Special Operations Forces company commander evacuated a wounded soldier on foot, then went back for his comrade's body
"Eighteen", a company commander in the Special Operations Forces (SOF), would normally have been expected to coordinate the evacuation from the command post. But when four of his soldiers were no longer able to walk independently after a battle and an encounter with an improvised explosive device, he went into the area himself.
"The guys all had leg wounds. There were two uninjured operators left in the group, plus one medic.
That was when I realised I had to go into the area and get my people out. Nobody could have imagined that out of a group of eight we'd end up with four seriously wounded men and one slightly wounded. Four of them couldn't walk," Eighteen recalls.
It took 15 hours to carry the most seriously wounded soldier, Malyi (Little One), to the medics. The young man had severe injuries to his arm and abdomen and a ruptured liver.
"There were moments when he couldn't take it any more and lost heart. He'd say: 'I don't want to. You don't need to carry me anywhere.' But painkillers make all the difference. Obviously he was in a lot of pain. But he did well and held on," Eighteen says.
As soon as Malyi had been handed over to the doctors, Eighteen went back for the body of his fallen comrade, Sava. The rescue operation took five days in all, and the soldiers covered more than 50 km. All but Sava survived.
This remarkable operation proved once again that even in the era of ground robots, those who operate on their own two feet still have the decisive say in battle.
"I thought about tightening the tourniquets and bleeding to death so I wouldn't suffer": how a badly wounded infantryman hunted by six drones was rescued
Herodotus is a private first class in the 3rd Mountain Assault Battalion of the 128th Separate Mountain Assault Brigade. After 18 months fighting in an assault unit, he miraculously survived being hunted down by six Russian drones.
Herodotus was alone in a wooded area. He had already lost a foot, and as he was being evacuated, a Russian drone destroyed the ground robot and mangled his other leg.
He crawled, hid from FPV drones, and even played "cat and mouse" with one of them around a dugout, moving in such a way as to stay out of the Russians' line of sight. His comrades watched him from a drone throughout, dropping water, painkillers and food and trying to find a way to get him out.
Eventually three soldiers came to retrieve him and carried him for about 2.5 km. Herodotus lost both legs, but he survived. He says that in his darkest moments he remembered that he had promised his family he would return.
"There, look at what I've got now instead of legs. Ta-da! What am I supposed to do now – cry? It's already happened... I'm alive, so everything should be all right. Life can be a complete pile of shit sometimes, but we'll get through it," he says cheerily.
"We accepted that we were going to die": the military anaesthesiologist who volunteered to go to the besieged Azovstal steelworks
In spring 2022, military anaesthetist Oleksandr Demchenko volunteered to fly to the besieged Azovstal steelworks in Mariupol by helicopter. He realised that it could be a one-way trip. He later learned that the helicopter was shot down on its return journey.
At Azovstal, Oleksandr operated on wounded soldiers in an underground hospital, in cold and damp conditions and with a dwindling supply of medicines: even amputations had to be performed under local anaesthetic.
After one airstrike, five floors of the building above the medics collapsed while hundreds of people were inside.
"We all accepted that we were going to die there, because, essentially, there were no other options," Oleksandr recalls. But he was lucky – he made it out of there.
He survived Azovstal, Russian captivity and the Olenivka prison camp. When he returned home, he went back to medicine.
"I returned to the profession because I love it. I genuinely love my work," he admits.
"I'd serve for another six years, as long as my son never sees all this": the nurse who swapped her uniform for combat fatigues
Before joining the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Tamila had worked as a nurse at a district hospital for 15 years. Then she swapped her uniform for combat fatigues, eventually becoming head of the medical station of the 3rd Mountain Assault Battalion of the 128th Separate Mountain Assault Brigade.
In autumn 2022, when the brigade was conducting a counteroffensive in Kherson Oblast, Tamila was constantly going out to evacuate the wounded.
"I provided first aid in the vehicle. I had to stop the bleeding from severed arms and legs, apply tourniquets and administer painkillers. The brigade was carrying out assault operations, and guys were dying both on the battlefield and in front of me," she recalls.
Once, two years later, she happened to meet a soldier whom she had once evacuated with a severed arm. He recognised her first: "You were the one who evacuated me back then. Thank you."
Tamila's first contract ended long ago and she could have left the military, but she stayed. She still goes out on evacuations sometimes, even though her current position does not require her to.
She says she is ready to serve for as long as necessary, as long as her 16-year-old son never has to follow in her footsteps.
"I've been in the Armed Forces of Ukraine for six years now, and they haven't been easy years for me – they've been really hard. Because war is the worst nightmare there can be. But I'm ready to serve for another six years, as long as my son never sees all this, as long as he never has to fight," Tamila admits.
"Several times we had enemy infantry jumping into our trenches": the company commander who spent 343 consecutive days on the front line
Three hundred and forty-three days is enough time to celebrate Christmas, New Year and Easter. But for company commander Oleksii, aka Botanik (Nerd), it was the length of time he spent at positions on the Orikhiv front without rotation.
About half of the soldiers in Botanik's company are over 50, and many suffer from chronic health problems. This makes normal rotations almost impossible, so they have to remain on the line of contact for long periods.
Oleksii's longest combat deployment took place in June 2025. The Russians would attack the Ukrainian positions using infantry fighting vehicles, motorcycles and quad bikes and on foot. When they managed to reach the trenches, machine gunners and drone operators would join the fighting. Evacuation crews collected the wounded under fire.
"I tried to make the fighters' time at the combat positions as bearable as possible. I made sure everyone had a chance to talk to their families every day – that helps a lot," the company commander says.
Oleksii finally left the line of contact on 8 March 2026 and immediately went on leave to celebrate his daughter's 10th birthday. Then it was back to the front line.
"I see my primary role as a commander as minimising personnel losses – ideally ensuring there are none at all," he says.
Pastry chef by day, air defence operator by night: the woman from Bucha shooting down Russian drones
Liudmyla, from Bucha, isn't your typical volunteer. By day she makes exquisite cakes and pastries, but after dark, she protects the skies over Kyiv Oblast.
It all began in 2024, when an acquaintance told Liudmyla about the Bucha Witches – a women's unit of mobile air-defence fire groups established as part of the Bucha Volunteer Formation of the Territorial Community. Liudmyla couldn't stand idly by.
The first time she shot down a Russian Shahed drone, the adrenaline rush was overwhelming. Two years ago she knew almost nothing about the military – now she commands a mobile fire group.
Liudmyla does all this as a volunteer and receives no pay. After a night shift, she returns home, puts down her weapon, and gets back to making cakes.
"It can be difficult at times – exhausting night shifts and winter cold when your hands quite literally freeze to the machine gun – but I love this work. Now I see safety in a completely different way and always silently thank those who protect my sleep when I am off duty," the defender says.
"It was eating away at me that my country was at war while I was here": the Mariupol surgeon who returned from abroad to serve in the army
In March 2022, urological surgeon Dmytro Hetmanov was operating on wounded civilians in besieged Mariupol. The hardest moment came when a father carried in his wounded teenage son. The injury looked minor from the outside, but the boy's heart and blood vessels had been virtually torn apart. The boy could not be saved.
On 16 March, Dmytro decided to try to escape the city with his parents and neighbours. On the way, he saw the bombed-out Drama Theatre still smouldering. It took him a long time to get through the Russian checkpoints.
Two years later, Dmytro was working as a surgeon at the University Hospital in Katowice, Poland. He had a job and his life was gradually getting back on track, but thoughts of his homeland never left him.
"It was eating away at me that my country was at war while I was here. Some of my friends had joined the Armed Forces, while I was sitting here enjoying life," he admitted.
Dmytro resigned and left Poland to return to Ukraine. He completed basic military training, signed a contract and joined the Unmanned Systems Forces. Six months later, he realised that he was missing surgery.
Now Dmytro is serving as a surgeon once again, this time with the 4th Medical Battalion of the 3rd Army Corps. He deals with combat injuries, assists with amputations, and has even tried his hand at neurosurgery for the first time.
Although Dmytro's daughter lives in the United States and rarely sees her dad, he does not regret his decision to join the military.
"They actually listed me among the dead": Azov fighter Web on the Olenivka terrorist attack and rehabilitation after three years in captivity
Dmytro "Web" Tishchenko was listed among the dead after the Russian terrorist attack on the Olenivka prison camp. When he came to, he was lying in a pile of metal and concrete, with a punctured lung and a bleeding arm. He crawled out of the destroyed barracks by himself.
"We asked the Russians for at least some medical supplies, but all they brought us was a bag of army sheets. We tore the fabric into pieces and used them to dress our wounds," the Azov fighter recalls.
When he was finally taken to hospital, one of the Russians was surprised to hear his name called out: "You're alive? I'd already got a body bag ready for you."
Web was only 21 at the time of the terrorist attack on Olenivka. He became a soldier at 18, took part in the defence of Mariupol, was wounded in the leg, made it to Azovstal, and from there he was taken into Russian captivity.
Dmytro spent another two months in hospital after the attack, and then he was moved from one penal colony to another. He had to endure torture, cold, hunger, and being made to stand for hours on end.
Because of a shrapnel wound, his leg became so badly infected that the wound simply opened up. In order to be admitted to hospital and avoid losing the limb, he had to pretend to faint.
Dmytro spent almost three years in captivity. In April 2025, he was suddenly taken out of his cell, given clean clothes and driven to an unknown destination. It was a prisoner swap. Web came home on the eve of Easter – exactly when he had dreamed of returning.
Now Web is undergoing treatment for his injuries and the effects of captivity, while also helping other young soldiers who have returned from Russian captivity.
"Sometimes I forget I'm missing a leg": two Khartiia infantrymen who've returned to service after suffering severe injuries
Assault trooper "Bilyi" stepped on a mine 15-20 metres from his position. He applied a tourniquet himself and waited to be evacuated, but the team that set off to retrieve him was attacked by a drone. When dawn broke, he realised that help might not come in time, so he started crawling on his own.
Bilyi crawled for nearly a whole day before two reconnaissance soldiers found him. By then the tourniquet had been on his leg for about two days. Bilyi had realised immediately after the explosion that his leg would have to be amputated.
"Terry" went through a similar ordeal. During his third combat deployment, he stepped on a petal mine hidden in the grass.
"It didn't hurt, I didn't lose consciousness. I opened my eyes and saw these toes lying around. Only the heel was left. I thought, 'That's it. I've had my run,'" Terry recalls.
It took 25 hours to evacuate him. Along the way, the wounded man and the soldiers carrying him were pursued by Russian FPV drones. One drone missed them, but another exploded near the group, injuring all three of the soldiers who were carrying Terry. Despite their own injuries, however, they managed to carry him to shelter.
Both Terry and Bilyi had their legs amputated. Months of surgery, rehabilitation and prosthetic fittings lay ahead of them. Terry recalls that after receiving a temporary prosthesis, he started walking the very next day and soon left his crutches behind. Bilyi was also quick to learn how to use his prosthesis.
"After they cut off my leg, there were moments when I felt a bit down. Then I'd lie there and think: it's all good. I'm alive, I can eat and get around on my own, go to the toilet and have a shower – I can do all of that," Terry says.
Bilyi is equally convinced: "Life goes on. The main thing is that I'm alive."
Their service didn't end there. Less than a year after being wounded, Bilyi got a call from the company's senior sergeant, who offered him a new position. On 12 May, he rejoined the Khartiia Brigade. Terry later joined him.
The two former infantrymen began learning an entirely different role – they became ISTAR dispatchers at a command and observation post. Instead of going out on combat missions, they now monitor the battlefield through screens, work with reconnaissance personnel and drone operators, and pass on information about targets.
"If I sat at home, what would I do? At least this way I can help out here," Bilyi says.
For now, the Khartiia soldiers have no plans to return to civilian life.
Olena Barsukova
Translated by Tetiana Buchkovska and Anna Kybukevych
Edited by Teresa Pearce

articles.title: Faslane sees British and American subs arrive in one day
articles.body:
Two nuclear-powered attack submarines came in to HM Naval Base Clyde on Friday, a United States Navy Virginia-class boat arriving in the morning and the Royal Navy’s newest hunter-killer, HMS Agamemnon, following later in the day.
Neither navy has identified the American submarine, and visits of this kind are not usually announced in advance for reasons that need little explaining. American submarines call at Faslane regularly to take on stores, change crew members and rest their people, often after periods working in the North Atlantic and the waters north of Scotland.
The Virginia class is the current American attack submarine, displacing around 7,800 tonnes dived and armed with Mk 48 heavyweight torpedoes and Tomahawk cruise missiles, with the later blocks carrying additional vertical launch tubes. The United States Navy has more than twenty in commission and is building more at Groton in Connecticut and Newport News in Virginia, and the type is the same one Australia is due to buy under the first phase of the AUKUS agreement.
Agamemnon’s arrival was her first at the base that will be her home. The sixth Astute-class boat sailed from the BAE Systems yard at Barrow-in-Furness on 25 September for contractor sea trials, thirteen years after her keel was laid, and she completed the passage north over the following week.
Announcing the start of those trials, the First Sea Lord, General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, said: “In an increasingly dangerous world, sea power remains fundamental to keeping our country and people safe. Our submarine fleet is essential to that effort, which is why I am delighted that HMS Agamemnon, the sixth of our Astute-class submarines, has now begun sea trials.
“She embodies the best of British engineering and the professionalism of our submariners and will be one of the most advanced submarines ever operated by the Royal Navy. As we continue to strengthen our warfighting readiness, HMS Agamemnon will play a central role in keeping the United Kingdom safe, contributing to NATO’s collective defence and ensuring we are ready to lead, fight and win.”
The two boats are not far apart in size or in what they are asked to do. Both are built to escort ballistic missile submarines, hunt other submarines and surface ships, put special forces ashore, gather intelligence and strike inland with cruise missiles, and British and American attack boats have operated closely together in the North Atlantic for decades.
That relationship is also being built into the next generation of hardware as the Barrow yard is constructing the four Dreadnought-class ballistic missile submarines using a missile compartment designed jointly with the United States for its own Columbia class, and SSN-AUKUS, the British design that will replace the Astutes, is to be built with American technology and sold to Australia as well. Faslane, meanwhile, is in the middle of a long programme of work under the Clyde Transformation Programme, including three new floating docks that the Treasury confirmed last week will be competed among British yards only.

articles.title: Moscow says it will step up strikes on Ukraine after Kyiv vows to hit Russian oil refineries
articles.body:
Moscow says it will step up strikes on Ukraine after Kyiv vows to hit Russian oil refineries
Russia’s announcement came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country would “have to respond in any way we can” to Russian attacks.
Firefighters and medics are evacuating an injured person after a projectile hit a residential building in the city center on September 28, 2026 in Kyiv. | Alex Babenko/Getty Images
Russia will intensify its attacks on military and industrial facilities in Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine, Moscow announced Sunday.
Writing on Telegram, Russia’s Defense Ministry said, “Strikes by the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation against military and military-industrial facilities, as well as related infrastructure in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine, will be intensified.”
The threat came following Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s statement that Kyiv would respond to Russian attacks by targeting the country’s oil refineries.
Advertisement
“The people of Ukraine should blame only the head of the Kyiv regime for this,” the Russian Defense Ministry stated, referring to the Ukrainian president. “It is Zelenskyy who bears full personal and political responsibility for this.”
In an interview with Reuters, Zelenskyy said Saturday that Ukrainian forces “have to respond in any way we can” to Russian attacks, which are increasingly targeting bridges across the Dnipro River in the capital.
“With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners: what gives money to them for this war,” he added, while saying Ukraine would not retaliate by deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure.
The Russian government also accused Kyiv of attempts “to disrupt voting in the elections … through terrorist strikes on civilian targets on Russian territory.” President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party largely dominated the results of Russia’s legislative elections, held from Sept. 18 to 20.
Russia’s threat to intensify strikes on Ukraine came on the same day as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a surprise one-day visit to Kyiv in a show of support to Ukraine.
During Merz’s visit, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that Russia had struck the roadway of the North Bridge in the city. On Saturday, Russia’s foreign ministry issued a warning against foreign visitors and diplomats and urged them to leave Kyiv.
Merz is expected to renew Germany’s support for Ukraine with a new military aid package worth around €1 billion, in addition to generators, substations and repair kits worth €350 million to strengthen the Ukrainian power grid under attack.
Zelenskyy and Merz visited Kyiv’s National Academy of Sciences, which was recently hit by Russian drones in an attack that killed two people and injured seven others and “was deliberate,” the Ukrainian president said on social media.

articles.title: Russia’s drones keep targeting the bridges Kyiv can’t easily replace—now the Northern crossing is cratered
articles.body:
Russia struck Kyiv's Northern Bridge with a drone again on 4 October, the second hit on the crossing in two days, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. The attack damaged a heating main and rerouted public transport, as overnight and morning strikes also hit Kyiv Oblast, Dnipro, and Sumy, where one person was killed.
Russia's air attacks on Ukrainian cities are daily, and in recent days they have hit a Kyiv school sheltering children and turned supermarkets into targets. Strikes on the crossings between the capital's two banks add another layer: they disrupt how millions of people move through the city every day.
A crater on the Northern Bridge, no hot water across the river
The drone hit the bridge's roadway, and videos posted by local channels showed a crater, Liga reported. The strike also damaged a heating main, cutting hot water in Kyiv's Desnianskyi district on the left bank, Klitschko wrote. Repair crews are working to restore it, he added.
Kyiv's transport operator Kyivpastrans cut trolleybus routes short of the river. Routes 29, 30, 31, and 47 now run from the left bank only to Darnytsia Square, and routes 29, 30, and 31 run from the right bank only to Pochaina metro station. Buses 21, 73, 101, and 114 run only to Darnytsia Square because the bridge is closed to traffic.
Russia first hit the Northern Bridge on 3 October, damaging its roadway and trolleybus lines. Two people were injured, and one of them was hospitalized, Klitschko said. A day earlier, repeated drone strikes hit the Southern Bridge and forced its closure. Overnight on 4 October, drone debris also fell on two locations in Kyiv's Dniprovskyi district, Klitschko reported.
Russia adds new weapon to its jet-powered drones, even more dangerous: 40-kilogram charge made to sever high-voltage pylons and iron bridges
Ukraine's government has already begun work on earth dams and pontoon crossings in case the city's Dnipro bridges are knocked out, Restoration Minister Mykola Kalashnyk told Suspilne.
The strike came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Kyiv. Ukraine and Germany would reach important agreements during the visit, Zelenskyy said. This week alone, Russia launched more than 1,900 attack drones, 1,700 guided bombs, and 25 missiles at Ukraine, more than 800 of the drones jet-powered, he added.
135 drones overnight
Russia launched 135 attack drones at Ukraine overnight, 52 of them jet-powered Shaheds, Ukraine's Air Force reported. By 08:30, air defenses had downed or suppressed 123 drones and two Banderol or Dan-T missiles. Strikes hit five locations, and debris fell on five more.
In Kyiv Oblast, Russian drones damaged six detached houses, a car, a church, a primary school, a café, and a medical facility in Boryspil Raion, the Kyiv Oblast Military Administration said. No one was killed or injured.
Dnipro and Sumy
Russia attacked a communications company's building in central Dnipro, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha reported.
"The whole street there is covered in broken glass, debris, and branches," Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov wrote, adding that nearby homes and schools escaped damage.
In Sumy, Russian drones struck an ordinary medical supplies warehouse and killed one person, Zelenskyy said. Strikes across the city injured seven people, two of them seriously, the Sumy city council said. The attack also damaged gas networks and left 70 apartments without gas.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits Russian Buk-M3, Drone Hub, and Bryansk EW Station
articles.body:
Ukrainian Defense Forces struck a Russian Buk-M3 surface-to-air missile system, a drone storage and launch site, and an electronic warfare station inside Russia during operations on Saturday, Oct. 3, and early Sunday morning, Oct. 4.
According to a military dispatch published by the General Staff, precision strikes engaged high-value Russian air defense, unmanned aviation, and electronic countermeasure assets across three operational directions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In the southern Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian fire engaged a modernized Russian Buk-M3 medium-range surface-to-air missile system deployed near the settlement of Kuroshany. The Buk-M3 represents one of Moscow’s frontline mobile air defense assets, engineered to intercept cruise missiles, tactical ballistic ordnance, and combat aircraft.
In the Donetsk region, Ukrainian units delivered a precision strike against a Russian military facility near occupied Donetsk used for the storage, technical preparation, and launching of strike unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
“Storage, preparation, and launch sites of strike UAVs of the Russian aggressors are among the priority targets,” the General Staff emphasized.
“The systematic destruction of such targets is aimed at reducing the Russian Federation’s capabilities to use strike drones against Ukraine’s civilian population.”
Across the international frontier, Ukrainian forces struck an active Russian electronic warfare (EW) station deployed near the municipal core of Klimovo in Russia’s Bryansk region, suppressing Russian tactical jamming networks operating adjacent to the northern border.
Russian Drone Strikes in Kherson and Chernihiv Injure 6
Ukrainian precision units also targeted Russian military telecommunications hubs deployed across three contested sectors in the Donetsk region, striking signal installations near the town of Hirnyk, the railway hub of Yasynuvata, and occupied Donetsk.
Concurrently in the occupied sector of the Luhansk region, Ukrainian long-range strikes hit military equipment repair and maintenance installations located in the vicinity of Vesela Tarasivka and the industrial center of Lysychansk.
Sustained campaign against rear logistics and air defense
The overnight operations mark the latest phase of a systematic Ukrainian campaign targeting Russian air defenses, drone infrastructure, and logistical chokepoints across occupied territories and adjacent Russian border regions.
On Oct. 2 and Oct. 3, Ukrainian forces conducted precision strikes against another drone preparation facility near Donetsk alongside a tactical military crossing over the Mokri Yaly River near Novoocheretuvate, severing a key supply conduit for Russian units in the southern Donetsk sector.
Across the border in Russia’s Belgorod region, Ukrainian strikes destroyed a Russian command post near Novaya Tavolzhanka and hit an equipment warehouse in Voznesenovka, while follow-on fire damaged a vehicle repair facility near Hromivka in occupied Kherson region.
Degrading Russian air surveillance and air defense batteries remains a central priority for Ukrainian long-range strike units.
In late September, Ukrainian forces conducted targeted strikes against two Russian mobile radar complexes in occupied Zaporizhzhia region, damaging an advanced 35N6 Kasta low-altitude detection radar near Chekhohrad and a Soviet-designed P-18 early-warning radar operating near Akymivka.

articles.title: Zelensky Vows Proportional Retaliation for Russian Bridge Strikes
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned on Sunday, Oct. 4, that Ukraine has responded and will continue to deliver proportional retaliatory strikes against Russian infrastructure.
Speaking during a joint press briefing with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv, Zelensky questioned the strategic calculations behind Moscow’s intensifying strikes on civilian utilities, warning that critical Russian facilities – including telecommunications backbones in Moscow – remain vulnerable to reciprocal Ukrainian deep strikes.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Honestly, I am not surprised by such an approach to war – hatred toward Ukraine from Russia. But I am surprised by this specific approach, because they struck our warehouses: Nova Poshta, Ukrposhta, and others. They struck, and we gave them a worthy response against Wildberries,” Zelensky told reporters.
“Now they are striking bridges. Do they really think we will not respond?”
Symmetrical response
Zelensky highlighted that Russian forces have expanded strikes against Ukrainian civilian life-support systems, deliberately directing loitering munitions and ballistic missiles against corporate data centers and mobile telecommunications installations.
The president warned that such actions establish a precedent for reciprocal targeting, reminding Moscow that its own infrastructure operates under identical vulnerabilities.
“Does [Russian President Vladimir] Putin not realize that mobile communications are used not only in Kyiv, in Ukraine? They are used in Moscow as well,” Zelensky said.
Ukraine to Deploy Small Missiles, Turrets Against Jet Drones, Zelensky Says
“I am simply, honestly, surprised by this beastly desire to escalate every day. That is, he relies on continuous escalation; he wants this very much. This is an answer to all those who believe that one just needs to simply ask Putin and he will definitely end the war. It simply will not work.”
Zelensky emphasized that Moscow’s conduct demonstrates that the Russian leadership does not seek diplomatic off-ramps, but instead uses aerial barrages to compel political concessions through intimidation ahead of the winter heating season.
Consecutive strikes on Kyiv bridges
The president’s warning follows two consecutive days of Russian strikes targeting Kyiv’s North Bridge, compounding structural strain across the capital’s metropolitan transport network.
Earlier on Sunday morning, Russian munitions struck the road deck of the North Bridge for the second time in 24 hours, blasting a crater into the asphalt roadway spanning the Dnipro River.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that emergency services and transit engineers deployed immediately to assess structural integrity, confirming that two civilians sustained injuries in the Sunday attack, with one hospitalized and a second treated on-site.
The Sunday bombardment followed a direct hit on Saturday morning, Oct. 3, when a Russian turbojet loitering munition struck the North Bridge, damaging the road surface and severing overhead electrical contact wires powering municipal trolleybuses.
The consecutive hits on the North Bridge follow the complete closure of the capital’s South Bridge to vehicular traffic on Friday after repeated drone impacts damaged roadway spans, bridge piers, and structural barriers shielding the Green Line metro crossing.

articles.title: Putin Hugged the Man Behind Russia’s Jet-Powered Shahed Program—OSINT Identifies Him
articles.body:

Putin Hugged the Man Behind Russia’s Jet-Powered Shahed Program—OSINT Identifies Him
Ukrainian OSINT researchers have identified a senior executive at Russia’s Alabuga Special Economic Zone as the man who presented the new jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 attack drones to Vladimir Putin during Russia’s Center-2026 military exercises.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Evocation.info on October 3, the man seen briefing Putin was Ildar Tazutdinov, a senior executive at Alabuga, the Russian industrial complex involved in producing Iranian-designed Shahed-type attack drones.
The identification followed the publication of footage from the Chebarkulsky training ground in Russia’s Chelyabinsk region, where Putin inspected new Russian weapons on October 2.
In the video, Tazutdinov described the capabilities of the Geran-4 and Geran-5 before concluding: “We are ready to continue striking the enemy in the same way. That concludes my report!” Putin then shook his hand and embraced him, according to footage analyzed by Evocation.info.
Interfax reported on October 2 that Putin had been shown both jet-powered Geran variants during his visit to the training ground. According to the presentation, the Geran-4 uses a jet engine allowing it to reach approximately 350 km/h, carry a 50-kilogram warhead, and operate at a range of around 750 to 800 kilometers.
The larger Geran-5 was described as having a speed of up to 450 km/h, a 90-kilogram warhead, and a maximum range of roughly 900 kilometers. Evocation.info identified Tazutdinov as one of the executives connected to Alabuga’s drone program.
His involvement with the facility has previously been documented by the US government. In February 2024, the US Treasury Department sanctioned Ildar Rashitovich Tazutdinov, identifying him at the time as Alabuga’s deputy director general of corporate affairs.
Treasury said he had been involved in the shipment and import of materials and disassembled Iranian UAVs to Russia in connection with drone production at Alabuga.
The US Treasury said Alabuga officials were involved in producing Iranian-designed UAVs, including the Shahed-136 and its Russian Geran-2 variant, as well as importing components from Iran for the program.
The Geran-4 and Geran-5 represent newer jet-powered additions to Russia’s expanding family of long-range attack drones. Their higher speeds make interception more difficult than with earlier propeller-driven Shahed-type UAVs, prompting Ukraine to develop and deploy faster drone interceptors designed specifically to engage such targets.
Earlier, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence identified 20 pieces of foreign-made industrial equipment being used at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone to produce various Geran drone modifications, including machinery from China, Germany, Japan, Switzerland, and Iran.

articles.title: Germany to Provide Ukraine with €1 Billion in Military Aid
articles.body:
Germany will provide Ukraine with €1 billion in military aid, along with an additional €350 million to help repair energy infrastructure.
Reuters reported the news.
According to German government officials, Chancellor Friedrich Merz is expected to announce the new support package during his visit to Kyiv on October 4. Germany and Ukraine are also expected to finalize an agreement on jointly producing various types of drones.
“I came to Kyiv today because Ukraine needs all the support we can give in the coming weeks. If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn against us,” Merz said, noting that Russian forces are bombing cities, residential buildings, and heating infrastructure.
The German chancellor is accompanied by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and a business delegation that includes executives from energy and defense companies, including Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defence, and Quantum Systems.
Merz is also expected to push for progress on reforms that Ukraine’s EU partners have called for, particularly efforts to combat corruption.
On Wednesday, following a phone call with Merz, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported that Ukraine and Germany would soon finalize an agreement on the production of drones, missiles, and related software.
A key priority will be the rapid production of drones designed to intercept Russian attack drones. The agreement will also cover the joint development and production of weapons with a range of more than 1,000 km, which Ukraine could use to strike targets deep inside Russian territory.
Overall, Germany has allocated a record €11.5 billion in aid to Ukraine for 2026. However, not all of this funding will go directly toward supporting Ukraine. For example, around €1.8 billion is planned to replenish Bundeswehr stocks after Germany transfers weapons to Ukraine. Another €688 million will be contributed to the European Peace Facility, which primarily reimburses EU countries for the cost of military aid they provide to Ukraine.
Germany’s Defense Ministry has received around €8.4 billion specifically for direct military assistance to Ukraine. An additional €515 million has been allocated to the Enable & Enhance Initiative Ukraine, which funds long-term contracts to produce weapons for Ukraine, supports the logistics of military aid, and finances repair hubs outside Ukraine.
The remaining funds are earmarked for non-lethal assistance, including demining and medical support, as well as treatment for wounded Ukrainian service members in Germany.
In 2027, according to the preliminary draft budget, the German government plans to increase funding for military assistance to Ukraine to a record €11.6 billion. Although the overall funding will formally increase by only €65 million, the new budget allocates €664 million less for replenishing Germany’s military stocks than in 2026. As a result, the share of direct assistance provided to Ukraine will increase significantly.

articles.title: Ex-PM says Russia’s Putin cannot admit ‘mistake’ over Ukraine war
articles.body:
Ex-PM says Russia’s Putin cannot admit ‘mistake’ over Ukraine war
- Former Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Kasyanov said Putin realises invading Ukraine was a mistake but refuses to admit it and continues the war, confident of winning a war of attrition.
- Kasyanov warned of a harsh winter for Ukraine and urged the West to unite, apply psychological pressure on the Kremlin, and supply Patriot missile systems to defend against Russian strikes.
- Despite fear and tension in Russia's ruling class and society, Kasyanov sees no revolt yet but warns that large military mobilisations could spark protests; he described Putin as a calculating provocateur seeking respect, not open war with Europe.
AI generated
PARIS - Despite growing economic trouble and rising unease among ordinary Russians and the elite, President Vladimir Putin is not ready to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, his former prime minister said on Oct 3.
Speaking to AFP in an interview, Mikhail Kasyanov, Russia’s prime minister from 2000 to 2004, said he believed his former boss understood he had made a mistake by invading Ukraine in 2022 but would persist with the course he had set.
“He made a mistake that he cannot bring himself to admit,” Kasyanov, 68, said in Paris.
“He believed the reports from his security services that Ukraine was weak.”
The former prime minister said he was not convinced the war would end in 2027, adding that Putin was buoyed by high oil prices resulting from the US-Iran conflict and by disagreements between the United States and Europe over how to deal with the Kremlin on Ukraine.
“Putin is, of course, rubbing his hands with glee,” Kasyanov said.
“He clearly believes he can continue the war without making any concessions. And he is convinced that he is winning a war of attrition against Ukraine.”
He warned that the coming winter could be particularly brutal for Ukraine, urging Western countries to apply “psychological pressure on the Kremlin” by closing ranks, and urgently supply Kyiv with Patriot missile interceptors to protect skies from intensifying Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure.
Putin, a former KGB agent who turns 74 on Oct 7, has insisted that millions of Russians support Moscow’s war. In September, his ruling party won a record supermajority in elections that critics said were tightly controlled, with Putin portraying the vote as a show of support for the hostilities.
‘Sense of fatalism’
Kasyanov, who left Russia in 2022, lives in exile in Riga. In 2023, Moscow designated him a “foreign agent”, a term reminiscent of the Soviet-era label “enemy of the people”.
The Kremlin critic said he remained in contact with some members of Russia’s ruling elite.
“Fear reigns there – I am talking about the ruling class.
“Everyone wants the war to end. An overwhelming majority does,” he said.
“The difference lies in what kind of ending people want: some want the war to end in victory, some want it to end in Putin’s defeat, and others simply want it to stop, regardless of the outcome.”
Among ordinary Russians, Kasyanov said he saw “no grounds for a revolt”, despite mounting war casualties and rising food prices.
“Russians have lived with high inflation for the past 30 years,” he said. “They have grown accustomed to putting up with it.”
But a new wave of large-scale military mobilisations could trigger street protests, he added.
Speaking on the sidelines of a conference organised by the Paris-based association Russie-Libertes for anti-Putin exiles, Kasyanov said Russia had become “practically totalitarian” over the past few years.
“There is a sense of fatalism, hostility toward one another, and serious tension in society,” he said. “People are retreating into their own families, while negative feelings towards one another grow.”
After being dismissed by Putin, Kasyanov joined the opposition and became one of the Kremlin’s most vocal critics. Like many others, the start and duration of the war were a shock for him. Kasyanov told AFP in 2022 that the war could last about two years.
‘Calculating cynic’
After the Kremlin chief on Oct 1 said Russia would consider using “all types of weapons” if its exclave of Kaliningrad were attacked, Kasyanov said Western countries should not be intimidated by Putin’s sabre-rattling.
“The West’s and Europeans’ biggest mistake is that they are too afraid of Putin. He is not as strong as he appears,” Kasyanov told a packed audience in Paris.
“Putin fears the nuclear button more than many Europeans do.”
Kasyanov suggested that Putin wants foreigners to believe that “he is a psychopath” when in reality he is simply a “highly calculating cynic”.
“And he is raising the stakes in the game.”
Kasyanov said that with an increase in “hybrid attacks” Putin was provoking the West into taking measures that he could then exploit.
“He is a provocateur,” he added. “The only modus operandi he understands is the one he learned at the KGB academy. He told me that himself.”
But, Kasyanov said, he did not believe Putin was preparing for open war with Europe.
“What Putin wants is respect. He wants to force all of Europe to give it to him.” AFP

articles.title: Drones Strike Russian Khanskaya Air Base in Adygea
articles.body:
Ukrainian strike drones targeted the Khanskaya military airfield near the city of Maykop in Russia’s North Caucasus Republic of Adygea early Sunday morning, Oct. 4, sparking a large fire across the facility, open-source monitoring channels and satellite thermal tracking indicated.
Local residents reported that the drone assault began shortly after 1:00 a.m. local time and continued through the early morning hours, with regional monitoring channels reporting repeated drone passages and active air defense fire around Maykop.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Geolocation footage published on social media confirmed an active fire at the military airfield, situated approximately six kilometers outside Maykop and roughly 500 kilometers from Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Thermal anomalies at the airfield were independently corroborated by NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which detected high-temperature fire signatures across the operational perimeter of the air base.
The airfield serves as the home station for the Russian Aerospace Forces’ 272nd Training Aviation Base, formed after the disbandment of the 761st Training Aviation Regiment in 2009.
Beyond its training designation, Russian forces actively utilize the installation as an operational logistics, staging, and refueling facility to support tactical aviation units executing missile and glide bomb strikes against Ukrainian territory.
Vilnius Airport Closes as NATO Jets Scramble Over Suspected Drone
Satellite imagery of the airfield recorded in recent months showed multiple combat and support aircraft deployed at the facility, including Su-24 strike aircraft, Su-30, Su-34, and Su-35S multi-role fighters, L-39 jet trainers, Mi-8 utility helicopters, and military transport aircraft.
The installation was previously targeted by Ukrainian deep-strike operations in December.
Deep-strike campaign against Russian air and drone assets
The overnight strike against Khanskaya marks the second consecutive long-range engagement targeting major Russian aviation and launch infrastructure within a 24-hour window.
Early Saturday morning, Oct. 3, Ukrainian strike drones hit the Tsymbulovo droneport in Russia’s western Oryol region, sparking multiple fires across storage and launch facilities identified by open-source intelligence and NASA thermal sensors.
The Oryol complex functions as Moscow’s primary launch hub for high-speed, turbojet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 loitering munitions directed against Kyiv.
Satellite monitoring throughout September documented rapid construction at the Tsymbulovo base, including eight reinforced domed shelters, new paved launch ramps, and 14 hangars, alongside efforts to convert surface-level storage shelters into underground bunkers to withstand drone strikes.

articles.title: Three Banderol Missiles and Two UAVs Entered Moldova and Exploded: Damage Reported
articles.body:
On the morning of October 3, Banderol missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles entered Moldova and subsequently exploded near a number of settlements in several districts.
This was reported by Moldovan President Maia Sandu.
“Five Russian air attack vehicles, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated our airspace and exploded on our territory,” she wrote on social media platform X.
Moldova’s national airspace monitoring system recorded the passage of five unmanned aerial vehicles between 7:45 a.m. and 8:00 a.m.
Subsequently, Moldovan Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatîi reported that there were three missiles and two drones, according to Newsmaker.
The Ministry of Defense of Moldova clarified that the incursion of Banderol missiles and UAVs occurred amid Russia’s massive strikes on Ukraine.
According to monitoring system data, explosions were heard near the towns of Krokmaz, Ștefan Vodă, Delacău, Puhăceni, Anenii Noi, Bozieni, and Hîncești, as well as near Dubovka, Konstantinovka, and Căușeni. Police officers and National Army soldiers were dispatched to the scene to investigate the incident.
The police added that reports of explosion sounds had been coming in since the morning from residents of the Kaushan, Ștefan Vodă, Anenii Noi, and Hîncești districts. On the outskirts of Căușeni, law enforcement officers discovered debris from a drone, from which smoke was rising.
Debris from drones was also found near Dubrovka in the Hîncești district, between the villages of Delacău and Puhăceni.
In Krokmaz, a drone crashed into a vineyard, causing dry vegetation to catch fire, and shattered the windows of a nearby house.
According to police, there were no casualties as a result of the incidents. Law enforcement officials are currently documenting all cases and determining the circumstances of the events.
The missile was developed by the Russian company Kronstadt. Its maximum speed is 620–650 km/h, and its cruising speed is 520–560 km/h. Banderol is equipped with an OFBCh-150 high-explosive fragmentation warhead with a total mass of 114.3 kg, of which 49.5 kg is explosive material.

articles.title: Iran FM says war has no military solution, Trump mulls strikes
articles.body:
Good morning and welcome to The New Arab's live coverage of the war in the region. Here are the top stories:
In Yemen, the Houthis have reportedly cut the vital Aden-Taiz road, operationally encircling the city, according to sources speaking with AFP.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said that there is no military solution to the conflict, warning: "If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force."
US President Donald Trump is pondering an escalation of the war and is expected to decide on a move soon, saying, "the only question is, it'll either be the easy way or the hard way."
Now, onto our live coverage:
Yemen leader announces military operations against Houthis
The leader of Yemen's Saudi-backed government announced the beginning of a major military operation against the Iran-backed Houthis on Sunday, aimed at seizing the territory under their control.
Regional and Western officials had previously told Reuters that Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies were planning to launch an assault on the Houthis, with the Saudis leading aerial combat and Yemeni forces fighting on the ground.
"Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory," Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address.
Yemen's Houthis on Sunday cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden -- the interim capital of the internationally recognised government -- according to four security sources.
"We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station," a police source in the area told AFP.
Three sources with the Yemeni military confirmed Houthi control over the area and supply route, with the group effectively encircling Taiz city.
An Israeli airstrike has killed a Palestinian in the city of Khan Younis in Gaza, according to Palestinian news agency Wafa, which added that another person was seriously injured in the strike.
Iranian army says will increase the range of its missiles
Iran will upgrade the range of its missiles following the war with the US as American forces are now positioned as much as 1,000 km (621 miles) away from the Iranian coast, Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia told Fars news on Sunday.
"During this war, we concluded that we absolutely must increase the range of our missiles, and we have now moved in that direction," he said.
How Israel is weaponising archaeology to annex the West Bank
In late September, Israeli troops raided the Tulkarem area and posted notices on the Banat Yaqub shrine in Irtah, south of the city.
The two-story building, with its Roman-era lower floor and Mamluk-era prayer room above, would now be under the control of the Israel Antiquities Authority.
The shrine and its grounds cover no more than 300 square meters, according to Suhail Salman of the Popular Campaign Against the Wall and Settlements, a Palestinian grassroots group, yet the notices claimed more than 10 dunams (about 2.5 acres) of surrounding land, taking in dozens of inhabited homes.
The shrine is the latest site in a campaign that uses heritage protection to seize land and override Palestinian jurisdiction, rights groups and archaeologists say.
From Silwan in East Jerusalem to Shiloh, Tel Rumeida in Hebron, and Sebastia near Nablus, excavations have arrived alongside roads, visitor centres, and restrictions on access that turn Palestinian land into settler-run tourist sites.
Iraq's state-owned Oil Tanker Company transported 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude aboard a very large crude carrier (VLCC) through the Strait of Hormuz, in what its director general described on Saturday as the company's first such operation in decades.
The announcement means the company is transporting the crude through the strait rather than delivering it at the port of Basra, giving state oil marketer SOMO greater flexibility in how and where it sells the crude.
The company's director general, Ali Qais Abdul Jabbar, said in a statement that the move could allow SOMO to take advantage of better sales and pricing opportunities.
Iraq's Oil Tanker Company is also working to buy and own specialised crude oil tankers to expand its fleet and strengthen its ability to compete with regional shipping companies, he added.
Iraq has previously secured Iranian permission for Iraqi oil tankers to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has effectively closed during its conflict with the US.
Tanker hit by unknown projectile in Strait of Hormuz
A tanker was hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, causing damage to its engine room, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said on Sunday, without specifying when the incident occurred.
The crew was safe and no environmental impact had been reported at the time the notice was issued, UKMTO added.

"If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force," Araghchi said at a gathering of foreign ambassadors. "There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions."
The US aircraft carrier George H.W. Bush arrived in Thailand's resort island of Phuket on Sunday with about 4,800 personnel aboard for a rest-and-recreation break after six months supporting US operations in the Middle East.
For the last six months, the Nimitz-class aircraft carrier and its strike group supported Operation Epic Fury and the US naval blockade in the US Central Command area of responsibility to secure maritime security and stability in the Middle East, according to the US Navy.
Phuket is the first port call for the George H.W. Bush Carrier Strike Group since departing Norfolk, Virginia, and Mayport, Florida, in March, the US Navy said in a statement.
Iran says Hormuz will not reopen until conditions met
The Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions set out in a June interim agreement with the US are met, Nournews reported Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf as saying on Sunday, a few days after Tehran received Washington's reply to its diplomatic proposal.
“The Americans, who say something different in the media, have recently put forward proposals through a mediator. But they must understand that the period of dragging out the process and dictating one-sided demands is over," Ghalibaf was quoted as saying.
"The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, are met."

articles.title: Houthis blame Saudi air strikes as loud blasts rock Yemen's capital Sanaa
articles.body:
Houthis claim strike on oil facilty near Riyadh, accuse Saudi forces of pounding Yemen's capital
Houthi rebels accused Saudi forces of launching 26 strikes on Sanaa on Saturday after loud explosions rocked the Yemeni capital. The Iran-backed group said it struck an oil facility south of Riyadh, where flames and a large plume of smoke were seen rising from a plant belonging to oil giant Aramco.
Yemen's Houthis claimed an attack on an oil facility near the Saudi capital on Saturday, where an AFP journalist saw flames and smoke, and accused the Gulf kingdom of striking Sanaa dozens of times.
The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen's Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandab strait in a lightning offensive last month.
Houthi-affiliated channel Al-Masirah TV reported that "Saudi enemy aircraft" hit Sanaa with 26 strikes, after earlier reporting "Saudi aggression" against the Yemeni capital, without providing details on the targets or casualties.
Two correspondents in Sanaa reported hearing loud explosions and seeing warplanes firing missiles at the city.
In neighbouring Saudi Arabia, flames and smoke were seen rising on Saturday afternoon from an Aramco facility south of Riyadh, an AFP journalist said.
While the Saudi authorities are yet to comment, late on Saturday, the Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted an oil facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones, adding that they sparked fires at the targeted sites.
The AFP journalist reported seeing firefighters attempting to extinguish a blaze at Aramco's Riyadh refinery, located south of the capital, while ambulances and police vehicles were stationed near the facility.
The Houthis' Al-Masirah channel earlier on Saturday also reported missile strikes on the telecommunications network in Yemen's northwestern governorate of Saada, one of the group's strongholds.
Read moreSaudi-led coalition accuses Houthis of striking Medina power station
It comes after the Houthis said that Saudi Arabia bombed the Yemeni capital itself on Thursday night for the first time since renewed fighting broke out between the two sides in July.
Hunger warning
After several years of calm, Yemen was plunged back into civil war that month, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of northwest Yemen including Sanaa, against Yemen's internationally recognised government.
The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of the country's south and east -- a region that is larger but much less populated.
Hostilities were reignited after four years of a fragile truce when Iran sent a plane to Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation.
The flight did not seek authorisation from Saudi Arabia, contravening a practice in place for a decade.
Riyadh retaliated with strikes on Sanaa airport, and in response the Houthis attacked Saudi territory for the first time since 2022.
Since then, fighting has intensified with the Houthis launching a lightning offensive in which they seized control of coastal regions along the Bab al-Mandab strait.
Read moreYemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels seize strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha
They have also struck multiple Saudi targets including oil infrastructure and the capital Riyadh while also announcing a naval blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea.
The renewed fighting has worsened the already appalling humanitarian conditions in Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, with the World Food Programme warning on Friday that three-quarters of the population was unable to meet its basic food needs.
Battle for Taiz
Fighting in recent days has centred on Taiz, where dozens of combatants were reported killed on Friday by sources on both sides.
The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed while government sources told AFP that 26 troops had died.
The battle for Taiz is taking place on several fronts, including highlands overlooking coastal areas recently seized by the Houthis.
While the Houthis have conquered swathes of territory, they have yet to take control of Taiz city, which is Yemen's third-largest after Sanaa and Aden.
The Houthis also on Friday said Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the past 24 hours.
Saudi authorities meanwhile reported a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemen border.
Riyadh has reportedly requested help from the United States, a call so far rebuffed by US President Donald Trump.
On Saturday US media outlet Axios reported that top cabinet members in the Trump administration met the day before to discuss Yemen as well as the Iran conflict, citing three US officials.
The meeting was not officially announced.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
