articles.title: Tory conference 2026: What POLITICO reporters are watching for
articles.body:
BIRMINGHAM, England — Britain’s largest opposition party wants to show it’s still on the electoral pitch during an annual gathering that kicks off Sunday.
Despite Conservative Leader Kemi Badenoch consolidating her position and seeing improved personal ratings, the party is still far from its government heyday, and faces an ongoing challenge on the right from Nigel Farage’s populist Reform UK.
Here’s what POLITICO’s team of reporters will be watching for as the Conservatives gather in Birmingham.
Advertisement
U.K. Political Editor Dan Bloom
My biggest question for Badenoch’s speech at 11 a.m. Wednesday will be: can she end Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s honeymoon?
Since July, Labour has jumped to 26% in the polls while the Tories lag behind Reform on 19%. There will simply be fewer lobbyists and hangers-on than at Labour’s jamboree.
Badenoch will spend this week arguing that Burnham, with his crusade against “40 years of neoliberalism,” has ushered in the kind of classic left-right ideological fight that she relishes. Expect her to bang on about cutting welfare to fund defense — two weak points for Labour. And the self-described “badass Kemi” plans to be more abrasive than Burnham, who went out of his way not to attack anyone in his speech.
I reckon two things will decide if she can cut through: her personal brand, and how far she can differentiate the Tories from Labour and Reform (plus, well, her own party from 2024). She will try to paint the Tories as the party of fiscal responsibility but that’s a crowded marketplace. It’s worked for the Conservatives in the past but we aren’t in two-party politics anymore — though admittedly, the five-party split has become less dramatic since the summer.
There will be economic policy announcements but perhaps not on the scale of last year’s pledge to scrap stamp duty. Badenoch has talked about getting rid of inheritance tax but aides appear to be suggesting an announcement isn’t ready.
I can’t wait to see the peacocking by would-be candidates for a general election. Tory aides are shouting from the hills that they are on a “war footing” and candidate selection is ramping up. Some of the high-profile Tories who were rejected for being too centrist are swerving this year’s conference, but former West Midlands Mayor Andy Street will be prominent on the fringe. Critics complain that Badenoch has bulldozed the transepts off her party’s ideological church.
Advertisement
And, of course, I’d ask questions about a coalition. There is no love lost between the Tories and Reform but all recent polls suggest they would have to team up to have any chance of running a government. Will she pull any punches against Farage … or Restore Britain chief Rupert Lowe, whose vote-splitting might help her in the end?
Senior Foreign and Defense Correspondent Esther Webber
I’ll be really interested to see how the party is positioning itself against what we know so far about Ed Miliband’s agenda as foreign secretary — so whether there’s any dissent over new sanctions introduced by Labour on Israeli E1 settlements.
Miliband has just begun to signal a potentially more conciliatory approach to China as an alternative locus of power and investment versus the U.S., so I’ll be looking at whether the Conservatives think this is a weak point where they can redouble attacks on Labour.
There’s also the question of artificial intelligence regulation and which camp the Tories are situating themselves in. Will they agree with the government on the need for a globally coordinated effort, or back U.S. President Donald Trump’s zero-regulation stance?
Finally, here’s a side plot: Are there any signs that former Home Secretary Priti Patel, traditionally a conference fan favorite, is actually doing anything in her new role in coordinating cooperation between the Tories and other parties internationally?
London Influence Reporter John Johnston
With little detail so far about Burnham’s plans for business, and many corporate execs pondering if Farage’s Reform has hit its peak, this Tory conference will be a vital opportunity for the party to try and show it is building back towards being a credible alternative.
Advertisement
Since the 2024 general election, many businesses and lobbying firms have sent only a skeleton staff to Tory conference. But I’ve heard that extra corporate passes and tickets to the standalone Business Day have been snapped up in the last few months. So, attendance may be healthier — even if most still won’t be splashing out on panel events or exhibition stands.
Business leaders remain skeptical about the prospect of an early general election. But as the official opposition, the Conservatives have the potential to help industry shine a spotlight on concerns and push issues up the political agenda if one comes. At last year’s conference, many public affairs pros felt the Tories lacked the ideas, unity and leadership to do that. My focus this year will be figuring out if that assessment has shifted.
Energy Reporter Abby Wallace
The Conservatives have come a long way from the party that, in government, enshrined net-zero targets in law. Badenoch has been clear about the direction she wants to take the party in: ditching legally-binding climate targets and drilling for more oil and gas in the North Sea.
The party’s leader has even suggested that former colleagues who still support the target will not be welcome back on the Tory benches. I’ll be looking out for whether that U-turn at the top has fully filtered through the party.
While energy bills have surged on the back of war in Iran, the party has been pressing Labour ministers to prioritize cutting costs in the system. For the Conservatives, that means ditching some support for renewables and a bigger role for gas and nuclear in the future. I’ll be keeping an ear on whether there is any pressure from the opposition for ministers to intervene ahead of what will be a difficult winter of price rises too.
The future of the North Sea, including looming decisions on Rosebank and Jackdaw, will no doubt spring up on the fringes — especially after the Conservatives clinched the Aberdeen South by-election following a campaign focused on oil and gas drilling.
Advertisement
Financial Services Reporter Eleanor Myers
Andrew Griffith will be stepping up this party conference, having been promoted to shadow chancellor earlier this year to replace his more mild-mannered colleague Mel Stride.
Griffith was a bigwig in business before he entered parliament, and as a former City minister, I’ll be watching whether he focuses his ire on the prospect of Labour raising bank taxes in the budget, which is now less than a month away.
Griffith will make his big speech on how to get Britain growing again at 2 p.m. Monday. Growth was the favored buzzword of former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, and has been heartily adopted by her successor John Healey, although how to achieve it remains a challenge amid soaring debt and rising interest rates. I’m interested to see whether the Conservatives propose a solution.
Senior Technology Reporter Frank Hersey
This conference is a chance for Badenoch’s team to establish any sort of differentiation between Tory tech policy and that of the other parties. This has been getting harder as parties’ approaches have coalesced. Labour committed to a pro-growth agenda for AI under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer with planned regulatory reforms to match. Tory plans for a social media ban for under-16s were eventually (and reluctantly) grasped by Labour. The Tories were further hemmed in by Reform banking the low-tax, low-regulation space.
I’ll be looking to see if the party can get ahead in any policy areas or if it has to pick new ones to do so. Among all the parties, there’s perhaps most interest in what the Conservatives say on tech — as their policy ideas in this space are feeling overdue.
Senior Trade Reporter Sophie Inge
The fightback against Burnham’s pledge to explore closer ties with the EU is expected to continue in Birmingham, after Badenoch warned that Britain shouldn’t be “having arguments which started 10 years ago.”
Deputy Leader Alex Burghart has already pledged to “reverse” the Brexit reset, warning that plans for an agrifood deal with the bloc risk undermining the U.K.’s trading relationship with the U.S., among other countries.

articles.title: Ukraine’s FP-2 Strike Drones Destroy Russian Pantsir-S2 Air Defense System
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s FP-2 Strike Drones Destroy Russian Pantsir-S2 Air Defense System
Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian Pantsir-S2 air defense system using FP-2 strike drones, with footage showing the system burning before its ammunition detonated and tore the vehicle apart.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian open-source monitoring channel Exilenova+ on October 3, the Pantsir-S2 had been interfering with Ukrainian drone operations and preventing UAVs from reaching targets deeper behind Russian lines.
Video published by the channel shows a Ukrainian FP-2 striking the Russian air defense system at night. A fire subsequently broke out on the vehicle, followed by secondary explosions that destroyed much of the system.
Additional footage recorded nearby reportedly captured another FP-2 approaching the Pantsir-S2 after the initial strike. By that point, however, the system had already sustained extensive damage.
Images taken after the attack show the burned remains of the crew cabin and components of the rotating combat module scattered around the site.
Exilenova+ did not disclose where or exactly when the strike occurred. The channel said the Pantsir-S2 had been obstructing Ukrainian drones attempting to penetrate farther into Russia’s rear areas.
The Pantsir-S2 is an upgraded version of Russia’s Pantsir family of short-range air defense systems. It combines surface-to-air missiles with 30 mm automatic cannons and is designed to engage aircraft, missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles.
The S2 variant features an upgraded target-detection radar intended to improve the system’s ability to detect and track aerial targets.

articles.title: U.S. Air Force adds $12M for AI agents on doomsday plane
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force added $12.1 million to Scale AI's contract for agentic AI on the E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center, raising it to $44.3 million.
- The work runs through Nov. 5, 2027, with $5 million in fiscal 2026 research funds obligated at award.
The U.S. Air Force has added $12.1 million to a contract with Scale AI to develop artificial intelligence agents for the E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center, the new “doomsday plane” meant to keep U.S. leaders in command of the military, including nuclear forces, if ground command centers are destroyed.
The modification raises the total value of the San Francisco company’s contract from $32.2 million to $44.3 million, the U.S. Department of War said. The work will be done in San Francisco and is expected to run through Nov. 5, 2027. The U.S. Air Force obligated $5 million in fiscal 2026 research and development funds at award.
The notice does not say what tasks the AI agents will perform aboard the aircraft, whether they will run on the plane itself or on ground systems that support it, or how much human control will be built in.
Agentic AI goes a step beyond chatbots that answer questions. These systems can plan and carry out multi-step tasks on their own, such as gathering and sorting information, drafting options or managing workflows, with people supervising or approving key decisions. On a command aircraft packed with communications gear and a battle staff, that could mean helping crews handle large volumes of messages and data during a crisis, though the U.S. Air Force has not described its plans.
The original contract was awarded earlier this year through the Air Force Research Laboratory’s Information Directorate in Rome, New York. The latest modification was issued by the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Hanscom Air Force Base, Massachusetts.
The E-4C will replace the E-4B Nightwatch, a fleet of four heavily modified Boeing 747-200s that first flew in the 1970s and serve as the National Airborne Operations Center. The aircraft are hardened against the effects of nuclear blasts and can be refueled in flight, allowing them to stay aloft for long periods while the president, defense secretary and senior commanders direct forces from the air.
Sierra Nevada Corp. won a $13 billion contract in April 2024 to build the replacement. The company bought used Boeing 747-8I airliners from Korean Air and is converting them in Dayton, Ohio, adding protection against radiation and electromagnetic pulse, new communications antennas, computers and mission systems. The first E-4C test aircraft flew on Aug. 7, 2025, and flight and ground testing is continuing through 2026 before mission equipment is installed. Deliveries are scheduled to finish by July 2036.
Scale AI, best known for labeling data used to train AI models, has become a major supplier of AI tools to the U.S. military. In March 2025, it won the Defense Innovation Unit’s Thunderforge project to bring AI agents into military planning and operations, working with Anduril and Microsoft. Earlier this year, the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office raised the ceiling on another Scale AI agreement from $100 million to $500 million. Meta holds a minority stake in the company.

articles.title: Italy’s Ustica enigma: Can French files solve mystery crash blamed on stray missile?
articles.body:
Italy’s Ustica enigma: Can French files solve mystery crash blamed on stray missile?
France’s decision to share defence documents with the Italian judiciary has raised hopes of a breakthrough in investigations into the 1980 crash of a passenger jet near the island of Ustica, which a former Italian president claimed was mistakenly shot down by a French fighter jet. Sceptics caution that the files are unlikely to shed light on one of Italy’s most enduring mysteries, let alone reveal a culprit.
A rocky outpost of Italy in the Tyrrhenian Sea, the island of Ustica owes its name to the smouldering volcanic lava that gave its striking rock formations their dark hue.
For many Italians, however, the picturesque island is synonymous with a notorious plane crash that claimed 81 lives, and the intricate cover-up that buried its causes in a thick fog of lies, decoys and mysterious deaths.
The fate of Itavia Flight 870, which plunged into waters off Ustica on June 27, 1980, remains a subject of fierce debate after countless expert reports and judicial enquiries spanning several decades. The most widely accepted theory suggests the plane was caught up in an aerial dogfight and mistakenly shot down by a fighter jet, which a former Italian president has claimed was French.
News this week that French authorities would hand over defence documents to Italian investigators has been greeted as a potential gamechanger in Italy, where prosecutors and plaintiffs have long accused France and other Western allies of withholding evidence.
The 11th-hour twist led prosecutors on Wednesday to abort plans to shelve the latest investigation into the crash, throwing a lifeline to families of the victims who have relentlessly lobbied Italian governments and the judiciary to pursue the case.
Cover-up
The DC-9 plane operated by the now-defunct Itavia carrier was in the final stretch of its journey from Bologna to Palermo on a clear summer evening when it suddenly broke up and crashed into the sea, killing all 77 passengers and 4 crew members, all of them Italian.
The incident is known in Italy as the strage di Ustica, a term commonly used to refer to the deadly terrorist attacks that rattled the country in those years, many of which also remain shrouded in mystery.
Watch moreVictims of Italy’s deadly ‘Years of Lead’ demand justice
“At first, it was labelled an ‘accident’ or a ‘tragedy’. But as efforts to cover up the incident became apparent over time, people started calling it a ‘strage’ (massacre),” said historian Cora Ranci, who has written a book about the Ustica affair and the many smokescreens she says have hampered investigations.
Like other unsolved civilian massacres, she added, the Ustica affair “has contributed to the erosion of trust between citizens and institutions in Italy, fuelling the sense that those in power are bound by a code of silence and that their actions are shrouded in secrecy”.
Following the crash, officials hastily concluded that it had been caused by mechanical failure, precipitating the demise of the already struggling carrier Itavia. Judicial inquiries resumed only years later under pressure from victims’ families, spurred by an investigative journalist convinced that the plane had been shot down.
Progress was slow, hampered by the fact that tracking data and radar scans had been wiped clean at all but one of the various Italian bases within range of the incident, leaving investigators with little hard evidence to work on. Four air force generals were eventually tried on charges of treason and withholding evidence, though none were convicted.
The untimely deaths of at least 15 military personnel and others connected to the case – through transport accidents, shootings, stabbings and suicides by hanging – furthered muddied the waters, compounding the sense of a conspiracy to hide the truth.
In 2013, Italy’s highest court ruled that the plane had been brought down in an aerial battle, either by a missile or through a near-collision, without identifying a culprit. It ordered the state to compensate families of the victims, adding that cover-ups in the investigations were considered “definitively ascertained”. The ruling was in line with the conclusions of an earlier, decade-long inquiry, which determined that the intended target of the operation was a smaller aircraft travelling in the DC-9’s slipstream to evade radar detection.
“We’ve known for years that the passenger plane was downed in a combat operation,” said former senator Daria Bonfietti, the head of the association of families of the victims that lobbied the authorities to recover the wreckage and reopen investigations decades ago. But, she added, “we still don’t know who did it.”
The Libya link
Despite the court rulings, some remain deeply sceptical of the missile scenario, leaning instead towards the theory of a bomb exploding on board the plane. They point to the numerous terrorist attacks that shook the country in those years, including the strage di Bologna, a train station bombing that killed 85 people and injured score more just weeks after the Ustica crash.
Potential culprits cited by proponents of the bomb theory – which has never been upheld in court – include far-right activists, Palestinian militant groups and Muammar Gaddafi’s Libya.
The late Libyan strongman is also at the heart of the missile hypothesis, which gained further traction in 2007 when former Italian president Francesco Cossiga claimed that the passenger jet had been shot down by French military planes who were after Gaddafi.
Cossiga, who was prime minister in June 1980, cited Italian intelligence but offered no evidence to back up the allegation. He claimed Italian sources had tipped off Gaddafi, ensuring that he was not on board the smaller plane allegedly tailing the Itavia flight.
Proponents of the Libyan link say it is substantiated by the recovery, three weeks after the Ustica disaster, of the wreckage of a Libyan MiG fighter on a mountain in Calabria, which may have been chased and downed on the same night as the DC-9.
“We know from declassified documents that Italy at the time was covertly allowing Libyan aircraft to fly though its airspace to Yugoslavia for purposes of training and maintenance,” said Ranci, adding that it was common practice for those jets to evade detection by tailing commercial flights. On top of creating dangers for civilian planes, this tacit agreement infuriated the Americans and even more so the French, who were fighting a proxy war with Gaddafi’s Libya in Chad.
The Ustica crash came months after France’s embassy in Tripoli was ransacked and after a botched Libyan attempt to shoot down a French surveillance aircraft over the Mediterranean, which sent tensions spiralling.
Bonfietti, whose elder brother was on board the Itavia flight, said successive judicial inquiries had established that multiple military aircraft were operating over the Tyrrhenian on the day of the crash, including US, French and other NATO aircraft. “Now we need those countries to tell us what they were up to and why they kept quiet about it,” she said.
Watch moreGladio: NATO’s secret cold war operation in Italy
“If Gaddafi was indeed their target, it’s obvious that whoever carried out the operation could not openly claim it – not in a Cold War context,” Bonfietti added. “Instead, they decided to cover up what happened and pretend the plane experienced a mechanical failure.”
Locating the Foch
Allegations of French involvement resurfaced in 2023 when former Italian prime minister Giuliano Amato urged France to come clean on the mysterious plane crash, asking President Emmanuel Macron to look into the matter.
“If he shows that the allegation is unfounded, so much the better. If it is true, he should apologise,” Amato, who served as deputy PM at the time of the incident, told a news conference, suggesting it would be easier for someone Macron’s age to overcome old taboos.
Bonfietti said she had personally asked Italy’s current Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to raise the issue with Macron when they met for a summit in June. According to Italian media reports, it was those talks that helped pave the way for the release of French documents.
The former senator said she hoped the new files would help expose what she described as France’s “past lies”, including about the whereabouts of a French aircraft carrier that Cossiga claimed was involved in the Ustica incident. Italian prosecutors say testimony from witnesses contradicts French claims that the Foch carrier was docked at Navy headquarters in Toulon on June 27 and that the Solenzara base in Corsica had closed and ceased all radar recordings hours before the Ustica crash.
“If the Foch was instead in the Tyrrhenian, as witness accounts suggest, it would have been in a position to detect and record what happened,” said Ranci, adding that the same applied to a US Navy carrier stationed in the Tyrrhenian – which US officials claimed had switched its radar off that night – and an AWACS mobile radar station believed to have been flying overhead.
Contacted by FRANCE 24, France’s defence ministry said it had “always responded to requests from the Italian judicial authorities” in connection with the case. It said it “recently confirmed (to Italian authorities) that a batch of documents could be used in legal proceedings”, adding that these documents “had been brought to the attention of the Italian authorities several years ago”.
The ministry did not say whether classified documents previously withheld would this time be handed over.
Analysts have voiced scepticism that the French documents would lead to any breakthrough, stressing that the decision to make them available to Italian prosecutors in no way constitutes an admission of guilt. According to Professor Gregory Alegi, a professor at LUISS University in Rome and a prominent critic of the missile hypothesis, France’s willingness to share more information “suggests they know they have nothing to fear”.
Some families of victims have expressed hopes that French cooperation might open new lines of investigation, urging prosecutors to also pursue the terrorism lead. All agree the French move will at least ensure the inquiry is not shelved.
“It’s quite possible the French sent us nothing new – their shopping list or something – but the important thing is they sent us documents and so investigations go on,” said Bonfietti. “We owe it to our loved ones to keep fighting for the truth.”

articles.title: Diplomatic path to ending war remains open: Iran FM Araghchi
articles.body:
Iran’s top diplomat made the remarks during a meeting with ambassadors and heads of diplomatic missions in Iran on Sunday, stressing that the diplomatic path to ending war remains open.

Referring to the meetings held with the Persian Gulf Arab states’ officials, Araghchi stated, "All of these meetings were held in a friendly atmosphere, and we have embarked on a new path for relations with these countries. Our brothers in the Persian Gulf are aligned with us, and a shared determination to establish stability—with the participation of the countries themselves—is being pursued."
Referring to the meetings held with European countries, he stated, "We hope the Europeans will reconsider their approach toward Iran. The NATO Secretary General’s admission regarding participation in a war against Iran was a grave matter. He [NATO chief] stated that over 5,000 fighter jets took off from bases in Europe, and we await an explanation from European countries. Our proposal to these nations is to engage in dialogue with Iran and avoid being drawn into any warmongering by the US and the Zionist regime."

In the past, the US has lost in both war and diplomacy. Sanctions, too, are of no avail. There is no military or sanctions-based solution; only a diplomatic solution will prove effective and serve to end the aggression against Iran.”
The US claim that Iran’s delegation was expelled is absurd. The Iranian delegation traveled to and from the US as scheduled, the Iranian foreign minister reiterated.

articles.title: Moscow vows to ramp up strikes on Ukraine after Zelensky’s threat
articles.body:
Moscow vows to ramp up strikes on Ukraine after Zelensky’s threat
Russia will intensify strikes on military and defense-related facilities in Ukraine in response to Vladimir Zelensky’s threat to increase attacks on Russian oil refineries, the Defense Ministry warned.
In a statement on Sunday, the ministry said it has “taken note” of the Ukrainian leader’s promise a day earlier to step up attacks on Russian oil refineries in response to strikes on bridges across the Dnieper River in Kiev.
Russia has already ramped up strikes on military-related logistics – including the key port of Odessa – and the defense industrial base in recent weeks in response to Zelensky’s botched 40-day PR ‘pressure campaign’, which included long-range strikes targeting oil refineries and civilian infrastructure deep inside Russia.
“Following Zelensky’s statement today, strikes by the Russian Armed Forces on military and military-industrial facilities, as well as related infrastructure in Kiev and other regions of Ukraine, will be intensified,” the ministry said in a statement on Sunday.
People in Ukraine should blame only the head of the Kiev regime for this. It is Zelensky who bears full personal and political responsibility for it.
The Defense Ministry reiterated that the Russian military has been responding to Kiev’s attacks on civilian targets in Russia that were meant to disrupt the State Duma election. It cited strikes on polling stations that killed six civilians, an attempted mass attack involving more than 1,600 Ukrainian strike drones against civilian sites in Moscow on September 19-20, and drone attacks aimed at disrupting the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum in June.
It also cited a strike on residential areas in Belgorod that killed and wounded civilians and damaged apartment buildings, houses, and vehicles.
President Vladimir Putin acknowledged that the strikes on oil refineries have cost around 1% of Russia’s GDP, but noted that the damaged facilities are being quickly restored, and that the nation’s energy system is operating with significant reserve capacity. Following Russia’s retaliatory strikes, Ukraine no longer has a steelmaking industry, he added.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: US must not forget it is a hundred times stronger than Russia in negotiations
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: US must not forget it is a hundred times stronger than Russia in negotiations
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US must not forget how strong it is in negotiations with Russia, noting that Vladimir Putin has begun to think that he is the one who gets to make decisions.
Source: Zelenskyy in an interview with Reuters, an excerpt from which he posted on social media, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy said he believes the US genuinely wants to end Russia's war.
Quote from Zelenskyy: "I think the US really wants to stop Russia's war. I trust them. Then, I understand it's difficult to stop somebody who's big and doesn't want to stop. That's why you're trying to find some compromises with Russia. But I think we are losing time if we want to play with Russian compromises."
Details: Zelenskyy emphasised that President Donald Trump now wants to achieve some kind of victory before the midterm elections, but, he said, Putin will do all he can to encourage the Iranians and make negotiations impossible.
Quote: "President Trump wants to have some kind of victory before the midterms. But Putin will do everything to push the Iranians and make this whole situation non-negotiable.
The same with Russia's war against Ukraine. If Putin sees that President Trump needs some victory, he will decide what to give and what not to give. And this is the problem – Putin has started to think that it is he who can decide. But America is one hundred times stronger than Russia. Absolutely. They just have to remember that."

- The New York Times previously reported that the White House is considering signing certain business deals with Russia as a way of demonstrating its good intentions.

articles.title: Iran army says prepared to face any scenario
articles.body:
Iran army says prepared to face any scenario
TEHRAN– Iran’s Armed Forces are closely monitoring developments and remain fully prepared to respond to any scenario, the spokesperson for the Islamic Republic of Iran Army said on Saturday, as he referred to repeated threats by the country’s adversaries.
Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia made the remarks during a visit to the Army’s 65th Airborne Special Forces Brigade, a unit widely recognized for its specialized capabilities and role in missions requiring a high degree of operational readiness.
Highlighting the brigade’s position within Iran’s defense structure, Akraminia said its personnel, combining commitment, specialized training and operational capabilities, have turned the unit into an important asset for both the Army and the country.
He stressed that the missions assigned to the 65th Brigade extend beyond conventional tactical operations, arguing that the unit’s activities can produce consequences at the strategic level and affect Iran’s national security interests as well as the wider regional and international environment.
Against the backdrop of continued tensions and threats, the Army spokesperson said Iran’s military capabilities have been undergoing continuous development and that the Armed Forces are prepared to confront whatever circumstances may arise.
Akrami-Nia also addressed the calculations of the United States and Israel in the conflict with Iran, saying the resilience of the Iranian Armed Forces, coupled with the steadfastness of the Iranian people, had disrupted the adversaries’ calculations.
According to the Army spokesperson, the United States and Israel had initially anticipated that Iran’s defensive capabilities could be dismantled and their objectives achieved within a matter of days. He said those calculations did not materialize.
Akraminia further argued that the objectives pursued by Iran’s adversaries went beyond the country’s nuclear and missile programs or their confrontation with the Resistance Front. He said the broader objective was to undermine the Islamic Republic and fragment Iran as a country, but that none of those objectives had been achieved.
The remarks come as Iranian military officials have repeatedly emphasized the importance of maintaining a high level of readiness amid continuing regional tensions and threats of renewed confrontation. Iranian authorities have also stressed that the country’s defense posture is based on deterrence and the ability to respond to threats against its territorial integrity and national security.
The Army spokesperson attributed the Armed Forces’ ability to withstand the pressure to their faith, motivation and spirit of resistance. He also pointed to the role of public solidarity in sustaining the morale of military personnel.
Akraminia said the nightly presence of people in public squares during the conflict was not merely a manifestation of national unity and cohesion, but also had a direct psychological effect on servicemen stationed on the frontlines, strengthening their morale and determination.
His comments underscored the Iranian military’s continued emphasis on preparedness, national cohesion and the integration of specialized military capabilities into the country’s broader defense posture.

articles.title: US claims it ‘kicked out’ Iranian diplomats
articles.body:
US claims it ‘kicked out’ Iranian diplomats
The US has expelled two more members of the Iranian delegation that attended the UN General Assembly in New York after they allegedly ignored an order to leave the country, AFP and Axios reported on Saturday, citing a State Department official.
US and Iranian negotiators separately met with mediators last month without reaching a breakthrough, leaving the Middle East bracing for a potential resumption of hostilities. US media reported that after the sides failed to reach an agreement on Monday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and other diplomats to leave the country earlier than planned.
“Two more members of the Iranian delegation were found still in [New York] long after the United Nations General Assembly had passed. They have now been kicked out of the US,” a US official told AFP, adding that Rubio “means business.”
According to Axios, one diplomat left on Friday night and the other on Saturday morning.
The Iranian mission to the UN previously disputed Washington’s account of the delegation’s departure, saying its members left in accordance with a schedule communicated to the US before the General Assembly session.
“Having achieved nothing, the State Department has resorted to propagating baseless and worthless news,” the mission wrote on X on Thursday.
US President Donald Trump has resumed threats to “annihilate” Iran’s leadership in recent weeks, hinting that he could order new strikes unless Tehran accepts his terms.
Iranian officials and the military say they are prepared for further escalation.
“After one failure after another, the worst president in American history just keeps talking – and talking – and now his words have even outrun his own fantasies. You can win every day in your own imagination. But reality is shaped by Iran – by its people, its soldiers, and its missiles,” Mohsen Rezaei, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, wrote on X on Friday.
The standoff comes as the US reinforces its military presence in the Middle East. The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and USS Makin Island amphibious ready group are heading to the region, adding 9,000 to 10,000 sailors and Marines.
The USS George Washington and USS George H.W. Bush are already operating there. If both remain when the Theodore Roosevelt arrives, the US could have three aircraft carriers in the Middle East by late October.
Some US officials reportedly believe Trump could resume major combat operations after the midterm elections in early November. The war remains unpopular among Americans, with 71% of registered voters saying the Trump administration lacks a clear strategy for ending the conflict, according to a recent Fox News poll.

articles.title: The G7 Is Releasing Emergency Fuel Reserves. How Much Will It Help Americans?
articles.body:
The Group of Seven (G7) countries said Friday that the nations would release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming months, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel. The move comes amid a global shortage largely attributed to slowdowns of the passage of oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
A joint statement from the G7 nations—Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the U.S.—confirmed that the International Energy Agency (IEA) will coordinate the release over the next four months.
It calls the move a part of “decisive, coordinated measures to stabilize immediate energy supplies” amid record-high fuel prices driven by the war in Iran and the recent escalation of fighting between Russia and Ukraine.
Read More: Once Again, Energy Is Power
“Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil,” President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social on Friday. “The process will begin immediately.”
In talks leading up to the announcement on Friday, Trump had been pushing European partners for the release, citing high fuel prices for Americans. Last month, the Trump Administration threatened to temporarily suspend its exports of diesel—earning immediate backlash from countries that rely on it, including Canada, Mexico, and much of Europe.
European leaders and oil executives at the time said that such a ban would be disastrous for long-term oil flow. For that reason, experts believe the threat helped pressure those nations to release their fuel reserves.
The agreement could offer some relief for Americans even if the released diesel stays in Europe, because Europe buys some of its diesel from the U.S. Releasing European reserves could ease competition for U.S. diesel and potentially reduce prices for American buyers.
This is especially critical as the cost of Brent crude oil sits at $102 per barrel as of Oct. 3 and on-highway diesel hit a high of $6.529 per gallon as of last month, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
But how much relief consumers will actually see—and how quickly—will depend on what type of fuel is released, how much reaches the market and when, and whether supply disruptions persist.
What is actually being added to the market?
Although the G7 shared how much fuel it would release, it did not specify the full breakdown of the release by fuel type. Its statement did say, however, that there will be a “frontloaded” and substantial release of diesel fuel within the first 20 days.
While crude oil must be refined into products like gasoline before consumers can use it, diesel is already a finished fuel. That means a diesel release could address the immediate shortage more directly.
The planned release could help ease shortages of both crude oil and refined fuels, with supplies disrupted by the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
The supply of crude oil has been heavily disrupted this year after the U.S. and Israel launched joint strikes that ignited a war with Iran in February. In response, Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in March. More recent negotiations to end the war have largely failed to address differing opinions on ownership and control over the Strait. This has critically restricted the passage of oil-carrying vessels through the waterway, with daily shipping traffic in the single digits last month, down from pre-war averages of roughly 138 to 140 daily transits.
Diesel, meanwhile, is essential to U.S. transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing: Most goods, food, and manufacturing supplies across the country are transported by heavy-duty trucks and trains running on diesel engines. The war in Iran has driven diesel prices up and lowered supply, but Russia and Ukraine’s targeting of one another’s energy infrastructure has further exacerbated the issue.
While the U.S. in particular does not heavily rely on Russian diesel, America is vulnerable to the volatility caused by Russia removing it from the global market. Trump has claimed outright that Ukraine’s targeting of Russian oil infrastructure is to blame for diesel shortages.
What could Americans feel, and when?
Jason Bordoff, founding director of the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, says it’s difficult to predict the consumer impact given the scarce details shared so far.
“It makes a big difference if the release is in the next two weeks or if it's four months from now,” Bordoff says.
“I think if we saw some announcement tomorrow from Germany or France that gave concrete, specific numbers for a substantial amount—50 million barrels or so—of diesel, then it could have a real impact if this release actually happens in a timely fashion,” Bordoff says.
At the same time, Jeff Colgan, a professor of political science at Brown University, cautions that American consumers may see limited benefits.
“Releasing diesel could make a difference on price, especially in tight markets in Europe,” Colgan says. “But American consumers are unlikely to see much of a price drop from this policy move unless the diesel share of that 100 million barrels is very large.”
With a timely release of diesel, Bordoff predicts that Americans could see a drop by as much as 25 cents per gallon after a few weeks—but, he adds, the markets seem pretty unsure that that will actually happen.
And market perception is central to whether or not prices drop in the short term.
“I think they’re saying: Show me the barrels, so I have confidence this is real, and it's going to happen quickly,” he says.
David Bieri, an economist and associate professor of urban affairs and planning at Virginia Tech, tells TIME that international interventions like this help “signal” to markets that governments are a credible safety net in prolonged periods of uncertainty.
“That's the main mechanism, because they want to influence market sentiment,” Bieri says. “Then, futures markets begin to price more optimistically, and then eventually the hope is that prices will come down.”
The effect Bieri is describing has already begun: The price of diesel futures in the United States fell 8% on Friday morning, a sign of more optimism in the market.
Bordoff adds that they are also, in part, a response to Trump dropping his threat of a diesel export ban—a threat that was lifted as a condition of the G7 agreement.
The release itself may not impact the markets “an awful lot,” Bieri says, given the broader context of the war with Iran.
“In fact, consumers might not necessarily notice it, ever. That's how insignificant the quantity itself is,” he says of the 100 million barrels. “But it's the importance of the cooperative signal that hopefully will make things better this fall.”
Bieri also cautions that any savings could take time to reach consumers, as carriers and other distributors may use lower fuel costs to rebuild their margins.
“[They] have been bleeding on increased fuel costs,” he says. “This is going to be, if anything, a welcome reprieve for their profit margins, and they're not going to pass that on immediately to consumers.”
What happens if the supply gap is still there when releases taper off?
This October announcement is not the first of its kind: Following the initial market shock of the war in Iran, IEA member countries announced a 400-million-barrel release in March—80% of which has already been released. Notably, the latest announcement did not clearly establish how much of the forthcoming release would be additional to earlier commitments.
In March, the IEA said that the majority of the barrel release would be crude oil; however, reports show that Europe has primarily contributed refined oil, like diesel—which could suggest more of the same in this latest round.
In either event, such fuel releases are just a matter of sticking a bandage over the larger issue of two unresolved wars and continued global energy disruption, says Bordoff.
“We're going to continue to have oil, gasoline, and diesel price shocks until that conflict comes to some sort of resolution, and energy flows can get going again,” he says. “Inventories, and stocks and other schemes like waiving state fuel taxes or something can help on the margin for temporary disruptions, but at some point this isn't temporary anymore.”
Michael Noel, economist at Texas Tech University, agrees with Bordoff, telling TIME that “unless something dramatic happens to end the Ukraine and Iran conflicts, the supply shortage will persist.”
Negotiations between Iranian leadership and the Trump Administration have stalled multiple times in the last six months. Trump said on Sept. 9 that he expected a resolution to come after the midterm elections, which take place in the U.S. on Nov. 3.
“I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer,” he said last month. “Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward.”
Axios reported, however, that senior Trump Administration officials met at Camp David to discuss the war on Friday. The talks come as the U.S. last week added economic pressure in the region with a series of sanctions aiming to curtail funding streams and stymy industrial lifelines for Iran.
Experts argue that the fuel crisis and volatility exposes the need for the U.S. to adapt to a changing energy ecosystem. Notably, Colgan says that would include “the national security advantages of clean technologies like EVs, batteries, and renewable energy.”

articles.title: ‘Everyone knows’ Kiev is embezzling Western aid – ex-Polish PM
articles.body:
‘Everyone knows’ Kiev is embezzling Western aid – ex-Polish PM
Ukrainian officials are embezzling foreign financial aid, former Polish Prime Minister Leszek Miller has said, adding that Kiev’s backers are well aware of the corruption but prefer not to ask questions.
Speaking on the ‘Jankowski Kontra’ podcast on Polsat News on Saturday, Miller called for suspending aid to Ukraine until Kiev accounts for previously supplied weapons and funds.
“Nobody’s asking what happened to the 300 tanks we sent in the first phase. What happened to the heavy equipment, the lighter equipment... Nobody’s asking what happened to the billions of euros we donated. Mr. Zelensky simply comes and says, ‘Give it’, and we give it,” Miller stated.
Asked whether he suspected that funds transferred to Ukraine were being embezzled, Miller replied: “Of course, everyone knows it.”The veteran politician argued that Warsaw should demand an accounting of how its assistance has been used and halt further support if Kiev fails to provide one.
“This is a fundamental issue: I’ll lend you the money, but give me a report on what you did with the previous installment,” Miller stated. “Without that help, there is no Ukraine… But we are not a country that is overflowing with wealth… We have obligations to our own citizens, and we cannot simply throw away money and equipment indiscriminately.”
Poland has been one of Kiev’s staunchest backers in its conflict with Russia, pouring billions into military, financial and humanitarian aid while serving as a crucial hub for Western supplies. Yet relations have increasingly soured over Kiev’s honoring of Ukrainian Nazi collaborators linked to the World War II-era Volhynia massacres, in which UPA militants, linked to the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), killed at least 100,000 ethnic Poles.
Warsaw recognizes the killings as genocide, while Kiev honors figures including OUN leader Stepan Bandera. Tensions flared again this year after Zelensky bestowed the title ‘Heroes of the UPA’ on the Ukrainian Special Operations Center North military unit. In the aftermath, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped him of the country’s highest honor, politicians on both sides renounced state decorations, and Warsaw threatened to obstruct Ukraine’s EU accession.
Relations have also been strained by mounting opposition to Ukrainian refugees. A July CBOS survey found that 52% of Poles now opposed accepting them, against 42% in favor – a sharp reversal from the overwhelming support seen after Kiev’s conflict with Moscow escalated in 2022. Tensions deepened earlier this month after a 31-year-old Ukrainian man stabbed five people at a Benedictine abbey in Jaroslaw, killing a priest.
Poland is also not alone in questioning funding for Kiev. Despite receiving billions in Western assistance over the past four years, Ukraine faces a severe cash squeeze and has been pressing European backers for more money. But a string of high-level graft scandals has heightened scrutiny in Brussels, the largest of which centers on an alleged $100 million kickback scheme at state nuclear operator Energoatom, which was reportedly led by Timur Mindich, a former business partner of Vladimir Zelensky.
Western-backed investigators have uncovered multiple other graft schemes involving Ukrainian officials, including one reported earlier this month in which they allegedly embezzled more than $3 million through the delivery of used Soviet-made metro cars donated by Poland.
Against that backdrop, the EU this week rebuffed Kiev’s bid to fast-track its latest €90 billion support loan, making clear that further funds depend on Ukraine delivering promised anti-corruption and governance reforms.

articles.title: Israeli forces attempt to assassinate Hamas' 'new Gaza leader'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli forces attempt assassination of senior Hamas leader in Gaza
Israeli forces have attempted to assassinate a senior Hamas leader Ali al-Amoudi in Gaza, Israeli media reported on Saturday.
The attacks took place on Friday evening, when Israeli airstrikes killed five Palestinians, including four women and a child, though al-Amoudi's fate remains unclear.
Hamas has not issued a statement acknowledging an attempted assassination.
After Hamas' Gaza leader Khalil al-Hayya was elected to succeed slain leader Yahya Sinwar in August 2026, al-Amoudi was considered the most likely candidate to take over as the group's chief in Gaza, a source close to Hamas told The New Arab in August.
The source noted that al-Hayya remains the official head of Hamas in Gaza, while al-Amoudi serves as his deputy. Israeli media reports on Friday alleged that al-Amoudi is in charge of the the group in Gaza.
Al-Amoudi has remained relatively out of the spotlight for years, though is considered to have been close to slain Hamas leader Sinwar. He was released from Israeli detention as part of the 2011 prisoner swap involving captured Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit, and later progressed to higher positions within the movement.
He was also among the key figures within Hamas who pushed within the group for acceptance of UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process Nikolay Mladenov's roadmap for Gaza in late July.
The assassination attempt comes as Israel continues its attacks on Gaza, despite a ceasefire agreement that came into force last October. Israeli forces have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians in Gaza since the truce deal, and has increased its area of military control in the enclave.

articles.title: North Korea launches ballistic missile over 700 kilometers as hostilities heat up
articles.body:
North Korea fired a ballistic missile toward the sea off its east coast on Saturday, South Korea and Japan said, its latest missile launch this year, which came a day after it rejected Seoul's accusation that its mines wounded soldiers.
The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at around 6:30 a.m. on Saturday and flew more than 700 kilometers (434 miles), the South Korean military said in a statement. Seoul and Washington were analyzing the test for details, it added.
Japan's coast guard, in an emailed statement citing the Japanese defense ministry, said the object may have been a ballistic missile and appeared to have come down, warning ships to take precautions.
South Korea's military said it has raised its monitoring of any further missile tests and will share intelligence with the US and Japan.
The South Korean presidential office's national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation after the missile launch, the office said in a statement.
North Korea tested missiles at least 10 times this year, ramps up hostility
North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Pyongyang has sometimes said it was testing new types of weapons systems. Some of the tests have come after North Korea protested joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.
The launch came after Pyongyang's Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong Un, issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul's demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarised Zone, a heavily fortified area between the two Koreas.
South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that seriously injured two South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4-km-wide (2.5-mile) border that stretches across the Korean Peninsula.
The missile test may be an attempt by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister's statement, said Cheong Seong-chang, vice president at the Sejong Institute in Seoul, a research center on North Korean affairs. North Korea may also have tested a new type of missile, he added.
North Korea has sharply ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its "primary foe."

articles.title: Trump says Iran has 'virtually given up' any plans for nuclear weapons
articles.body:
Ahmet Salih Alacaci
04 October 2026•Update: 04 October 2026
US President Donald Trump suggested on Saturday that Iran has “virtually given up” any plans to develop nuclear weapons, one of his administration’s most frequently stated objectives in the war with Tehran, now in its eighth month.
Trump also claimed oil prices were currently decreasing, long elevated after Israel and the US launched strikes against Iran on Feb. 28.
“Oil is coming down. Oil is right now lower, and it's been lower than it was under the Biden administration, and they did nothing about the fact that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters as he departed the White House to attend a rally in the state of Ohio.
“By the way, Iran, as you know, has virtually given up any plans of a nuclear weapon,” he added.
Iran has long denied accusations by the US and Israel that it seeks to develop nuclear weapons, a position reiterated by President Masoud Pezeshkian during his visit last month to New York for the UN General Assembly.
Pezeshkian said Tehran is not seeking nuclear weapons because of a religious prohibition, and offered to dilute its enriched uranium stockpiles under international verification.
Iran, however, has maintained that it will not compromise on its peaceful civilian nuclear program or make structural concessions unless the US lifts economic sanctions.

Germany pledges new €1.3bn-plus support package for Ukraine

Source: European Pravda, citing Zelenskyy during a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv; Zelenskyy on X (Twitter)

The German chancellor stressed that the package will rapidly and tangibly strengthen Ukraine's air defence and that this reinforcement is urgently needed. articles.title: Drones Attack Khanskaya Military Airbase in Russia’s Adygea Region
articles.body:
Strike drones attacked the Khanskaya military airbase in Russia’s Republic of Adygea during the night of October 4, 2026.
Footage published by the Exilenova+ outlet appears to show the attack.
The military airbase is located about 6 km northwest of Maykop and 3 km east of the village of Khanskaya.
Reports of a drone threat began coming in at 1:42 a.m. and continued until 5:34 a.m.
During this time, Russian monitoring channels reported detecting drones and active air defense operations in the region and around the airbase.
NASA FIRMS data from geostationary satellites also confirmed a fire in the area of the military airbase.
Russian military aviation currently uses the airbase. It is located at coordinates 44°40′47″N, 40°02′00″E. The site is approximately 500 km from Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Historically, the airbase hosted military aviation training units, including the 761st Training Aviation Regiment. After the regiment was disbanded in 2009, the 272nd Training Aviation Base was established.
Military Unit 55661 is part of the A. K. Serov Krasnodar Higher Military Aviation School for Pilots.
Despite the presence of training aviation units, the airbase has previously been targeted by Ukrainian strikes.
On October 10, 2024, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported that Su-34, Su-27, and Su-35 aircraft were based at the airfield and were being used by Russian aviation in the war against Ukraine.
Militarnyi previously reported that drones attacked the airbase on December 25, 2025. Another attack took place on December 29 of the same year.

articles.title: Russia rebukes US, defends Iran’s ‘inalienable’ nuclear rights
articles.body:
Russia rebukes US, defends Iran’s ‘inalienable’ nuclear rights
TEHRAN – Russia has strongly rebuked the United States over its calls for Tehran to abandon its peaceful nuclear program, reaffirming that the Islamic Republic possesses an inalienable right to pursue peaceful nuclear energy under international law.
In a post on X on Friday, Mikhail Ulyanov, Russia’s permanent representative to Vienna-based international organizations, slammed Washington for relying on “wrong assumptions” regarding non-proliferation norms and the mandate of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).
“Iran is not obliged to abandon its nuclear program. It is Iran’s inalienable right,” Ulyanov emphasized. “Unfortunately, the position of the Republican administration is based on wrong assumptions of non-proliferation norms and the IAEA activities.”
The Russian diplomat made the remarks in response to US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz, who claimed Tehran had “broken the rules” by enriching uranium to 60 percent.
Iran has maintained a firm, principled stance regarding its peaceful atomic activities, particularly in the aftermath of the unprovoked US-Israeli military aggressions in June 2025 and February 2026. In both instances, the aggressors struck civilian and nuclear infrastructure in flagrant violation of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) and the UN Charter.
Following the initial aggression, which occurred amid indirect diplomatic engagements, the Iranian Parliament unanimously passed legislation in June 2025 suspending all cooperation with the IAEA. The decisive move came after the agency adopted a politically motivated resolution that set the stage for foreign strikes, followed by the UN nuclear watchdog’s refusal to condemn the illegal attacks on Iranian facilities.
Under the law, IAEA inspectors will not be permitted to resume monitoring unless verifiable security guarantees are established, subject to the approval of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC). Senior Iranian officials, including Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, have repeatedly stressed that neither Tehran’s legitimate nuclear rights nor its conventional deterrent capabilities are up for negotiation.
China also rallied behind Tehran. Addressing a recent UN General Assembly session, China’s deputy permanent representative to the UN, Sun Lei, reiterated that “Iran’s legitimate right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy should be respected.”
Sun held Washington responsible for the current crisis, pointing to its unilateral withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear deal (JCPOA), brutal “maximum pressure” campaigns, and military escalations during ongoing diplomacy.

articles.title: Pontoon crossings coming to Kyiv following Russian strikes on key bridges, media reports
articles.body:
Pontoon crossings coming to Kyiv following Russian strikes on key bridges, media reports
Following Russian attacks on vital bridges in central Kyiv, the capital plans to construct pontoon crossings across the Dnipro River, Ukrainian media reported on Oct. 3.
"Urgent solutions are a dam and a pontoon crossing, which are being built quickly," Ukraine's Reconstruction, Infrastructure, and Transport Minister, Mykola Kalashnyk, told Suspilny news about responding to the bridge attacks. "This work has already begun. A corresponding coordination meeting was held with the president."
From Oct. 1 to Oct. 3, Kyiv's Southern and Northern bridges over the Dnipro River were targeted in multiple Russian drone strikes amid Moscow's unrelenting attacks on the civilian infrastructure across Ukraine. This week alone, the capital had 56 air raid sirens, lasting over 87 hours in total, emergency services said on Oct. 2.
Kalashnyk said that the construction of pontoon crossings could take up to three months and would help traffic move through the capital, which remains heavily restricted after the bridge attacks.
The Kyiv City Military Administration (KMDA) announced new restrictions on movements over Kyiv's bridges during air raid alerts on Oct. 3.
"On average, about 600,000 cars cross the left and right banks [of the Dnipro] during the day and the task is to maintain this throughput," Kalashnyk said. "Therefore, the locations where construction will begin have been determined accordingly."
Kalashnyk also revealed that plans for constructing underground tunnels beneath the Dnipro were being considered, though construction could "cost tens of billions of hryvnias."
Before constructing alternative crossings, Kalashnyk said that protecting the capital's existing bridges should remain the priority.
"Our first task is to provide protection from the sky, which we are doing in coordination with the military," Kalashnyk said. "The first step is to prevent strikes. The second part is to provide protection. The third is rapid recovery. And the fourth is to make decisions regarding alternative reserve crossings, i.e., the construction of new alternative bridge infrastructure facilities."
To counter Russia's growing use of jet-powered attack drones, Ukraine will be able to produce up to 400 interceptor drones by the end of October, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times published on Oct. 2.

articles.title: Trump says Iran dropped nuclear weapon plans
articles.body:
AA Photo
US President Donald Trump said on Oct. 3 Iran has virtually abandoned its drive to develop nuclear weapons because severe financial exhaustion and regional setbacks crippled Tehran's strategic leverage.
Speaking to reporters, Trump said Iranian authorities no longer possess the capability or ambition to produce an atomic bomb and are eager to negotiate a new settlement. "They have virtually given up any plans for nuclear weapons," he said.
Trump reiterated his position an Iranian nuclear weapon remains unacceptable, asserting earlier maximum pressure sanctions and subsequent economic isolation had drained Tehran's revenue before recent regional conflicts further weakened the government.
The remarks come as international observers continue to monitor Tehran's atomic program. The International Atomic Energy Agency reported earlier this year Iran had accumulated an enriched uranium stockpile with purity levels reaching 60 percent, just below the 90 percent threshold required for weapons-grade material.
Tehran has consistently maintained its atomic work remains exclusively civilian, focused on energy generation and medical research. The diplomatic dispute intensified in 2018 when the US unilaterally pulled out of the 2015 nuclear accord, formally known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, before reimposing sweeping banking and oil sanctions on the Islamic republic.

articles.title: Russia to never sacrifice its relationship with Iran
articles.body:
Speaking to Iranian media, Medvedev said Russia is ready to act as a mediator between the US and Iran to end the war and that Moscow would never sacrifice its relationship with Tehran.
 
Medvedev also said that relations between Iran and Russia are at an “unprecedented level”, and trade between the two countries increased by 20 percent last year.
"Russia and Iran face extensive sanctions and must seek other mechanisms on financial cooperation. About 90 percent of trade between Shanghai Cooperation Organisation member states is conducted in national currencies," he said.
He went on to say that the planned Rasht-Astara railway, which will link the Iranian city of Rasht to Astara on the border with Azerbaijan, will be transformational. "The project, financed by Russia and Iran, is key to the International North-South Transport Corridor that connects Europe and Russia to the [Persian] Gulf and India via Azerbaijan and Iran."
Medvedev continued that Russia has plans to build a new nuclear power plant in Iran in addition to the Bushehr facility.
"Iran plays a key role in ensuring security in the Strait of Hormuz," he emphasized.

articles.title: EU responds to Russian threats against European diplomats in Kyiv
articles.body:
EU responds to Russian threats against European diplomats in Kyiv
European Commission spokesman Christian Wigand has said that, despite Russia's threats of massive attacks against foreign diplomats and embassies remaining in Kyiv, the EU delegation will continue to work in the Ukrainian capital, and that Russia will not intimidate Europe or force it to stop supporting Ukraine.
Source: Ukrinform and Ukrainian public broadcaster hromadske, citing Wigand's comments
Details: Wigand said this was not the first time Russia had resorted to such threats, which he said shows that the Kremlin is losing its war and losing its nerve. The spokesman noted that Moscow is trying to intimidate Europe into scaling back its support for Ukraine, adding that this will not happen, and that the EU will continue to support Ukraine, expose Russia's irresponsible and dangerous actions, and keep increasing pressure on it.
The European Commission spokesman was responding to a statement by Russia's Foreign Ministry on 3 October, in which Russia once again called on foreign citizens and diplomats to leave Kyiv and refrain from visiting Ukraine.
Russia said it will continue carrying out massive strikes on Ukrainian cities, including the capital, and claimed that those who ignore the warning will themselves be responsible for any negative consequences and will be "knowingly putting their lives in mortal danger".
Wigand, however, said that the EU's diplomatic mission in Kyiv remains operational.
The spokesman said the EU is currently preparing the largest sanctions package against Russia in its history, and had already introduced new restrictions this week in response to the deportation of Ukrainian children.
He cited EU High Representative Kaja Kallas as saying that Russia is prepared to take greater risks, but noted that the EU is also stepping up its own actions to make Russia pay an even higher price.
Separately, Wigand stressed the increase in volumes of military aid to Kyiv. In particular, the EU has approved plans for defence procurement for Ukraine worth €28.3 billion for this year and is allocating an additional €6.6 billion directly for military aid.
Background:
- Ahead of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, a number of European countries evacuated their embassies from Kyiv to Lviv and Poland.
- On 2 October, The Guardian reported that, amid intensifying Russian attacks, some Western embassies are drawing up contingency plans for evacuation to Lviv or eastern Poland, despite public statements about their intention to remain in the Ukrainian capital.
- Foreign Ministry spokesman Heorhii Tykhyi later said that foreign partners had not informed Ukraine of any intentions to relocate their diplomatic missions from Kyiv.

articles.title: Defence Minister Herem: Ukraine receives billions in effective EU support to boost combat capabilities
articles.body:
At EU Defence Ministers’ meeting in Brussels, the release of €6.6 billion from the European Peace Facility (EPF) to support Ukraine was welcomed.
“This is a powerful step forward to ramp up aid to Ukraine and increase pressure on the Russian Federation,” said Minister of Defence Martin Herem. From the EPF allocation, €900 million will fund assistance measures for the EU Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine (EUMAM Ukraine) for 2026–2027, €1 billion will fund support for Ukraine through joint procurement, and €4.7 billion will reimburse Member States for the assistance delivered to Ukraine.
“Our most critical task ahead of this winter is ensuring Ukraine receives urgently needed military aid. This means delivering on Estonia’s aid commitments and ensuring the immediate implementation of the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan,” he added. Estonia continues to support Ukraine bilaterally with military assistance worth at least 0.25% of GDP annually.
Estonia also emphasized the need to continue discussions on leveraging frozen Russian assets to ensure more extensive and sustained support for Ukraine. In May of this year, the Riigikogu passed a law enabling the use of assets belonging to entities of the Russian Federation – frozen under international sanctions – to compensate for war damages caused to Ukraine.
The second key topic addressed was Russian sabotage operations across EU nations. “Russia has intensified dangerous provocations in Europe. We must respond to this by enforcing robust sanctions, including an EU-wide restriction on issuing tourist visas to citizens of the Russian Federation. We must remember that Russia’s provocations aim to undermine our collective support for Ukraine by sowing distrust in our societies and our relations with Allies and partners, while fueling fear of escalation. Our support for Ukraine remains steadfast,” the Minister of Defence stated.
During today’s meeting, Defence Ministers were also briefed on the European Defence Agency’s (EDA) Annual Defence Readiness Report. While EU Member States’ defence spending, capability development, and defence industrial capacity are growing rapidly, further cooperation is required to secure a sufficient volume of ready and deployable armed forces.
